Operating long-term assets refer to non-current assets held and used by an enterprise in its daily business operations, with an expected useful life exceeding one accounting year. They constitute a significant component of net operating assets and are used to measure the scale of resource investment in the enterprise's long-term operational activities.

name: Operating Long-term Liabilities
definitions: Operating long-term liabilities refer to debts arising from a company's daily business operations with a repayment period exceeding one year. They are typically presented directly under the long-term liabilities section of the balance sheet and represent financial obligations undertaken to support long-term business activities.

Operating long-term liabilities refer to non-financial debts generated from a company's daily business operations with a repayment period exceeding one year. They primarily arise from operating activities rather than financing activities and typically do not require collateral or interest payments.

name: Operating Loss
definitions: Operating loss represents the shortfall from a company's core operations when operating expenses exceed gross profit. It excludes the effects of non-operating items such as interest, taxes, and extraordinary gains or losses, and is commonly used to assess operating performance and efficiency.

Operating loss represents a negative operating income arising from a company’s core business activities before interest and taxes. For analytical purposes, an adjusted operating result may be derived by excluding non-recurring expenses, adding back one-time items to present a normalized view of ongoing operational performance.

name: Operating Margin
definitions: Operating margin is a profitability ratio that measures the percentage of revenue remaining after deducting operating expenses, indicating a company's operational efficiency in generating profit from sales.

Operating margin measures the proportion of operating profit generated from each unit of revenue, expressed as a percentage. It reflects a company’s operating efficiency before interest and taxes, indicating how well core operations convert sales into profits.

Operating margin measures the proportion of sales revenue that remains as operating profit after covering operating expenses. It is expressed as a percentage and indicates a company's operating efficiency and cost control effectiveness.

Operating margin is a profitability ratio that measures the proportion of revenue remaining after covering operating expenses. It is calculated as operating earnings divided by revenue and typically expressed as a percentage, indicating the efficiency of a company's core operations.

Operating margin is a profitability ratio that indicates the percentage of revenue remaining after covering operating expenses, measuring how efficiently a company generates profit from core operations before interest and taxes. It is calculated as EBIT divided by revenue and expressed as a percentage.

name: Operating Net Income
definitions: Operating net income refers to the net profit earned by a company through its core business operations (excluding non-recurring gains and losses). It is a key metric for measuring the profitability and operational efficiency of a company's main business and serves as the basis for calculating disposable income.

name: Operating Net Profit
definitions: Operating Net Profit (After-tax Operating Net Profit) refers to the profit generated by a company from its core operating activities after deducting income tax. It excludes the impact of non-operating items (such as non-operating income and expenses, investment income, etc.) and financing activities (interest expenses), serving as a core indicator for measuring the profitability and operational efficiency of a company's main business.

name: Operating Performance Adjustment
definitions: Operating Performance Adjustment refers to the modification or calibration of relevant financial metrics or transaction prices based on the comparison between a company's actual operating performance and predetermined targets or benchmarks, typically within specific transactions or agreements such as repurchase price determination.

name: Operating Period
definitions: The operating period is a critical time parameter in investment project evaluation, referring to the entire duration from when a project commences operations to the end of its useful life. It is used to define the scope for calculating operating cash flows. It is not an accounting line item itself, but rather a timeframe defined by concepts such as project life and construction period, or determined through specific business plans.

name: Operating Profit
definitions: Operating profit is the profit generated from a company's normal business activities, representing pre-tax earnings before deducting interest expenses.

Operating profit refers to the profit earned by an enterprise from its core business activities, such as selling goods and providing services. It reflects the profitability of the company's principal operations and is a key component of the income statement.

Operating profit represents the profit generated from core business operations after deducting cost of goods sold and operating expenses, excluding interest, taxes, and non-operating items. It reflects a company's operational efficiency and profitability.

name: Operating Profit Before Depreciation and Amortization
definitions: A metric that measures the profitability of a company's core business operations, calculated before deducting depreciation, amortization, interest, and taxes. This indicator reflects earnings generated solely from operating activities, excluding the effects of capital structure, tax jurisdictions, and non-cash expenses related to asset maintenance.

name: Operating Profit Before Interest and Taxes
definitions: Operating Profit Before Interest and Taxes refers to the profit generated solely from core business operations before deducting interest expenses and income taxes. It excludes the impact of non-recurring or non-operating items such as investment income and gains/losses on asset disposals, focusing on reflecting the profitability of a company's main business.

name: Operating Profit Margin
definitions: In business, operating profit margin refers to the ratio of operating profit (also known as operating income) to net sales or operating revenue, usually expressed as a percentage. This metric is used to measure the proportion of revenue remaining after deducting operating expenses (including depreciation and amortization) but before paying interest and taxes.

Operating profit margin is a profitability ratio that measures the proportion of revenue remaining after covering operating expenses, calculated as operating income divided by revenue. It indicates the efficiency of a company's core operations in generating profit before interest and taxes.

name: Operating Profit in the Final Period of the Forecast Horizon
definitions: Operating profit in the final period of the forecast horizon refers to the projected operating profit expected to be achieved in the last forecast period (e.g., the final year) within the defined forecast timeframe (such as the next 3 or 5 years) in a corporate financial forecasting model. It is calculated based on projections of operating revenue, costs, expenses, etc., and serves as a key indicator for assessing the profitability of a company's core operating activities at the end of the forecast period. It is commonly used in subsequent cash flow forecasts or business valuation calculations.

name: Operating Profit of Previous Period
definitions: Operating profit of the previous period refers to the profit earned by an enterprise through its core operating activities in the preceding accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). It is the profit amount after deducting operating costs, various period expenses, taxes and surcharges, asset impairment losses, etc., and after adding gains from fair value changes and investment income, but before considering non-operating income and expenses.

name: Operating Ratio
definitions: Operating ratio measures total operating cost—cost of goods sold plus operating expenses—as a proportion of net sales, indicating the share of revenue consumed by core operating costs. Lower values generally reflect better operating efficiency and cost control.

name: Operating Revenue
definitions: Operating revenue, also known as sales revenue or revenue, is the income generated by an enterprise from its normal business activities. It is one of the most important indicators for measuring a company's business scale, market performance, and core profitability, and is typically presented as the first item on the income statement.

Operating revenue refers to the income earned by an enterprise or individual through its principal business or daily operating activities (such as sales of goods, provision of services, etc.), and is a key indicator for measuring the profitability of its core business.

name: Operating Revenue to Working Capital Ratio
definitions: The Operating Revenue to Working Capital Ratio measures the amount of working capital required to generate a certain level of operating revenue, reflecting the efficiency of a company's working capital utilization. A lower ratio typically indicates that the company achieves more revenue with less capital, demonstrating higher capital efficiency.

name: Operating Risk
definitions: Operating risk refers to the volatility of a company's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) without the use of debt financing, reflecting the inherent uncertainty in generating profits from asset operations.

name: Operating Spread
definitions: The operating spread is the difference between the net operating asset return rate and the after-tax interest rate. It measures the additional rate of return provided to shareholders after paying after-tax interest from the net profit generated by the enterprise's use of net operating assets. This indicator serves as a key bridge connecting operating activities with shareholder returns and is used to decompose the return on equity in the modified DuPont analysis system.

name: Operating Surplus
definitions: Operating surplus refers to the balance of value added created by resident units after deducting compensation of employees, net taxes on production, and consumption of fixed capital. It reflects the residual income generated from business operations and is an important indicator in national economic accounting and corporate financial analysis.

name: Operating Surplus of the Secondary Industry
definitions: Operating surplus of the secondary industry refers to the balance of value added created by resident units in the secondary industry, such as industry and construction, within a certain accounting period in the national economic accounting system, after deducting compensation of employees, net taxes on production, and consumption of fixed capital. It reflects the surplus obtained by production units in the secondary industry from their production activities and serves as an important source of funds for their investment and expanded reproduction.

name: Operating Surplus of the Tertiary Industry
definitions: Operating surplus of the tertiary industry refers to the balance of value added created by producers in the tertiary industry during the reporting period, after deducting compensation of employees, net taxes on production, and consumption of fixed capital. It reflects the operational efficiency and profitability level of the tertiary sector and is a key indicator in national economic accounting.

name: Operating Transportation Expense
definitions: Operating transportation expense refers to the costs incurred by an enterprise in its daily business activities related to the transportation of goods for the sale of products or provision of services. It is a significant component of transportation costs and is typically recorded directly as a specific expense item in accounting.

name: Operating Working Capital
definitions: Operating working capital is the funds required to maintain normal operations based on managerial financial statements, reflecting short-term solvency and operational efficiency. It is calculated as the difference between operating current assets and operating current liabilities.

name: Operating Working Capital Percentage
definitions: Operating Working Capital Percentage is a derived financial metric calculated by dividing operating working capital by a relevant base (such as total assets). It measures the proportion of operating working capital in assets and is used to assess a company's short-term liquidity risk, operational efficiency, and fund utilization.

name: Operating Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period
definitions: Operating working capital in the first year of the continuing period refers to the net current assets required to support daily business operations in the first year after entering the stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or terminal period) in enterprise valuation or project cash flow forecasting. It typically equals the operating current assets minus operating current liabilities for that year, reflecting the level of working capital employed by the enterprise at the beginning of the stable growth phase.

name: Operating Working Capital in the Year Preceding the Continuing Period
definitions: Operating Working Capital in the Year Preceding the Continuing Period refers to the base value used in business valuation to calculate the increase in operating working capital for the first year of the continuing period (also known as the terminal period or stable growth period). It represents the amount of net current assets required to maintain daily business operations in the year immediately before the company enters the stable growth phase, typically estimated based on the financial data of the final year of the forecast period.

name: Operational Functional Obsolescence
definitions: Operational functional obsolescence refers to the portion by which an asset's market value falls below its replacement cost due to outdated design, technology, or functional characteristics, resulting in reduced operational efficiency, increased costs, or diminished output value.

name: Operational Risk
definitions: Operational risk refers to the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems, or from external events (including legal risk), i.e., the difference between actual loss and expected loss. This risk encompasses fraud, security breaches, privacy violations, legal issues, physical disruptions, and environmental events. It is not voluntarily assumed, not revenue-oriented, and cannot be diversified or transferred.

name: Opportunity Cost
definitions: Opportunity cost refers to the value of the best alternative forgone when making a choice under conditions of limited resources.

Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative foregone when a decision is made to allocate resources to a particular option, representing the benefits that could have been obtained by choosing the alternative.

name: Opportunity Cost Rate
definitions: The opportunity cost rate is a ratio used to quantify the cost of forgoing other investment opportunities. It is typically estimated based on financial metrics such as market interest rates, investment return rates, or cost of capital rates, and is employed in financial decision-making (e.g., optimal cash holdings, capital budgeting) to assess the potential loss from resource utilization.

name: Opportunity Cost Rate of Holding Cash
definitions: The opportunity cost rate of holding cash refers to the potential rate of return that a company forgoes by holding cash instead of investing the funds in other marketable securities or projects. It is typically measured by the interest rate on marketable securities or the company's cost of capital.

name: Optimal Cash Balance
definitions: The optimal cash balance is the cash level that minimizes the sum of the opportunity cost of holding cash and the transaction costs, while meeting the payment requirements of the enterprise.
Optimal cash balance is the level of cash holdings that minimizes total costs after weighing the opportunity cost and transaction cost of holding cash.

name: Optimal Debt-to-Equity Ratio
definitions: The optimal debt-to-equity ratio represents the target leverage level that balances the benefits of debt (such as tax shields) against the costs of financial distress and volatility. In this estimation approach, the target ratio is derived by scaling the industry average by a factor that decreases with higher cash flow volatility.

name: Optimal Number of Orders Per Year
definitions: The optimal number of orders per year is the number of orders that should be placed under the Economic Order Quantity model to minimize total costs.

name: Optimal Order Cycle
definitions: The optimal order cycle refers to the time interval between two orders under the Economic Order Quantity model that minimizes total costs.

name: Option Boundary Conditions
definitions: Option boundary conditions define the theoretical minimum and maximum prices that an option can take, based on factors such as the underlying asset price, exercise price, and option style (American or European).

name: Option Break-even Price
definitions: Option break-even price is the underlying asset price at which an options position neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss, typically calculated by adjusting the strike price for the paid premium. For a long call, the break-even price equals the strike price plus the option premium.

Option break-even price is the underlying asset price at expiration at which the option holder realizes zero profit, accounting for the premium paid. For a call option, the break-even price equals the strike price plus the premium; for a put option, it equals the strike price minus the premium.

Option break-even price is the underlying asset price at expiration at which an options position yields zero profit and zero loss, considering only the option premium paid (for buyers). For a call option, the break-even price equals the strike price plus the premium per share; for a put option, it equals the strike price minus the premium per share. This measure excludes commissions, taxes, and other transaction costs.

name: Option Contract Cost
definitions: Option contract cost refers to the total premium paid to acquire an options contract, calculated as the product of the premium per share and the number of shares controlled by the contract.

name: Option Current Price
definitions: Option current price refers to the market price of an option at the current time or its theoretical value calculated using methods such as the single-period binomial option pricing model.

name: Option Delta
definitions: Option Delta measures the sensitivity of an option's price to changes in the underlying asset's price, estimating the change in the option's price for a small change in the underlying price. Delta for call options typically ranges from 0 to 1, and for put options from -1 to 0. It is widely used for risk management, hedging, and scenario analysis.

Option Delta measures the sensitivity of an option's price to a small change in the price of the underlying asset, representing the first derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying price. Under the Black–Scholes framework, call deltas range from 0 to 1 and put deltas from -1 to 0, and depend on the underlying price, strike, time to expiry, volatility, and the risk-free rate.

name: Option Delta (Moneyness-Based Approximation)
definitions: Option delta is the first-order sensitivity of an option’s price to changes in the underlying asset price. This simplified approach assigns fixed delta values based on moneyness classifications (Out of The Money, At The Money, In The Money) for calls and puts, providing an intuitive estimate of price responsiveness per $1 move in the underlying.

name: Option Expiration Date Value
definitions: Option expiration date value refers to the profit that can be obtained if the option is exercised at its expiration.

name: Option Expiration Time
definitions: Option expiration time refers to the pre-determined final date or point in time specified in an option contract when the contract rights become void. It is a fundamental and fixed parameter of an option contract, determining the final deadline by which the option holder may exercise their rights.

name: Option Extrinsic Value
definitions: Option extrinsic value, also called time value, is the portion of an option's premium that exceeds its intrinsic value, reflecting factors such as time to expiration, implied volatility, interest rates, and expected dividends. It is non-negative.

name: Option Gamma
definitions: Option Gamma measures the rate of change of an option’s Delta with respect to changes in the underlying asset’s price. It captures the curvature (second-order sensitivity) of the option’s price and indicates how much Delta is expected to change for a given change in the underlying price.

name: Option Holding Value
definitions: Option holding value is the current fair market value of an option contract, comprising the profit obtainable from immediate exercise (intrinsic value) and the premium arising from future uncertainty in the underlying asset price over the remaining term (time value). This value is a composite metric calculated from a series of input variables based on financial models (such as the Binomial Model or Black-Scholes Model) and serves as a core quantitative parameter for evaluating and managing option-based financial instruments like American options.

name: Option Intrinsic Value
definitions: Option intrinsic value is the immediate exercise value of an option, equal to the in-the-money amount based on the relationship between the underlying price and the strike price, excluding any time value or extrinsic value.

Option intrinsic value is the immediate exercise value of an option, reflecting the in-the-money amount. For a call option, it equals the positive difference between the underlying price and the strike price; for a put option, it equals the positive difference between the strike price and the underlying price. Negative values are floored at zero.

Option intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount of an option at a given moment, defined as the nonnegative difference between the underlying asset's market price and the strike price for a call, and the nonnegative difference between the strike price and the underlying asset's market price for a put. It excludes time value and option premium.

Option intrinsic value is the immediate exercise value of an option, representing the non-negative difference between the underlying asset's market price and the option's exercise price. For a call option, it equals max(0, S − K), and for a put option, it equals max(0, K − S). It excludes time value and premiums, indicating how much an option is in the money.

Option intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount of an option and represents the portion of the option premium attributable to immediate exercise value. For a call, it is the excess of the underlying price over the strike price; for a put, it is the excess of the strike price over the underlying price. Intrinsic value is never negative and excludes time value.

name: Option Moneyness
definitions: Option moneyness describes the relationship between the underlying asset's market price and the option's exercise (strike) price, indicating whether a contract is in-the-money (ITM) or out-of-the-money (OTM). For call options, ITM occurs when the market price exceeds the exercise price; for put options, ITM occurs when the market price is below the exercise price. Moneyness guides trading, hedging, and valuation decisions by reflecting the option's intrinsic value status.

Option moneyness describes the relationship between the underlying asset price and the option's strike price, indicating whether an option is in-the-money (ITM), at-the-money (ATM), or out-of-the-money (OTM). It is fundamental to interpreting exercise likelihood, intrinsic value at expiration, and sensitivity to market movements.

name: Option Net Profit
definitions: Option net profit is the final gain or loss from an option trade after subtracting the total premium paid from the total intrinsic value realized, accounting for the number of contracts traded.

name: Option Premium
definitions: Option premium is the price paid by the buyer of an options contract, representing the sum of intrinsic value and time value. In this simplified formulation, the time value is adjusted by market volatility and the option's maturity period, reflecting how uncertainty and time to expiration influence the premium.

Option premium is the fair value (price) of an option contract. Under the Black-Scholes framework for European options, it equals the present value of the expected payoff under risk-neutral valuation. This implementation evaluates the Black-Scholes price assuming a zero risk-free rate (r = 0).

Option premium is the total amount paid by the buyer to acquire options contracts. For equity options, the total premium equals the number of contracts multiplied by the quoted price per contract and the contract multiplier, which typically represents 100 shares per contract. It reflects the upfront transaction cost for obtaining option rights.

Option premium is the upfront cost paid by the option buyer to acquire the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying asset. For multiple option contracts, the total option premium equals the premium per share multiplied by the number of shares per contract and the number of contracts. In most markets, one option contract typically represents 100 shares.

name: Option Premium Cost (Options on Futures)
definitions: Option premium cost for an option on a futures contract is the total cash outlay required to purchase one contract, calculated as the quoted option premium per index unit multiplied by the contract multiplier. It excludes commissions, fees, and other transaction costs. While the index level and strike price affect moneyness and valuation, they do not change the initial premium paid per contract.

name: Option Present Value
definitions: Option present value is the current value obtained by discounting the option's value at expiration to the present moment using the risk-free interest rate.

name: Option Price
definitions: Option price is the premium paid by the option buyer to the option seller to acquire the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying asset at a specified price on or before a specific future date. This premium consists of two components: intrinsic value, which is the favorable difference between the current price of the underlying asset and the strike price; and time value, which represents the additional value attributable to the potential for market fluctuations during the remaining life of the contract.

name: Option Price Change
definitions: Option price change is a key output variable in option valuation models, referring to the change in option value resulting from variations in its underlying parameters (such as stock price, strike price, risk-free interest rate, volatility, time, etc.). This change is calculated through complex mathematical models (e.g., Binomial Tree Model, Black-Scholes Model) rather than being raw data directly obtained from financial statements.

Option price change refers to the calculated variation in the value of an option based on specific pricing models (such as the Binomial Model or the Black-Scholes Model), given changes in underlying variables (e.g., stock price, risk-free rate, strike price, time to maturity, volatility). It is a calculable composite metric commonly used to measure the sensitivity of an option's value to changes in a single factor, such as the Delta value.

name: Option Price Change (due to Interest Rate Change)
definitions: Option price change due to interest rate change is the first-order estimate of how an option’s value varies with a small change in the risk-free interest rate, calculated as the product of the option’s Rho and the interest rate change. Rho measures the interest rate sensitivity of the option’s value and is used for risk management and hedging.

name: Option Price Sensitivity Parameter
definitions: A key parameter in the Black-Scholes model that reflects the relative relationship between the underlying asset price and the strike price, as well as the impact of time value.

name: Option Profit
definitions: Option profit refers to the net profit or loss realized from an options position at expiration, calculated as the intrinsic value of the option minus the premium paid or plus the premium received, scaled by the number of contracts and the contract size (shares per contract). It reflects the economic outcome of call or put strategies excluding transaction fees and taxes.

name: Option Profit at Expiration
definitions: Option profit at expiration is the net gain or loss from a long options position when the contract expires. It equals the option’s intrinsic value per share minus the premium paid per share, multiplied by the standard shares per contract and the number of contracts. Intrinsic value per share is max(0, S_T - K) for a call and max(0, K - S_T) for a put. This measure typically excludes commissions, fees, and taxes.

name: Option Risk-Adjusted Parameter
definitions: Another key parameter in the Black-Scholes model, representing the probability-adjusted value of an option being exercised before expiration, used to calculate the present value portion of the strike price.

name: Option Time Value
definitions: Option time value is the portion of an option's premium that exceeds its intrinsic value, reflecting factors such as time to expiration, implied volatility, interest rates, expected dividends, and market supply-demand conditions.

name: Option Value
definitions: Option value is the value of an option contract, reflecting the potential economic benefits of holding the option at a specific point in time. It consists of intrinsic value and time value, and is central to the pricing of financial derivatives. Its specific numerical value can be calculated through various theoretical models such as the basic decomposition formula, the Black-Scholes model, and the binomial model, rather than being directly taken from financial statements.

name: Option Value After Down Then Up Movement
definitions: Option Value After Down Then Up Movement is a composite metric that relies on the option value in the down state as an input. Combined with other factors such as the risk-free rate, volatility, and time, it is calculated through option pricing models (such as the Binomial Model or the Black-Scholes Model), representing the option value along the price path where the underlying asset first declines and then rises.

name: Option Value After Two Consecutive Declines
definitions: Option Value After Two Consecutive Declines refers to the expected value of an option when the underlying asset price experiences two consecutive declines in option pricing. This value depends on underlying data such as the underlying asset price, strike price, risk-free interest rate, volatility, etc., and is derived through calculations using financial models like the binomial tree model or the Black-Scholes model. It is a composite indicator, commonly used in calculating the value of options in a down state.

name: Option Value After Two Consecutive Up Movements
definitions: In the binomial option pricing model, this refers to the intrinsic value of a call option at the corresponding node after the underlying asset price experiences two consecutive upward movements. It typically serves as one scenario of expiration value and is used to calculate intermediate node values such as the option value in the up state.

name: Option Value After Up-Down Movement
definitions: Option value after an up-down movement refers to the expected present value of an option when the underlying asset price follows an up-then-down path in the binomial option pricing model. It is a composite metric that depends on underlying data such as the underlying asset price, risk-free rate, volatility, etc., and is calculated through the risk-neutral pricing principle, rather than being a direct fundamental data point. This concept is used in option valuation to calculate derivative metrics such as the option value in the up state.

name: Option Value After Up-Up Movement
definitions: "Option Value After Up-Up Movement" is an intermediate state value in the binomial option pricing model. It depends on underlying data such as the underlying asset price, strike price, and risk-free interest rate, and is calculated through specific discounting and probability-weighted formulas, rather than being raw data directly obtained from financial statements.

name: Option Value Change
definitions: Option value change refers to the variation in the theoretical value (option premium) of an option over a specific period, caused by changes in parameters such as the underlying asset price, volatility, time to expiration, and the risk-free interest rate. In professional analysis, this change is typically measured and decomposed using Greek Letters to gauge the sensitivity of the option price to different risk factors. The hedge ratio (Delta) is a core metric for measuring the impact of changes in the underlying asset price on the option value.

name: Option Value at Expiration in Downward Price Scenario
definitions: Option value at expiration in a downward price scenario refers to the value of an option contract at expiration when the underlying asset price is below the strike price (for call options) or above the strike price (for put options) under specific conditions. Its value is typically determined based on variables such as option type, underlying asset price, and strike price, and serves as the basis for calculating risk management metrics like hedge ratios.

name: Option Value at Expiration in Up State
definitions: Option value at expiration in the up state refers to the value of a call option at expiration when the stock price rises.

name: Option Value in Up State
definitions: Option value in the up state refers to the intrinsic value of a call option at expiration when the underlying asset price rises, calculated as the difference between the up-state stock price and the strike price. This concept is commonly used in option pricing models (such as the binomial model) as a fundamental component for calculating the fair value of an option.

name: Option Writer Profit or Loss
definitions: Option Writer Profit or Loss measures the total monetary outcome for an investor who sells (writes) options, combining premium income with the payoff from intrinsic value at expiration or exercise and, if covered, the change in value of the underlying shares held.

name: Option on Futures Profit
definitions: Option on futures profit refers to the monetary gain or loss realized from buying and later selling an option written on a futures contract. It equals the change in the option premium multiplied by the contract multiplier, excluding commissions, taxes, and other transaction costs.

name: Options Breakeven Point
definitions: The options breakeven point is the market price of the underlying asset at which an options position neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss, accounting for the premium paid.

name: Options Contract
definitions: An options contract is a derivative giving the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an underlying asset at a specified strike price on or before expiration. An option is in-the-money when its immediate exercise would yield positive intrinsic value: for a call when the current price exceeds the strike price, and for a put when the current price is below the strike price.

name: Options Spread Net Cost
definitions: Options spread net cost is the premium paid for the long option minus the premium received for the short option in an options spread. It represents the initial cash outflow (net debit) to establish the position and typically caps the maximum potential loss for debit spreads, excluding commissions and fees.

name: Order Cycle Demand
definitions: Order cycle demand refers to the quantity of products or raw materials that a company expects to consume or sell during the time interval between two consecutive orders. It is a key parameter in inventory management and procurement decisions, used to determine the size of each order.

name: Order Frequency
definitions: Order frequency refers to the total number of purchase orders issued by a company to suppliers to replenish inventory within a specific period (e.g., one year). It is a key metric in inventory management and procurement decisions, directly impacting ordering costs and inventory holding costs.

name: Order Quantity
definitions: Order quantity refers to the planned or actual quantity of a specific raw material, commodity, or supply that a company purchases or orders in a single procurement or ordering activity. It is a fundamental operational data point in inventory management and procurement decision-making, used for subsequent calculations of ordering costs, holding costs, and other financial metrics.

Order quantity refers to the amount of goods or raw materials that an enterprise or organization orders from a supplier at a specific point in time to meet future production or sales needs. It is a key parameter in inventory management and procurement decision-making.

name: Order Quantity per Order
definitions: Order quantity per order is the quantity of goods ordered each time, calculated using formulas such as the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model or the periodic ordering method in inventory management. It is used to optimize ordering strategies to minimize total costs or meet inventory requirements, relying on indicators such as annual demand, ordering cost, and holding cost per unit. It is not a raw data item in financial statements.

name: Order Type
definitions: Order type refers to the specific form and conditions of trading instructions that investors send to brokers when buying or selling securities or derivatives. It stipulates how a trade is to be executed, including key parameters such as price, timing, and quantity.

name: Ordering Cost
definitions: Ordering cost refers to the total cost incurred by a company to acquire inventory related to placing orders, including both fixed costs per order and variable costs.

Ordering cost refers to the various expenses incurred by an enterprise for ordering inventory, typically consisting of fixed costs and variable costs, and is a key component of total inventory management cost.

name: Ordering Cost per Order
definitions: Ordering cost per order refers to the total of various expenses incurred by an enterprise from placing an order to receiving goods into inventory for a single procurement of raw materials or merchandise. These expenses typically include salaries of purchasing personnel, travel expenses, order document processing fees, communication costs, and indirect costs such as transportation arrangements. It is directly proportional to the number of orders placed but is not directly related to the quantity ordered each time.

name: Ordering Fixed Cost
definitions: Ordering fixed cost refers to a fixed fee that a company must pay each time it places an order, regardless of the quantity ordered. This cost is independent of the specific order quantity and is incurred whenever an order is placed, such as salaries of procurement personnel, administrative expenses for order processing, communication fees, and fixed logistics starting prices.

name: Orderly Transaction
definitions: An orderly transaction refers to a transaction that has been publicly available in the market for a period prior to the measurement date, where both parties are knowledgeable, acting voluntarily and not under compulsion, and the transaction is conducted under fair conditions. It is a fundamental prerequisite that must be met when determining the fair value of an asset or liability.

name: Ordinary Annuity Factor
definitions: The ordinary annuity factor is a financial calculation metric used to determine the present value or future value of an equal series of cash flows paid or received at regular intervals, given a fixed interest rate and time period. It relies on fundamental data such as the interest rate and number of periods, is a composite metric rather than a fundamental data point, and is widely applied in finance, accounting, and investment decision-making.

name: Ordinary Annuity Future Value Factor
definitions: The ordinary annuity future value factor is a composite indicator used to calculate the future value of a series of equal payments (ordinary annuity) at a specific interest rate and number of periods. It is derived from basic data such as interest rate and number of periods through mathematical formulas and is commonly used in financial calculations such as sinking fund contributions.

name: Ordinary Annuity Present Value Factor
definitions: The ordinary annuity present value factor refers to the ratio of the present value sum of a series of future equal end-of-period payments to each periodic payment under a specific discount rate and number of periods, serving as a key parameter for calculating the present value of an ordinary annuity.

name: Ordinary Income
definitions: Ordinary income is income subject to standard tax rates, typically including wages, salaries, interest, rental income, and business income, excluding items such as long-term capital gains that may be taxed at preferential rates. When measured annually, it represents the sum of recurring income streams received within a tax year.

Ordinary income refers to income subject to standard marginal income tax rates, such as wages, salaries, interest, business income, and non-qualified dividends. The tax liability on ordinary income is computed by applying the marginal tax rate schedule to successive portions of income within statutory tax brackets.

Ordinary income (operating income) is the profit generated from a company's core business activities before interest and taxes. It is calculated as total revenue minus cost of goods sold, selling, general, and administrative expenses, and depreciation. It excludes non-operating items, financing costs, and income taxes, and reflects operating efficiency and profitability.

name: Ordinary Loss
definitions: Ordinary loss is a loss arising from non-capital transactions and normal business operations (e.g., operating expenses exceeding ordinary income). Under U.S. tax rules, ordinary losses are generally fully deductible against ordinary income, unlike capital losses, which are subject to limitations (e.g., the $3,000 annual cap on net capital losses offsetting ordinary income for individuals).

name: Ordinate
definitions: The ordinate is the numerical value in a Cartesian coordinate system that represents the vertical position of a point (typically on the Y-axis). It usually appears paired with the abscissa (X-axis coordinate) to precisely determine a point's location on a plane.

name: Organic Reserve Replacement Ratio
definitions: The Organic Reserve Replacement Ratio measures the volume of proved reserves added (typically through exploration and development, excluding acquisitions and divestitures when calculated on an organic basis) relative to the volume of oil and gas produced over the same period. A ratio of 100% or higher indicates that a company is fully replacing its produced reserves, supporting sustainability of its reserve base.

name: Organic Sales Growth
definitions: Organic sales growth is the percentage increase in revenue attributable to a company's core, internal operations, excluding the impact of acquisitions and other inorganic activities. It isolates the growth driven by existing products, pricing, and volumes without the effects of newly acquired businesses.

name: Original Amount
definitions: Original amount refers to the initial numerical value in a financial or accounting transaction before any adjustments, deductions, interest, or fee calculations. It can be the initial principal of an investment, the original acquisition cost of an asset, or the base amount upon which a calculation (such as a deduction rate calculation) is based.

name: Original Asset Value
definitions: Original asset value refers to the initial cost or value of an asset recognized and recorded on the books according to accounting standards at the time of its initial acquisition or construction. It reflects all necessary expenditures incurred before the asset is put into use and serves as the basis for subsequent accounting treatments such as depreciation, amortization, and impairment.

name: Original Average Collection Period
definitions: The Original Average Collection Period is a financial metric that measures the average number of days required for a company to convert sales of goods or services into cash receipts. It reflects the efficiency of accounts receivable turnover and the effectiveness of credit policy implementation.

name: Original Calculation Result
definitions: The original calculation result refers to the value directly derived from initial data, assumptions, or specific formulas during financial or computational processes, which has not been subsequently adjusted or revised. It serves as the starting point for subsequent analysis, comparison, or decision-making.

name: Original Cost
definitions: Original cost refers to the total price paid by an enterprise to acquire an asset (such as a fixed asset), as well as all reasonable and necessary expenditures incurred before the asset reaches its intended usable state. It serves as the basis for the initial recorded value of the asset and possesses objectivity and verifiability.

name: Original Cost of Asset
definitions: Original cost of asset refers to the total necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise when acquiring, constructing, or obtaining a specific asset (primarily fixed assets), including purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, loading and unloading fees, installation and commissioning costs, etc. It represents the initial cost of the asset upon recognition in the accounts.

name: Original Cost of Fixed Assets
definitions: Original cost of fixed assets refers to the total monetary expenditure incurred by an enterprise in acquiring, constructing, installing, renovating, expanding, or technically upgrading a fixed asset to bring it to its intended usable condition. It typically includes the purchase price, packaging fees, transportation and handling charges, installation and commissioning costs, and related construction expenses.

name: Original Cost of Fixed Assets at Beginning of Period
definitions: Original cost of fixed assets at the beginning of a period refers to the total historical cost incurred during the acquisition, construction, installation, and other processes of all fixed assets at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the scale of the enterprise's original investment in fixed assets at the beginning of the period.

name: Original Daily Sales
definitions: Original Daily Sales typically refers to the unadjusted daily sales revenue amount used as a benchmark or reference in specific analyses or calculations. In financial analyses such as accounts receivable management, it is often used as the base data for calculating changes in fund utilization.

name: Original Debt Amount
definitions: Original Debt Amount refers to the total original principal or face value of a debt at initial recognition or inception, excluding subsequent factors such as interest, fees, impairment, or restructuring. It serves as the base value for calculating debt-related ratios (e.g., adjustment factors).

name: Original Issue Discount (OID)
definitions: Original Issue Discount (OID) is the excess of a debt instrument's redemption (face) value over its issuance price when issued below par. The discount represents imputed interest that accrues over the life of the instrument and is recognized as interest income (or expense) for financial reporting and tax purposes.

name: Original Plan Highest Activity Level Cost
definitions: Original Plan Highest Activity Level Cost refers to the total cost corresponding to the historical activity level at its peak for the original or benchmark plan in cost behavior analysis (e.g., the high-low method). It is a key data point for calculating the unit variable cost or total fixed cost.

name: Original Plan Peak Activity Level
definitions: Original Plan Peak Activity Level refers to the data point representing the highest level of activity (such as production volume, sales volume, or operating revenue) within the original (or baseline) plan selected for analysis when using cost behavior analysis methods like the High-Low Method. It serves as a key reference data point for calculating unit variable costs or conducting cost forecasts.

name: Original Plan Total Cost
definitions: Original Plan Total Cost refers to the total sum of all costs initially established for developing or evaluating a project, plan, or technical solution, without considering subsequent changes or adjustments. It typically serves as a benchmark for cost comparison and decision analysis.

name: Original Plan Variable Cost per Unit
definitions: Original plan variable cost per unit refers to the cost incurred for producing or selling each unit of product under the enterprise's original production or operational plan, which changes in direct proportion to the level of business activity (such as production volume or sales volume). It serves as a critical foundational data point for cost-volume-profit analysis, cost control, and plan comparison.

name: Original Price
definitions: Original price refers to the initial selling price of a good or service before any discounts, promotions, or price adjustments, serving as the base reference price for calculating discounts, profit margins, and other financial metrics.

name: Original Price of Goods
definitions: Original price of goods refers to the initial selling price before any discounts, promotions, or price adjustments, typically serving as the base price for calculating discounts, profits, or costs.

name: Original Sales Revenue
definitions: Original sales revenue refers to the total income obtained by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during a specific accounting period. It is typically calculated based on the product of sales volume and unit selling price, serving as a key indicator for measuring the scale and performance of the enterprise's core business.

name: Original Sales Volume
definitions: Original sales volume typically refers to the initially set or actually achieved quantity of product sales by an enterprise during a specific period (such as a financial cycle or planning period), serving as a baseline or reference data for subsequent revenue, profit, or budget analysis.

name: Original Share Capital
definitions: Original share capital refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and subscribed by founding shareholders or initial investors at the time of a company's establishment or initial public offering. It represents the initial source of corporate capital and historical factual data, typically determined by multiplying the par value per share (e.g., 1 yuan) by the total number of shares initially issued.

name: Original Stock Price
definitions: Original stock price refers to the initial stock price used as the starting point for calculation in stock market trading, which is unadjusted or not derived from further calculations. It serves as the fundamental raw data for market transactions and is typically used to compute derivative metrics such as stock price change percentages.

name: Original Value
definitions: In financial accounting, original value typically refers to the total reasonable and necessary expenditures incurred to acquire or construct an asset and bring it to its intended usable condition, representing the initial recorded amount of the asset in the accounting books.

Original value refers to the initial data or unadjusted starting point data used as a benchmark for calculating growth rates, change rates, or conducting financial analysis. For example, in calculating the overall growth rate, it represents the value at the beginning of the growth calculation.

name: Original Value of Assets at Beginning of Period
definitions: Original value of assets at the beginning of the period refers to the original acquisition cost of fixed assets at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month), including the purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, installation expenses, and all other necessary expenditures incurred to bring the asset to its intended usable condition. It is a fundamental historical data point obtained directly from accounting ledgers or asset cards, serving as the starting point for subsequent depreciation calculations and the determination of net asset value.

name: Original Value of Fixed Assets
definitions: The original value of fixed assets refers to the total sum of all reasonable and necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire a specific fixed asset and bring it to its intended usable condition. It represents the initial book entry value of the fixed asset in the accounting records, reflecting the actual investment scale in fixed assets and serving as the basis for subsequent depreciation calculations.

name: Original Value of Fixed Assets Disposed or Transferred Out
definitions: Original value of fixed assets disposed or transferred out refers to the original carrying value of fixed assets, intangible assets, or other long-term assets before they are transferred to the disposal process, i.e., the recorded acquisition cost when the assets were initially purchased or obtained.

name: Original Value of Intangible Assets
definitions: The original value of intangible assets refers to the initial cost or historical cost recognized and recorded on the books according to accounting standards when an enterprise acquires or forms an intangible asset. It serves as the basis for calculating subsequent amortization, impairment, and determining the net book value of intangible assets.

name: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets
definitions: Original value of operating long-term assets refers to the historical cost or book value at initial acquisition of tangible assets (such as plants, machinery, equipment, land use rights, etc.) purchased or constructed by an enterprise for its principal business activities, with an expected useful life exceeding one accounting year. It reflects the original cost incurred by the enterprise to obtain these long-term operating resources, without deducting subsequent accumulated depreciation or amortization.

name: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets Acquired in Current Period
definitions: The original value of operating long-term assets acquired in the current period refers to the initial recognized cost at acquisition of tangible assets (such as plants, equipment, vehicles, etc.) purchased or constructed for business operations during the current accounting period (e.g., the current year or quarter), with an expected useful life exceeding one year, excluding subsequent depreciation or impairment.

name: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets Disposed in Current Period
definitions: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets Disposed in Current Period refers to the historical cost value at initial recognition of fixed assets, intangible assets, and other long-term assets used in the enterprise's daily business operations that were disposed of during the current accounting period (such as the current quarter or fiscal year) through means such as sale, scrapping, damage, external investment, non-monetary asset exchange, or debt restructuring. It reflects the scale of historical cost of long-term assets withdrawn from operating activities during the current period.

name: Origination Fee
definitions: An origination fee is a lender-charged fee at the initiation of a loan, typically expressed as a percentage of the loan amount, to compensate for processing, underwriting, and administrative costs. It is usually calculated as a fixed rate applied to the total loan principal.

An origination fee is an upfront charge assessed by a lender for processing, underwriting, and funding a loan. It is typically expressed as a percentage of the loan amount and represents part of the loan's finance charges.

An origination fee is a lender-imposed upfront charge, stated as a flat amount or a percentage of the loan principal, intended to cover the costs of processing, underwriting, and funding a loan. When the fee is rolled into the loan principal, it increases the outstanding balance and total interest paid over the loan term.

name: Origination Points Fee
definitions: Origination points fee is the lender's charge for processing and underwriting a mortgage, typically quoted in points where 1 point equals 1% of the loan amount. The fee is calculated by applying the origination points percentage to the mortgage principal.

name: Orphan Drug Credit
definitions: The orphan drug credit is a U.S. federal income tax credit that allows eligible pharmaceutical companies to reduce tax liability by a specified percentage of qualified clinical testing expenses incurred in developing treatments for rare diseases.

name: Oscillator of a Moving Average (OsMA)
definitions: The Oscillator of a Moving Average (OsMA) is a technical analysis indicator that measures the deviation of an oscillator from its own moving average. It highlights momentum shifts and potential trend reversals by quantifying the difference between the oscillator and its smoothed value.

name: Other Adjustments
definitions: In financial accounting and tax treatment, it refers to the amount of items that require additional adjustments in financial statements or tax returns due to differences between accounting regulations and tax laws that cannot be classified into specific adjustment categories. Commonly used during corporate income tax final settlement to address differences not explicitly listed, such as deemed sales and special asset treatments.

Other adjustments refer to amounts that require tax increase or decrease adjustments during corporate tax filing, used to report other income or deduction items arising from differences between accounting treatment and tax regulations that are not separately listed in detailed tax adjustment schedules (such as Form A105000).

name: Other Alternative Investment Assets
definitions: Other alternative investment assets, in accounting, typically refer to non-trading equity instrument investments held by an enterprise that are designated as measured at fair value through other comprehensive income. They belong to a category of alternative investments, distinct from traditional assets such as stocks, bonds, and cash, and represent a specific asset account on the balance sheet.

name: Other Asset Investments
definitions: Other asset investments refer to the allocation of corporate funds into financial or physical assets beyond traditional stocks, bonds, and cash, such as long-term equity investments, real estate, commodities, artwork, or intangible assets, typically falling under the category of long-term investments.

name: Other Assets
definitions: Other Assets is an aggregated accounting item on the balance sheet, used to consolidate long-term asset items that are unique in nature, occur infrequently or irregularly, and cannot be clearly classified into major asset categories such as current assets, fixed assets, or intangible assets.

name: Other Attributable Costs
definitions: Other attributable costs refer to various costs in financial accounting that can be clearly and directly attributed to a specific cost object (such as a product, project, or department) but are not separately listed under major cost categories (such as direct materials or direct labor). They represent raw data in the cost accumulation process, used for more accurately calculating the true cost of a specific object.

name: Other Business Income and Expenses
definitions: Other business income and expenses refer to the revenue generated and corresponding cost expenditures from business activities other than the main operations of an enterprise. It is directly derived from accounting records and serves as a fundamental line item on the income statement, used to account for the operating results of non-core business activities such as material sales and asset leasing.

name: Other Capital Reserves
definitions: Other capital reserves is a detailed account under capital reserves, primarily recording gains and losses directly attributable to owners' equity other than capital premium (or share premium). It arises from specific accounting events, such as equity-settled share-based payments, changes in other equity of investees under the equity method excluding net profit or loss, etc. Its amount is directly recognized and not derived through calculation.

name: Other Cash Payments Related to Financing Activities
definitions: Refers to cash payments related to financing activities, as reported in the cash flow statement, other than principal repayments of debt, dividend or profit distributions, and interest payments. These expenditures typically do not constitute the main part of financing activities but are nevertheless related to raising funds or changes in capital structure.

name: Other Cash Payments Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period
definitions: Other cash payments related to financing activities in the next period refer to other cash payments associated with financing activities that an enterprise expects to occur in future periods (e.g., the next accounting period), excluding major financing cash outflows such as debt repayment, dividend or profit distribution, and interest payments. These payments typically include audit fees, consulting fees directly paid for raising funds, lease payments for finance leases, and cash payments for capital reduction (e.g., share repurchases).

name: Other Cash Payments Related to Investing Activities in the Next Period
definitions: Other cash payments related to investing activities in the next period refer to other cash outflows associated with investing activities that an enterprise expects to incur in the next accounting period (such as the next fiscal year or quarter), excluding the net cash paid for the purchase of fixed assets, intangible assets and other long-term assets, and for obtaining subsidiaries and other business units. These expenditures generally do not constitute major investing activities but are components of cash flows from investing activities.

name: Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities
definitions: Other cash received related to financing activities is an item in the cash flow statement that reflects various other cash inflows related to financing activities received by an enterprise, apart from major items such as absorbing investments and obtaining borrowings, for example, receiving cash donations.

name: Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period
definitions: Refers to other cash inflows related to financing activities that an enterprise expects to receive in future accounting periods (e.g., next period, next fiscal year), excluding primary financing methods such as capital absorption and borrowing. Examples include expected cash donations received and refunds of deposits related to finance leases.

name: Other Cash Received Related to Investment Activities in the Next Period
definitions: Other cash received related to investment activities in the next period refers to other cash inflows related to investment activities received in the enterprise's cash flow statement for the next accounting period (e.g., next period, next quarter, or next fiscal year), excluding major items such as the net cash received from the disposal of fixed assets, intangible assets, and other long-term assets, and cash received from investment returns. Examples may include dividends or interest received that were paid but not yet collected when purchasing stocks or bonds.

name: Other Cash Received Related to Operating Activities in Next Period
definitions: Other cash received related to operating activities in the next period refers to other cash inflows related to daily operations that an enterprise expects to receive in the next accounting period (such as the next quarter or fiscal year), excluding major operating activities such as sales of goods and provision of services. These inflows typically include non-core business cash receipts such as penalty income, rental income, scrap sales revenue, and refunds of deposits received.

name: Other Cash Received Related to Operating Activities in Year k
definitions: Other cash received related to operating activities in year k refers to cash inflows received by an enterprise during its operating activities in year k, apart from main business operations such as sales of goods and provision of services. These inflows typically include non-recurring or secondary cash receipt items such as penalty income, deposit refunds, rental income (non-core business), and cash overages.

name: Other Comprehensive Income
definitions: Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) refers to the difference between comprehensive income and net profit, representing certain gains and losses of an enterprise that are not recognized in the current period's profit or loss. These items are directly recorded in the equity account 'Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income' (AOCI) and include unrealized gains/losses on available-for-sale financial assets, the effective portion of cash flow hedges, foreign currency translation adjustments, actuarial gains/losses on defined benefit plans, and revaluation surplus.

name: Other Comprehensive Income by Scenario
definitions: Other comprehensive income by scenario refers to the gains and losses that, according to accounting standards, are directly recorded in changes of owners' equity but not recognized in the current period's income statement, excluding net profit generated from ordinary business activities during a specific accounting period. It primarily reflects unrealized or temporary gains and losses, which do not affect current period net profit but impact total comprehensive income.

name: Other Comprehensive Income for the Period
definitions: Other Comprehensive Income for the Period refers to the gains and losses recognized in a specific accounting period, as stipulated by accounting standards, that are not included in the current period's profit or loss but are directly recorded in owners' equity. It is a component of the statement of changes in owners' equity and a key element in calculating total comprehensive income.

name: Other Construction Costs
definitions: Other Construction Costs are a significant component of the construction investment within the total investment estimate for a construction project. They refer to various expenses incurred during the construction period that are related to land use rights acquisition, the entire construction process, and future production and operation, but are not classified under construction engineering costs, installation engineering costs, or equipment purchase costs. They are aggregated from a series of independently measurable specific cost items and are ultimately capitalized into the original value of fixed assets.

Other construction costs refer to the various expenses that must be incurred during construction investment, in addition to engineering costs such as construction engineering fees, installation engineering fees, and equipment purchase costs, to ensure the smooth construction and delivery of the project.

name: Other Costs Attributable to Inventory Purchase
definitions: Refers to other necessary and reasonable expenditures incurred by an enterprise during the inventory procurement process, beyond the purchase price, related taxes, transportation fees, loading/unloading fees, and insurance premiums, to bring the inventory to its intended salable or usable condition. These costs form part of the total inventory purchase cost and must be capitalized into the initial cost of inventory.

name: Other Costs Directly Attributable to Inventory Acquisition
definitions: Refers to other expenditures, besides the purchase price, related taxes, transportation fees, loading and unloading charges, and insurance premiums, that are necessarily incurred by an enterprise during the inventory acquisition process to bring the inventory to the location and condition necessary for it to be saleable or usable, and that can be directly attributed to the acquisition of that specific inventory.

name: Other Current Assets
definitions: Other current assets is a specific line item under current assets on the balance sheet, referring to short-term assets that do not belong to major current asset categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory, but are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle.

name: Other Current Assets as Percentage of Total Current Assets
definitions: A composition ratio that measures the proportion of Other Current Assets within Total Current Assets, indicating the materiality and mix of less common current asset categories in a firm's liquidity profile.

name: Other Current Liabilities
definitions: Other current liabilities refer to the aggregate of short-term debts that a company must repay within one year or one operating cycle, which do not fall under major current liability items such as short-term borrowings, accounts payable, or employee compensation payable. It is a collective account used to summarize short-term obligations that are either unique in nature or relatively insignificant in amount, making separate presentation impractical.

Other Current Liabilities is an aggregated account under current liabilities on the balance sheet, used to consolidate debts that are not separately presented in major current liability accounts such as short-term borrowings, accounts payable, and employee compensation payable, and are expected to be settled within one year or one operating cycle.

name: Other Debt Investments
definitions: Other debt investments are a type of financial asset held by an enterprise, typically referring to investments in debt instruments such as bonds that are held with the objective of both collecting contractual cash flows and selling the financial asset. In accounting treatment, they are designated as measured at fair value through other comprehensive income. Their carrying amount is directly formed through initial recognition and subsequent measurement (such as fair value changes and amortization of interest adjustments).

name: Other Deductions
definitions: Other Deductions refer to additional items, as stipulated by China's Individual Income Tax Law, that can be legally deducted when calculating the taxable income of a resident individual's comprehensive income, apart from the basic deductions, special deductions, and special additional deductions. They are original deduction items explicitly listed in the tax law, with specific content determined according to relevant laws and regulations, and cannot be derived or calculated through other financial indicators.

name: Other Direct Costs
definitions: Other direct costs refer to additional expenditures, beyond primary raw material costs and direct labor costs, that can be directly attributed to a specific cost object (such as a product, project, or service) during the production, construction, or service provision process. These costs are typically directly related to production or service activities and can be clearly traced and allocated to specific cost objects.

name: Other Direct Operating Costs
definitions: Other direct operating costs refer to other necessary expenditures directly related to the provision of products or services, beyond primary costs such as direct materials and direct labor, incurred by an enterprise in its daily business operations. These costs typically cannot be directly attributed to a specific production process or product but are indispensable components of operating activities. In accounting, they are treated as basic or detailed items under cost and expense categories.

name: Other Equity Instrument Investments
definitions: Other equity instrument investments refer to non-trading equity instrument investments that an enterprise actively designates as measured at fair value with changes in fair value recognized in other comprehensive income, in accordance with accounting standards. They are a type of financial asset whose value fluctuates directly with market fair value, and the holding purpose is typically for long-term strategic holding rather than short-term trading gains.

name: Other Equity Instruments
definitions: Other equity instruments refer to various financial instruments issued by an enterprise, other than ordinary shares, that are classified as equity instruments. They are used to account for funds raised by the enterprise through the issuance of these special financial instruments (such as perpetual bonds, preferred shares, etc.) that constitute part of the owner's equity.

name: Other Expenses
definitions: In financial statements (such as the income statement), 'Other Expenses' is an independent primary account used to aggregate and present various incidental or non-recurring expenditures that cannot be classified into major expense categories (such as Selling Expenses, Administrative Expenses, and Financial Expenses). It belongs to fundamental financial data and typically cannot be directly derived through calculations from other financial metrics.

Other expenses refer to various costs and losses incurred by an enterprise in its daily business operations or non-recurring activities, excluding clearly classified items such as main business costs and major period expenses (e.g., selling expenses, administrative expenses, financial expenses). They are typically used to account for infrequent or relatively minor expenditure items not warranting separate ledger accounts, such as fines, donations, and losses on disposal of non-current assets.

name: Other Financial Current Assets
definitions: Other financial current assets is a specific line item under current assets on the balance sheet, referring to short-term assets with financial characteristics held by an enterprise that do not belong to major current asset categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory. These assets are typically expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle and represent fundamental financial data directly obtained from accounting records.

name: Other Freight Charges
definitions: Other freight charges refer to the aggregate of various additional costs incurred during the freight transportation process, excluding basic freight (such as air freight, road tonnage charges) and declared value surcharges. These charges are typically applied to cover the costs of specific operations or services within the transportation service.

name: Other Income
definitions: Other income refers to various non-recurring or secondary revenues obtained by an enterprise or administrative unit in accordance with regulations, beyond its main business or primary appropriation income. In financial statements, it is typically presented as an independent revenue item directly, rather than derived through calculation.

Other Income is a line item on the income statement, classified as a profit and loss account under accounting standards. It primarily accounts for various gains that are not directly related to the enterprise's ordinary operating activities but result in an increase in owners' equity, excluding operating revenue and investment income. It serves as one of the fundamental data items for calculating operating profit.

name: Other Increases
definitions: In the field of finance and accounting, 'Other Increases' typically refers to the incremental amount in a specific statement or account (such as surplus reserves) that results from items not separately presented or classified, apart from the main, clearly defined components. It is an aggregated, supplementary item used to reflect increases that are not conveniently or separately disclosed within the primary items.

name: Other Interest-bearing Current Liability Items
definitions: Other interest-bearing current liability items refer to debts that a company must repay within one year or one operating cycle and on which interest must be paid. These items exclude major categories such as short-term borrowings and current portion of long-term debt, and constitute a part of interest-bearing current liabilities.

name: Other Investment Expenses
definitions: Other investment expenses refer to the various necessary costs incurred to complete a project's construction, beyond the main direct costs such as equipment purchase costs and construction engineering costs, during the preparation of project investment estimates or design budget estimates. These expenses typically include construction unit management fees, survey and design fees, engineering supervision fees, etc., and constitute an important component of the total project investment.

name: Other Investments
definitions: Other investments refer to long-term investments made directly by an enterprise in other entities in the form of monetary funds, physical assets, or intangible assets, typically not constituting control over the investee. In accounting, it is presented as a separate asset item on the balance sheet.

name: Other Items Meeting Regulatory Requirements
definitions: In financial statements, this specifically refers to items that comply with accounting standards or regulatory provisions but cannot be classified under major standard categories, and are therefore presented separately in specific statement line items (such as other comprehensive income for the period).

name: Other Long-term Assets
definitions: Other long-term assets refer to those long-term asset items on a company's balance sheet that are of a special nature, occur infrequently, or have an amortization period exceeding one year, and are not classified under specific categories such as current assets, long-term equity investments, fixed assets, or intangible assets. They typically include items like long-term prepaid expenses that cannot be categorized under the aforementioned major asset classes.

name: Other Long-term Assets Book Value
definitions: Other long-term assets book value refers to the net amount of other long-term assets presented on the balance sheet, excluding major long-term assets such as fixed assets, intangible assets, and long-term equity investments, after deducting relevant impairment provisions or allowance items.
