It reflects the actual accounting value of these assets on the books.

name: Other Monetary Funds
definitions: Other monetary funds refer to various monetary funds deposited in banks or other financial institutions for specific purposes, excluding cash on hand and bank deposits, in the daily business operations of an enterprise.

name: Other Non-Cash Expenses for Next Period
definitions: Other non-cash expenses for the next period refer to expense items that a company expects to incur in the next accounting period but do not involve actual cash outflow or inflow in the current period. These expenses are recognized under the accrual basis of accounting, affecting current period profits, while their cash impact occurs in future periods, such as prepaid expenses or deferred costs that require future amortization.

name: Other Non-Operating Activity Adjustments in the Final Forecast Period
definitions: Other non-operating activity adjustments in the final forecast period refer to the cash inflow or outflow items considered when adjusting the cash flow statement for the final period of the forecast horizon (typically the ending year of the detailed forecast period) in a financial forecast or valuation model. These items are not part of the company's regular operating activities and are of a non-recurring or one-time nature. The adjustments aim to make the cash flow in the final period better reflect the normalized operating condition of the company as it enters a stable or perpetual growth phase, thereby providing a more reasonable basis for subsequent terminal value calculation. Common adjustment items may include non-recurring gains or losses, significant asset disposals or acquisitions, one-time restructuring charges, litigation settlements, and other cash impacts unrelated to operations.

name: Other Non-cash Adjustments
definitions: Other Non-cash Adjustments is an aggregate adjustment item in the supplementary information of the cash flow statement, used to reflect all other non-cash adjustment items not separately listed during the process of reconciling net profit to cash flows from operating activities, apart from the explicitly enumerated items (such as asset impairment provisions, depreciation of fixed assets, etc.). It serves as a catch-all item to ensure the completeness of the reconciliation process.

name: Other Non-current Assets
definitions: Other non-current assets refer to long-term assets with a turnover or realization period exceeding one year, excluding those separately presented on the balance sheet (such as fixed assets, intangible assets, long-term equity investments, etc.). These assets typically do not meet the criteria for separate presentation or have relatively unique characteristics.

name: Other Non-current Financial Assets
definitions: Other non-current financial assets are items in the balance sheet used to aggregate financial assets that are not separately presented in the financial statements and have a holding period exceeding one year. They typically include infrequent or immaterial long-term financial assets that are not practical to present separately.

name: Other Non-current Liabilities
definitions: Other non-current liabilities are items on the balance sheet used to aggregate long-term debts or obligations that cannot be classified into standard long-term liability categories such as long-term borrowings, bonds payable, and long-term payables. They form part of non-current liabilities and typically refer to non-standard liabilities with a repayment period exceeding one year.

name: Other Non-operating Assets
definitions: Other Non-operating Assets is a line item on the balance sheet used to aggregate various non-current assets held by an enterprise that are not directly related to its daily operating activities and are expected to be realized or consumed over a period exceeding one year (or one normal operating cycle). It typically includes specific assets with longer amortization periods, such as contract acquisition costs, contract fulfillment costs (net of the portion to be recovered within one year), and costs of expected returns.

name: Other Non-operating Current Assets
definitions: Other non-operating current assets refer to short-term assets presented on a company's balance sheet that do not fall into major operating current asset categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory, are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle, but are not directly related to primary business activities.

name: Other Operating Costs
definitions: Other Operating Costs is an enterprise accounting item used to record the direct costs incurred from operating activities other than the main business operations, such as the cost of selling materials, depreciation of leased fixed assets, amortization of leased intangible assets, and the cost of leased packaging materials.

name: Other Operating Current Assets
definitions: Other operating current assets refer to the operational portion under the 'Other Current Assets' account on the balance sheet. These are short-term assets arising from daily business operations that do not fall into major categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory. They typically include prepayments, deferred expenses, etc., and are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle.

name: Other Operating Current Assets at Period End
definitions: Other operating current assets at period end refer to other current assets, excluding major items such as cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, and inventory, that are used in daily business operations and are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle, as presented in the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end).

name: Other Operating Current Liabilities
definitions: Other operating current liabilities refer to other short-term debts arising from a company's daily business operations that are due within one year or one operating cycle, excluding major items such as accounts payable and employee compensation payable. It is a specific line item on the balance sheet used to account for and report these non-major operating short-term liabilities.

name: Other Operating Expenses
definitions: Other operating expenses refer to various expenditures related to business activities incurred by an enterprise in its daily operations, excluding main business costs and primary operating expenses (such as selling expenses, administrative expenses, and financial expenses). These expenses are typically accounted for under operating costs or operating expense accounts.

name: Other Operating Payables
definitions: Other operating payables are a current liability item on the balance sheet, referring to various amounts payable or temporarily received by an enterprise in its daily operating activities, excluding notes payable, accounts payable, advances from customers, employee compensation payable, taxes payable, interest payable, dividends payable, etc. The reported amount must be calculated and recorded based on an analysis of the balances of relevant subsidiary ledger accounts, involving reclassification adjustments.

name: Other Operating Revenue
definitions: Other operating revenue refers to the income realized by an enterprise from other operating activities besides its main business in daily operations, such as selling materials, leasing assets, and providing non-core business services.

Other operating revenue refers to income generated by an enterprise from sales or operating activities outside its main business operations. These activities are typically not the company's core business but form part of its daily operations, such as selling raw materials, leasing fixed assets or intangible assets, and providing services not related to the main business (e.g., transportation, purchasing and sales agency services). In accounting, it corresponds to 'Other Operating Costs' and is used to reflect the profitability of these activities.

name: Other Owners' Equity Items of Subsidiaries
definitions: Other owners' equity items of subsidiaries refer to the equity interests in the net assets of subsidiaries attributable to investors other than the parent company (i.e., non-controlling interests) as presented in consolidated financial statements. They represent the portion of the subsidiary's owners' equity that does not belong to the parent company.

name: Other Payables
definitions: Other payables refer to various amounts payable or temporarily received from other entities or individuals that occur in the course of daily business operations, excluding major transactions such as purchasing goods or accepting services. It is an account under current liabilities on the balance sheet, reflecting debts related to non-core business operations that the enterprise needs to repay or settle.

Other payables refer to various amounts payable or temporarily received by an enterprise in its daily operations, excluding major transactions such as purchasing goods or accepting services. It is an account under current liabilities on the balance sheet, reflecting debts related to non-core business activities that the enterprise needs to pay but has not yet settled.
Other payables refer to various special payments that an enterprise is required to remit to the state, excluding various taxes such as value-added tax and income tax.

name: Other Payables (Non-interest Bearing Portion)
definitions: Other payables (non-interest bearing portion) refer to amounts payable or temporarily received from other entities or individuals arising from transactions or events not directly related to the principal business operations in the course of daily business activities, and which do not accrue interest according to relevant contracts or agreements. It is a significant component of a company's non-interest bearing current liabilities, and its amount is directly sourced from accounting book records.

name: Other Payables - Prior Period
definitions: Other payables - prior period refer to various payable and temporarily received amounts, excluding those arising from main business operations such as accounts payable and notes payable, that remained unpaid or unsettled as of the balance sheet date of the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous fiscal year or quarter).

name: Other Payments to Individuals
definitions: Refers to various non-fixed or non-recurring expenses paid by an enterprise to individuals (such as sales personnel, consultants, freelancers, etc.) within intermediate inputs like selling expenses, excluding regular wages, bonuses, and commissions. Examples include travel allowances, business entertainment reimbursements, and temporary service remunerations.

name: Other Policy Tax Reduction Amount
definitions: Other Policy Tax Reduction Amount refers to the portion of tax reduction already granted by other independent tax incentive policies (such as employment of disabled persons, entrepreneurship of retired soldiers, etc.) that must be deducted from the tax payable in advance when calculating the tax reduction amount for a specific tax incentive (e.g., halved individual income tax on business income of sole proprietorships). It is used to ensure accurate calculation when multiple tax incentives are applied cumulatively and to avoid duplicate reductions.

name: Other Procurement Expenses
definitions: Other procurement expenses refer to other necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise during the procurement of materials or goods, in addition to direct costs such as purchase price, main transportation fees, and related taxes. These expenses typically include packaging fees, warehousing fees, loading and unloading fees, insurance premiums, inspection fees, etc., and constitute part of the total cost of inventory procurement.

name: Other Property Loss Value
definitions: Other Property Loss Value refers to the monetary measurement of economic losses incurred due to damage, destruction, or depreciation of various properties other than major assets such as buildings, structures, and equipment (e.g., inventory, office supplies, intangible assets) in specific events such as accidents, fires, etc.

name: Other Receivables
definitions: Other receivables refer to various amounts receivable or temporarily paid to other entities or individuals by an enterprise in its daily operations, excluding those arising from principal operating activities such as accounts receivable, notes receivable, and prepayments. Examples include travel advances to employees, petty cash funds, various deposits collected, insurance claims receivable, or fines receivable. On the balance sheet, it is presented as part of current assets.

name: Other Receivables - Prior Period
definitions: Other Receivables - Prior Period refers to the carrying value of various receivables and temporary payments due from other entities or individuals at the end of the previous accounting period (e.g., the prior year or quarter), excluding major receivable items such as accounts receivable, notes receivable, and prepayments. It is typically presented as the net amount of the ending balance in the 'Other Receivables' account from the prior period, less the corresponding provision for bad debts.

name: Other Related Expenses
definitions: Other related expenses refer to the directly associated, necessary additional expenditures incurred in specific economic activities (such as asset disposal or procurement), apart from the primary cost or revenue. These expenses typically do not constitute core costs but are essential for the complete accounting of the transaction.

name: Other Securities Investments
definitions: Other Securities Investments is a composite metric in financial statements, representing the total value of securities held by an enterprise beyond major categories (such as equities and bonds). It is typically derived by aggregating or calculating data from underlying securities investments and is used to reflect the diversification of the enterprise's investment portfolio and non-core investment activities.

name: Other Short-term Borrowings
definitions: Other short-term borrowings refer to non-core operating loans obtained by an enterprise from financial institutions such as banks, with a repayment period of one year or less. They are typically used for temporary working capital needs, specific project financing, or as bridge financing, and are separately presented as a current liability in the financial statements.

name: Other Short-term Liabilities Related to Operating Activities
definitions: Other short-term liabilities related to operating activities refer to various short-term debts that a company incurs in its daily business operations, excluding major items such as accounts payable and notes payable, which are due for repayment within one year or one operating cycle. They typically include liabilities directly related to core business operations, such as accrued employee compensation, deferred revenue, dividends payable, and short-term borrowings.

name: Other Statutory Deductions
definitions: Other statutory deductions refer to specific expenditure items that individuals are permitted to deduct from their comprehensive income according to relevant national laws and regulations, in addition to basic deductions, special deductions, and special additional deductions, when calculating the taxable income for individual income tax purposes.

name: Other Taxes and Fees Paid
definitions: Other taxes and fees paid refer to the actual cash disbursements made by an enterprise for various taxes and fees other than major tax categories (such as corporate income tax and value-added tax), including stamp duty, property tax, land use tax, vehicle and vessel tax, etc. It constitutes a significant component of the 'Cash Paid for Taxes' item in the cash flow statement and represents fundamental cash outflow data directly sourced from accounting records.

name: Other Tier 1 Capital Instruments and Their Premiums
definitions: Other Tier 1 capital instruments and their premiums are direct components of a commercial bank's capital structure, referring to capital instruments, other than common equity and retained earnings, that meet regulatory requirements and have the capacity to absorb losses on a going concern basis, along with the premium portion exceeding their par value at issuance. Common examples include preferred shares and their issuance premiums.

name: Out of The Money (OTM)
definitions: Out of the Money (OTM) describes an option with no intrinsic value. A call option is OTM when the underlying asset's market price is below the strike price; a put option is OTM when the underlying asset's market price is above the strike price. OTM options have zero immediate exercise value and consist solely of time value.

name: Out-of-Pocket Cost
definitions: Out-of-pocket cost refers to the expenses that a company needs to pay in cash during operational decision-making, directly impacting cash flow management, and is commonly used in production/operational decisions and cash flow analysis.

name: Out-of-Pocket Expenses
definitions: Out-of-pocket expenses are direct payments made by an individual for goods or services that are not reimbursed by an employer, insurer, or other payer. In accounting and finance, they are tracked to evaluate personal spending, employee expense claims, and patient cost burden in healthcare.

name: Out-of-Pocket Limit
definitions: The out-of-pocket limit (out-of-pocket maximum) is the annual cap on cost sharing a policyholder must pay for covered healthcare services, including deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. Once this limit is reached, the insurance plan pays 100% of covered, in-network allowed charges for the remainder of the year, excluding premiums and non-covered or out-of-network costs.

name: Outcome Probability
definitions: Outcome probability refers to the likelihood of a specific financial result or market event occurring in the future within financial and accounting activities, typically expressed as a percentage or a value between 0 and 1. It is a fundamental data point estimated based on historical data, statistical models, or expert judgment.

name: Outcome Value
definitions: Outcome value refers to the final economic value of a project or decision calculated through financial models (such as discounted cash flow or probability-weighted analysis) after considering future uncertainties. It is a core evaluation metric for capital budgeting and investment decision analysis and typically does not directly equate to the book value in financial statements.

name: Output
definitions: Output refers to the physical quantity of qualified products produced by an enterprise, production line, equipment, or worker within a specific period. It is the most fundamental physical measure or operational data in the production process, typically obtained through direct counting, weighing, or measurement, and is used to gauge the scale and efficiency of production activities.

name: Output Gap
definitions: Output gap measures the deviation of actual GDP from potential GDP, expressed as a percentage of potential GDP. A positive output gap indicates the economy is operating above potential (inflationary pressure), while a negative output gap indicates slack or underutilized capacity.

name: Output VAT
definitions: Output VAT is the value-added tax amount calculated based on sales revenue and the tax rate stipulated by tax laws, collected from the buyer when a taxpayer sells goods or provides taxable services. It is a key component in VAT calculation.

name: Output VAT Amount
definitions: Output VAT amount refers to the value-added tax calculated based on the current period's sales revenue and the prescribed VAT rate, which is charged to the buyer by a general taxpayer when selling goods, providing taxable services, or engaging in deemed sales activities. It is a key component in calculating the enterprise's current period VAT payable.

name: Output VAT Payable
definitions: Output VAT payable refers to the value-added tax amount calculated based on sales revenue and the prescribed VAT rate, which a general taxpayer should collect from the buyer when selling goods, providing taxable services, or engaging in taxable activities. It is a key component in calculating the enterprise's current-period VAT payable.

name: Output VAT for the Current Period
definitions: Output VAT for the current period refers to the amount of Value-Added Tax (VAT) that a taxpayer is required to collect from purchasers during the current tax period (e.g., a month or a quarter) arising from taxable sales activities, such as the sale of goods, provision of taxable services, intangible assets, or immovable property. It serves as one of the fundamental components for calculating the enterprise's VAT payable for the current period.

name: Output Value
definitions: Output value refers to the total market value of all goods and services created by an enterprise or individual through production activities within a specific period. It is an important economic indicator for measuring the scale and results of production activities, reflecting the final outcome of the production process, but it is not equivalent to profit, as production costs have not yet been deducted.

name: Output per Shift (Month)
definitions: Output per shift (month) refers to the actual quantity of products completed by a production team or individual within one work shift or one month, serving as important raw data for measuring production efficiency and capacity.

name: Output per Unit Time
definitions: Output per unit time refers to the quantity of products produced or the amount of work completed within a specific time period (such as per hour, day, or week), serving as a fundamental metric for measuring production efficiency.

name: Outright Forward
definitions: An outright forward is a foreign exchange forward contract that locks in a single all-in forward exchange rate for settlement on a future date. The outright forward rate (forward outright) is computed by adjusting the spot exchange rate with forward points, which reflect the covered interest rate differential; positive points indicate a forward premium and negative points a forward discount. It is used to hedge or manage exchange rate risk.

name: Outright Option
definitions: An outright option is a standalone position in a single call or put option, not combined with other option legs. The net profit or loss for a long outright option position equals the option's intrinsic value minus the premium paid, evaluated at a given spot price and strike, ignoring transaction costs and time value.

name: Outstanding Amount of Long-term Debt Securities
definitions: Outstanding amount of long-term debt securities refers to the total number of units or certificates of long-term debt securities (such as long-term bonds) that have been issued by an issuer (e.g., government, corporation) and are currently being traded among investors in the financial market, not yet matured or redeemed. It is a fundamental statistical value directly obtained from market records or issuer data, reflecting the supply scale of the security in the secondary market.

name: Outstanding Balance
definitions: Outstanding balance refers to the total amount in an account that has not been paid or settled at a specific point in time (e.g., statement date or reporting date). It typically includes unpaid principal, accrued interest, and other related charges, serving as fundamental data reflecting the current debt level.

name: Outstanding Common Shares
definitions: Outstanding common shares refer to the total number of common stock shares issued by a company and actually held by investors in the public market. It excludes shares repurchased and held as treasury stock by the company, serving as fundamental data for calculating key financial metrics such as earnings per share and net asset value per share.

name: Outstanding Invoices
definitions: Outstanding invoices refer to sales invoices issued to customers for which payment has not yet been received, or purchase invoices received from suppliers for which payment has not yet been completed. They represent a state of receivables or payables where the transaction has been confirmed but funds have not yet been settled.

name: Outstanding Principal Balance
definitions: Outstanding principal balance refers to the portion of the original loan principal that has not been repaid by the borrower at a specific point in time for an installment loan or debt. It serves as the basis for calculating current interest and is a core indicator for measuring the remaining liability scale of the debtor. It can be calculated through methods such as the total loan amount minus the present value of cumulative principal repaid or the present value of future repayment amounts.

name: Outstanding Shares
definitions: Outstanding shares refer to all shares that have been authorized by the company, issued, and purchased and held by investors. They are distinguished from treasury shares, which are shares held by the company itself and do not carry exercisable rights. The sum of outstanding shares and treasury shares equals the total number of issued shares.

Outstanding shares refer to all shares that have been authorized by the company, issued, purchased, and held by investors. They are distinguished from treasury stock, which are shares held by the company itself and do not carry exercisable rights. The sum of outstanding shares and treasury stock equals the total number of issued shares.

Outstanding shares are the total number of shares held by external shareholders, excluding treasury shares retained by the issuing company. It equals issued shares minus treasury shares and is used in key metrics such as market capitalization, earnings per share (EPS), and ownership calculations.

name: Outward Arbitrage Profit
definitions: Outward arbitrage profit is the gain realized by borrowing domestically at a given interest rate and lending the proceeds abroad at a higher foreign interest rate for the same period, ignoring transaction costs, taxes, and other frictions.

name: Over and Short
definitions: Over and Short (Cash Over and Short) is a general ledger account and reconciliation measure that records the discrepancy between the recorded cash sales expected to be collected and the actual cash received. A positive amount indicates a cash over situation (excess cash on hand), while a negative amount indicates a cash short situation (cash deficiency), typically arising from cash-handling errors, timing issues, or recording mistakes. It is used in cash-intensive operations to monitor internal control effectiveness and reconcile cash drawers to sales records.

name: Overall Capture Ratio
definitions: Overall capture ratio measures an investment manager's relative performance in rising versus declining markets. It is defined as the up-market capture ratio divided by the down-market capture ratio, indicating how effectively the manager participates in gains compared to losses. A value greater than 1 suggests stronger participation in up-markets relative to down-markets.

name: Overall Credit Utilization Ratio
definitions: Overall Credit Utilization Ratio measures the percentage of total outstanding revolving balances relative to total revolving credit limits across all credit cards. It is calculated by dividing the sum of balances by the sum of credit limits and is a key factor in credit scoring and credit risk assessment.

name: Overall Current Period Amount
definitions: Overall current period amount refers to the actual value of a specific indicator during the current statistical or analytical period. It is a fundamental concept in data analysis and can be calculated using the base period amount combined with the growth amount or growth rate.

name: Overall Growth Rate
definitions: Overall Growth Rate refers to the proportional increase in quantity or value over a specified period, serving as a fundamental composite metric for measuring the magnitude of change in scale or level, widely applied in financial, economic, and business analysis.

name: Overall Labor Productivity
definitions: Overall labor productivity measures the ratio of labor output (such as total output value or GDP) created by all employees in a country, region, sector, or enterprise over a specific period (typically one year) to the corresponding labor input (such as average annual number of employees or total labor hours), used to evaluate the overall input-output efficiency of the labor factor.

name: Overall Liquidity Ratio
definitions: The overall liquidity ratio measures an institution’s capacity to meet outstanding liabilities using assets on hand. It is calculated as total assets divided by net liabilities (total liabilities minus conditional reserves) and is commonly used in solvency assessment for insurers and financial institutions.

name: Overall Ratio
definitions: Overall ratio is a type of financial analysis metric, calculated by dividing the amount of a specific item in the financial statements by a relevant total base amount and multiplying by 100%, used to reflect the composition or proportion of that item within the total.

name: Overall Recorded Amount
definitions: Overall Recorded Amount refers to the total book value or aggregate amount recorded for a specific account, transaction category, or financial statement item during financial auditing or analysis. It serves as the base figure for calculating financial metrics such as misstatement rates and composition ratios.

name: Overcapitalization
definitions: Overcapitalization occurs when a company's capital employed exceeds the capitalized value of its maintainable earnings at the required rate of return, resulting in inadequate returns on capital and potential impairment of shareholder value. The capitalized value (fairly capitalized capital) is commonly estimated as earnings divided by the required rate of return.

name: Overcollateralization (OC)
definitions: Overcollateralization (OC) is a credit enhancement technique in which the value of pledged collateral exceeds the outstanding exposure. The Overcollateralization Ratio, also called the collateralization or collateral coverage ratio, measures the extent of coverage by comparing collateral value to loan value; a ratio greater than 1 indicates overcollateralization, while a ratio less than 1 indicates undercollateralization. It is widely used in lending, structured finance, and securitizations to assess credit protection and resilience against losses.

Overcollateralization is a credit enhancement technique in which the value of pledged collateral exceeds the outstanding loan or tranche to provide a loss-absorbing buffer. The required collateral value can be computed as the loan value multiplied by one plus the overcollateralization percentage.

name: Overextension
definitions: Overextension is a condition in which an individual or corporation assumes a debt burden that is unsustainably high relative to income, typically indicated by a debt service ratio at or above a defined threshold (here, one-third of net income). It signals elevated credit risk and potential stress on liquidity and repayment capacity.

name: Overfunded Pension Plan
definitions: An overfunded pension plan is a defined benefit plan whose fair value of plan assets exceeds its pension obligations (liabilities). The condition is assessed by the funded ratio, calculated as total plan assets divided by total plan liabilities and expressed as a percentage; a funded ratio greater than 100% indicates an overfunded plan, around 100% indicates fully funded, and less than 100% indicates underfunded.

name: Overhang
definitions: Overhang is a dilution metric that measures the potential future shareholder dilution from stock-based compensation plans. It is calculated as the total of granted stock options and authorized but unissued stock options relative to total shares outstanding, expressed as a percentage. Companies and investors use it to assess equity compensation impact and dilution risk.

name: Overhead Allocation Rate
definitions: The overhead allocation rate is a calculated ratio used to allocate indirect costs (such as manufacturing overhead), representing the amount of indirect cost to be borne per unit of allocation base (e.g., labor hours, machine hours, direct labor cost, etc.). Its core calculation formula is the total amount of indirect costs to be allocated divided by the total allocation base of all allocation objects.

name: Overhead Rate
definitions: The overhead rate is a predetermined allocation rate used to distribute total indirect costs to specific cost objects (such as products or projects). It is typically established based on historical data, budgets, or industry standards and serves as a key calculation parameter in cost accounting and management accounting.

Overhead rate is the ratio used in cost and managerial accounting to allocate total indirect (overhead) costs to cost objects. It expresses indirect costs per unit of an allocation base (such as direct labor hours, machine hours, or direct labor cost) and is applied to assign overhead to products, services, or departments.

name: Overhead Ratio
definitions: The overhead ratio measures a bank’s noninterest expenses relative to its average assets, indicating the institution’s cost efficiency in managing operating expenses.

The overhead ratio measures the proportion of operating expenses to income, here defined as operating expenses divided by the sum of taxable interest income and operating income. It evaluates cost efficiency in running the business, with a lower ratio indicating better control of overhead relative to income, commonly used in financial institutions and corporate performance analysis.

name: Overhead to be Allocated
definitions: Overhead to be allocated refers to the total amount of indirect costs that need to be apportioned to various cost objects (such as products, projects, or departments) according to specific allocation bases during the cost accounting process. It is typically aggregated from multiple common expenses that cannot be directly attributed to specific cost objects (such as management salaries, office expenses, utilities, depreciation, etc.) and serves as the basis for calculating the overhead allocation rate.

name: Overleveraged
definitions: Overleveraged refers to a condition in which a company has an excessive amount of debt relative to its equity and earnings capacity, elevating refinancing, liquidity, and default risks. A primary indicator is the Debt-to-Equity Ratio, which compares total debt to shareholders’ equity; higher values signal greater financial leverage and potential overleveraging.

name: Overnight Index Swap
definitions: An Overnight Index Swap (OIS) is an interest rate swap where the floating leg is linked to a compounded overnight rate over the accrual period, while the fixed leg pays a predetermined rate. The benefit calculated here represents the incremental gain from compounding at the overnight index rate over the swap horizon relative to the initial one-day accrual (adjusted for weekend conventions), using a 360-day money market day-count convention.

name: Oversold
definitions: Oversold refers to a market condition in which an asset has experienced sustained selling pressure, driving its price lower and momentum indicators (commonly the Relative Strength Index, RSI) to levels that suggest the decline may be overextended. A typical technical benchmark flags oversold when RSI falls below a predefined threshold (e.g., 30), signaling potential mean reversion risk but not guaranteeing a price rebound.

name: Overtime Pay
definitions: Overtime pay is the portion of wage expense compensated at a premium rate for hours worked beyond the standard workweek (commonly 40 hours). It represents incremental labor cost recognized when employees exceed standard hours under statutory or company policy.

name: Overwriting Yield
definitions: Overwriting yield measures the combined income rate generated by a dividend-paying stock when call options are written against the position (covered call). It is calculated as the sum of the stock's dividend yield and the option premium yield over the same period, typically expressed as a fraction.

name: Own Price of a Good
definitions: The own price of a good refers to the monetary amount a consumer must pay to purchase one unit of the good, serving as a direct factor influencing consumer purchasing decisions and market demand.

name: Owner Earnings Run Rate
definitions: Owner earnings run rate is an extrapolated measure that annualizes or scales recent owner earnings over a chosen forecast horizon, assuming consistent performance. It estimates future owner-oriented cash generation based on observed periods and is useful for forward-looking valuation and budgeting, but it may be unreliable for highly seasonal or volatile businesses.

Owner earnings run rate estimates the sustainable cash flow available to equity owners by adjusting reported earnings for non-cash expenses, required maintenance capital expenditures, and changes in working capital, aligning with Warren Buffett's approach to measure true owner cash generation.

name: Owner's Equity Translated into Renminbi
definitions: Owner's Equity Translated into Renminbi refers to the process, when an enterprise prepares consolidated financial statements or translates foreign currency financial statements, of converting owner's equity items denominated in foreign currency (such as paid-in capital, capital reserve, surplus reserve, and undistributed profits) into amounts denominated in Renminbi, in accordance with specific accounting standards (such as China's Accounting Standards for Business Enterprises) and exchange rates (such as the spot exchange rate on the balance sheet date, historical exchange rates, etc.). This process is a crucial component of foreign currency financial statement translation, and its results affect the balance of the translated statements and the calculation of translation differences.

name: Owners' Equity
definitions: Owners' equity refers to the residual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities, representing the owners' claim on the net assets. It reflects the financial position and operating results of an enterprise at a specific date, also known as shareholders' equity or net assets.

name: P/E 10 Ratio
definitions: The P/E 10 Ratio, also known as the CAPE or Shiller P/E, measures equity market valuation by dividing the current index level by the average of inflation-adjusted earnings per share (EPS) over the past 10 years. It smooths short-term earnings volatility and uses CPI-based adjustments to express historical EPS in current-year dollars.

name: PDCA Cycle
definitions: The PDCA Cycle is an iterative four-stage management method widely used in quality management and process improvement. It drives continuous improvement and optimization of work or projects through the cyclical repetition of the four stages: Plan, Do, Check, and Act.

name: Paasche Price Index
definitions: The Paasche Price Index is a price index calculated using the quantities of the reporting period (current period) as weights, used to measure the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services from the base period to the reporting period. It reflects the impact of price changes on total cost or total expenditure under the current consumption or production structure.

name: Packaging Costs
definitions: Packaging costs refer to all expenditures related to packaging materials incurred by an enterprise during the production, sales, or transportation of products, for the purposes of protection, decoration, storage, transportation, and sales facilitation. These expenditures typically include the procurement cost of packaging materials, labor costs for packaging operations, and related indirect expenses.

name: Paid-Up Capital
definitions: Paid-up capital is the amount of equity that shareholders have actually contributed to the company in exchange for issued shares. It equals the sum of the par (nominal) value of issued shares and the share premium (additional paid-in capital) received over par, and is presented within shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.

name: Paid-in Capital
definitions: Paid-in capital refers to the total amount of capital actually received from shareholders, reflecting the funds that shareholders have actually contributed. It represents the paid-up portion of the company's registered capital and is a significant component of shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.

name: Paid-in Capital Eligible Portion
definitions: The Paid-in Capital Eligible Portion refers to the capital actually contributed by shareholders to the enterprise and already credited to the account. This portion of capital forms the foundation of the enterprise's owner's equity, reflects the actual capital contribution by shareholders, and serves as a crucial component in calculating regulatory capital such as Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1).

name: Paid-in Capital at Beginning of Year
definitions: Paid-in capital at the beginning of the year refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed by shareholders to the enterprise at the start of a fiscal year (typically January 1st), in accordance with laws or the company's articles of association. It includes various forms of contributions such as cash, physical assets, intellectual property rights, and land use rights. It is a point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, reflecting the enterprise's capital base at the beginning of the year.

name: Paid-in Capital at End of First Quarter
definitions: Paid-in capital at the end of the first quarter refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and received by shareholders or investors as of the close of the first quarter (typically January 1 to March 31), reflecting the status of registered capital actually paid up by the company at the end of the first quarter.

name: Paid-in Capital at End of Q2
definitions: Paid-in capital at the end of the second quarter refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and received by all investors as of the close of the second quarter (typically April 1 to June 30), reflecting the status of registered capital actually paid up at the mid-year point.

name: Paid-in Capital at Period End
definitions: Paid-in capital at period end refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed by all shareholders and recorded in the accounts at the end of an accounting period. It is a core component of owners' equity. Its value is calculated from the opening balance, additions during the period, and reductions during the period, reflecting the final outcome of shareholders' actual investment in the enterprise.

name: Paid-in Registered Capital Ratio
definitions: The Paid-in Registered Capital Ratio refers to the proportion of a new shareholder's capital contribution to the company's total capital after capital increase (or company valuation) following an equity investment through capital increase. It is a key intermediate variable for calculating accounting items such as subsidiary capital surplus.

name: Pair Trade Profit (Long-Short Equity)
definitions: Pair trade profit in long-short equity is the net profit or loss from concurrently holding a long position in one stock and a short position in another, computed as the sum of the long-leg gain and the short-leg gain. The measure typically assumes simultaneous closure of both legs and excludes transaction costs, financing charges, and taxes.

name: Paired t-Statistic
definitions: The paired t-statistic measures the standardized mean difference between two related samples (matched pairs or repeated measures). In financial and accounting analysis, it is used to test whether pre- and post-event metrics (e.g., returns, costs, or efficiency measures) differ significantly, assuming normally distributed paired differences and independence across pairs.

name: Par Value
definitions: Par value is the stated face value of a bond that is repaid to the holder at maturity. It serves as the benchmark for assessing whether a bond is trading at par, at a premium, or at a discount by comparing the bond's current market value to its par value.

name: Par Value Per Share
definitions: Par value per share refers to the legal price per share set in the company's articles of association when a joint-stock company issues shares, usually denominated in yuan/share. It represents the amount of legal capital corresponding to each share and serves as the basis for share issuance and accounting. In China's A-share market, the par value per share for the vast majority of stocks is fixed at 1 RMB, with exceptions for individual companies (such as Zijin Mining).

name: Par Value of Preferred Stock
definitions: Par value of preferred stock refers to the nominal value per share explicitly stated on the stock certificate or in the company's articles of incorporation at the time of issuance. It serves as the basis for calculating financial data such as preferred stock dividends and share capital, and is itself a fixed original value, not derived through a formula.

name: Par Value of Stock
definitions: Par value of stock is the legal amount explicitly stated on the face of a stock certificate when issued by a joint-stock company, denominated in 'yuan per share'. It is the legal face value stipulated in the company's articles of association or determined at issuance, serving as the basis for calculating share capital and does not represent the actual market value of the stock.

name: Parabolic SAR (Stop and Reverse) Indicator
definitions: Parabolic SAR (Stop and Reverse) is a trend-following technical indicator that plots a trailing price level acting as dynamic support or resistance to indicate trend direction and potential reversals. The SAR for each period is derived from the prior SAR, the Acceleration Factor (AF), and the Extreme Point (EP)—defined as the highest high in a rising trend or the lowest low in a falling trend. AF typically starts at 0.02 and increases by 0.02 with each new extreme point, capped at 0.20.

name: Parent Company Currency Investment
definitions: Parent company currency investment refers to the investment made by a parent company in the form of cash, bank deposits, or other monetary funds to subsidiaries or affiliated companies. Such investments typically involve conversions between different currencies, requiring consideration of exchange rate fluctuations in accounting treatment.

name: Parent Company Net Profit
definitions: Parent company net profit refers to the final operating result generated by the parent company itself (excluding its subsidiaries) during a specific accounting period through operating activities, investment activities, and financing activities, i.e., the net amount after deducting all costs, expenses, and taxes from revenue. It reflects the profitability of the parent company as an independent legal entity.

name: Parent Company's Shareholding Ratio in Subsidiary
definitions: The parent company's shareholding ratio in a subsidiary refers to the percentage of shares or equity held by the parent company in the subsidiary, either directly or indirectly. This ratio is a key indicator for measuring the parent company's degree of control and financial influence over the subsidiary. Typically, a shareholding exceeding 50% constitutes control and requires consolidated financial statements.

name: Pareto Analysis
definitions: Pareto analysis is a prioritization technique that ranks causes or cost drivers by their frequency or impact to identify the vital few that account for the majority of outcomes (80/20 rule), supporting resource allocation, cost control, and process improvement in managerial accounting.

name: Parity Price
definitions: Parity price refers to the no-arbitrage forward exchange rate implied by interest rate parity, calculated by adjusting the spot exchange rate for the differential between foreign and domestic interest rates. It represents the forward price at which covered interest arbitrage yields no profit.

Parity price (conversion parity price) is the implied per-share price of the underlying common stock derived by dividing the market price of a convertible bond by its conversion ratio. It represents the break-even stock price at which converting the bond into equity yields the same value as holding the bond, aiding investors in conversion decisions and relative value assessment.

Parity price (put-call parity) is the no-arbitrage relationship between European call and put options on a non-dividend-paying underlying, stating that the call price plus the present value of the strike equals the put price plus the underlying price. This relationship is used to verify pricing consistency, identify arbitrage opportunities, and compute the implied parity price of one instrument given the others.

name: Partial Current Expenditure Amount
definitions: Partial current expenditure amount refers to the amount of cash outflow or resource consumption incurred by an enterprise or project during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year) that is part of current operations or investment activities. It is typically used for comparative analysis with base period data.

name: Partial Current Period Amount
definitions: Partial current period amount refers to the value of a specific component in the current period, calculated based on the base period amount and its corresponding growth amount or growth rate. It is a key metric used in financial forecasting, budgeting, and trend analysis to measure the growth of specific items.

name: Partial Expenditure Growth Rate
definitions: The Partial Expenditure Growth Rate is an indicator that measures the growth and change of a specific expenditure item (partial) over a certain period (e.g., comparing the current period with the previous period), reflecting the trend and speed of change in that partial expenditure.

name: Partial Growth Rate
definitions: Partial growth rate is a ratio that measures the relative change of a specific financial or economic indicator between two consecutive periods, used to analyze the growth or decline trend of that indicator.

name: Participating Preferred Dividend per Share
definitions: Participating preferred dividend per share is the total dividend allocated to a participating preferred share, consisting of the fixed preferred dividend rate plus an additional participation component tied to the dividend rate paid on common shares. If the common dividend rate exceeds the preferred dividend rate, the excess is added; otherwise, the participation component is zero. This measure reflects the contractual preference and participation rights of participating preferred stock.

name: Participating Preferred Liquidation Proceeds
definitions: Participating preferred liquidation proceeds represent the total distribution due to participating preferred shareholders in a liquidation event. It includes the return of their stated preferred equity (liquidation preference) plus a pro rata share of the remaining proceeds based on the participating preferred equity's percentage of the capital structure.

name: Participation Rate
definitions: The labor force participation rate measures the share of the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over that is either employed or actively seeking work, indicating the degree of workforce engagement in the economy.

name: Pattern Day Trader
definitions: A Pattern Day Trader (PDT) is a regulatory classification (commonly under U.S. FINRA/SEC rules) applied to a customer account that executes four or more day trades within five business days and where day trades exceed a specified proportion of total trades (commonly more than 6%). Accounts designated as PDT are subject to specific margin and equity requirements and increased supervisory oversight.

name: Pattern Day Trader Minimum Equity Compliance Margin
definitions: The Pattern Day Trader Minimum Equity Compliance Margin measures the difference between an account's equity and the regulatory minimum equity requirement (commonly $25,000) for pattern day traders. A non-negative margin indicates the account meets the minimum equity requirement and maintains PDT compliance.

name: Payback Period
definitions: The payback period refers to the time required for an investment project from the initial capital outlay until the cumulative net cash inflows equal the original investment amount, used to measure investment liquidity.

The payback period is the length of time required for an investment to generate cash inflows sufficient to recover the initial cash outlay, serving as a simple risk-assessment metric in capital budgeting.

Payback period is the length of time required for cumulative cash inflows from an investment to recover the initial investment outlay, typically expressed in years; it is a simple liquidity-focused metric that does not incorporate the time value of money or post-payback cash flows.

name: Payment
definitions: Payment refers to the act by which one party (such as an individual or company) delivers an item of value (such as currency or its equivalent) to another party in exchange for goods or services provided, to fulfill a legal obligation, or to achieve a charitable purpose.

name: Payment Probability
definitions: Payment probability refers to the likelihood or expected rate at which a debt or obligation (such as pension liabilities) will be actually paid in the future under specific conditions. It is commonly used to assess the expected present value of liabilities, particularly when considering time value and uncertainty.

name: Payment Timing Types
definitions: Payment timing types refer to the classification based on the timing of payment or receipt (such as beginning of period, end of period, lump-sum payment, installment payment, etc.) in financial management and time value of money calculations. They are used to distinguish cash flows occurring at different times and form the basis for time value of money calculations such as present value and future value.

name: Payment Type
definitions: Payment type refers to the specific method or channel used to complete fund transfers or value exchanges in economic activities, such as cash, bank transfers, electronic payments, etc. It is a fundamental business attribute describing how transactions are settled.

name: Payment of Accounts Payable from Prior Periods in Current Period
definitions: Payment of accounts payable from prior periods in the current period refers to the actual cash payment made by an enterprise during the current accounting period to settle debts owed to suppliers that were incurred and recognized in previous accounting periods. This cash outflow reflects the settlement of liabilities arising from historical purchases or services received.

name: Payment of Notes Payable from Prior Period in Current Period
definitions: Payment of notes payable from prior period in the current period refers to the actual payment or settlement by an enterprise during the current accounting period of funds for commercial drafts (such as bank acceptance drafts or trade acceptance drafts) that were issued or accepted in previous accounting periods but had not yet matured. This constitutes a cash outflow activity for the enterprise and reflects its settlement of prior period debts.

name: Payout
definitions: Payout refers to the cash amount disbursed from an annuity or investment account on a periodic basis. It can be derived from the annual payout, which is the product of the account balance and the annual payout rate, and then allocated across the payment frequency to determine the per-period payment.

name: Payout Ratio
definitions: Payout ratio measures the proportion of a company's net income distributed to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. A higher payout ratio often indicates a mature firm prioritizing shareholder returns, while a lower ratio may reflect a growth-oriented capital allocation strategy.

The payout ratio measures the proportion of a company's net income distributed to shareholders as cash dividends, typically expressed as a percentage. It indicates dividend policy, sustainability, and the balance between returning profits to shareholders versus retaining earnings for growth. A ratio exceeding 100% suggests dividends exceed current earnings.

name: Payroll Tax
definitions: Payroll tax is a statutory levy on earned income that funds Social Security and Medicare. Employees pay the employee portion of FICA taxes, while self-employed individuals pay the combined employee and employer portions as self-employment tax. This simplified calculation excludes the Social Security wage base cap and the additional Medicare surtax thresholds.

name: Peak Period Total Transportation Cost
definitions: Peak Period Total Transportation Cost refers to the aggregate sum of all actual costs incurred by an enterprise to complete transportation activities during a specific business cycle (e.g., a peak transportation period). It typically serves as the foundational raw data for cost decomposition (e.g., the high-low method) or cost analysis and can be obtained directly from accounting records.

name: Peak Price
definitions: Peak price refers to a derived financial metric calculated through statistical methods on historical price data (such as daily, monthly, or annual prices) to identify or measure its extreme or highest levels. It is typically measured using maximum value functions or statistical methods based on mean-variance (standard deviation), serving as a crucial reference in risk management, trend analysis, and investment decision-making (e.g., downside percentage calculation), rather than being directly sourced from standard financial statement line items.

name: Peak Transportation Volume
definitions: Peak transportation volume refers to the maximum quantity or scale of goods transported by an enterprise or logistics system during a specific analysis period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a specific operational observation data point, commonly used in cost behavior analysis (e.g., the high-low method), where it forms the high-point data pair with the corresponding transportation cost.

name: Pearson Correlation Coefficient
definitions: The Pearson correlation coefficient is a statistical measure that quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables, ranging from -1 (perfect negative linear relationship) to +1 (perfect positive linear relationship), with 0 indicating no linear relationship.

The Pearson correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. In finance and accounting analytics, it is widely used in trend analysis, factor modeling, and portfolio diversification to quantify co-movement between asset returns or financial metrics, ranging from -1 (perfect negative linear relationship) to +1 (perfect positive linear relationship), with 0 indicating no linear relationship.

name: Penalty Interest Rate
definitions: Penalty interest rate is the adjusted loan interest rate applied when a borrower becomes delinquent or in default, typically calculated by adding a penalty spread to the base interest rate. If the borrower is not delinquent, the interest rate remains at the base rate.

name: Penalty Ratio
definitions: The penalty ratio refers to the percentage of the penalty amount payable due to a party's breach of contract in a contract or financial transaction, relative to the total contract amount, the defaulted portion amount, or the value of the relevant underlying asset. It is used to measure the size of the default cost relative to the transaction scale.

name: Pension Funding Shortfall
definitions: Pension funding shortfall is the amount by which a defined benefit pension plan's projected benefit obligation (PBO) exceeds the fair value of plan assets. A positive shortfall indicates the plan is underfunded, while zero or negative values indicate a fully funded or overfunded plan.

name: Pension Insurance
definitions: Pension insurance is a social security system designed to provide long-term insurance for basic living security to workers after they reach the statutory retirement age or lose their ability to work due to old age. It is typically funded through contributions from individuals, employers, and the state, accumulating to form a pension fund used to pay retirement pensions to insured participants.

name: Pension Insurance Contribution Base
definitions: The pension insurance contribution base refers to the base amount used to calculate the monthly pension insurance premium payable by insured individuals (including enterprise employees, self-employed individuals, etc.). It is typically linked to the insured individual's wage income or the local social average wage, with upper and lower limits set. Multiplying the contribution base by the prescribed contribution rate yields the respective pension insurance premium amounts payable by the employer and the employee.

name: Pension Insurance Contribution Rate
definitions: The pension insurance contribution rate refers to the percentage of the contribution base that employers and employees are respectively required to bear when paying basic pension insurance premiums, as stipulated by national regulations. Typically, the employer contribution rate is approximately 20% of the total employee wages, while the individual employee contribution rate is approximately 8% of their own contribution wage. Specific rates may vary depending on the region and policy adjustments.

name: Pension Liability
definitions: Pension liability is a composite metric calculated based on a series of actuarial assumptions (such as employee service years, salary levels, discount rates, mortality rates, etc.) and the present value of future benefit payment obligations. It reflects an enterprise's present obligation for future pension payments to employees under a defined benefit plan and is not raw data directly taken from accounting books.

name: Pension Plan Funded Status (Percentage)
definitions: Pension Plan Funded Status (Percentage) measures the extent to which a pension plan's fair value of plan assets covers its Projected Benefit Obligation (PBO). A value of 100% indicates a fully funded plan, below 100% indicates an underfunded plan, and above 100% indicates an overfunded plan.

name: Per Capita
definitions: Per capita is a scaling metric that expresses a total economic or financial amount on a per person basis by dividing the aggregate value by the population, commonly used in indicators such as GDP per capita or income per capita to enable comparability across populations.

name: Per Capita Consumption Expenditure
definitions: Per capita consumption expenditure refers to the total monetary expenditure on final consumption per person over a specific period (typically one year), serving as a core composite indicator for measuring the consumption level of residents or specific population groups.

name: Per Capita GDP
definitions: Per Capita GDP measures the average economic output per person by dividing a country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by its total population. It is widely used to compare living standards and economic prosperity across countries and over time.

name: Per Share Value
definitions: Per share value refers to the intrinsic value of each share of stock, typically calculated using other financial metrics (such as company value, number of shares outstanding, etc.). It is a derived composite indicator used to assess the investment value of a stock and is often cited in valuation analyses such as adjusted average price-to-book ratio.

name: Per-Person Household Expense
definitions: Per-person household expense represents the average share of total household expenses attributable to each member, calculated by dividing total household expenses by the number of individuals in the household. It is used for budgeting, cost allocation, and household financial planning.

name: Percentage Change
definitions: Percentage change is a ratio that measures the relative magnitude of change from an old value (base period value) to a new value (current period value), typically expressed as a percentage. A positive value indicates growth, while a negative value indicates decline. It is one of the most fundamental tools in financial analysis, used to quickly understand the trend and degree of change.

Percentage change measures the relative change between an old value and a new value, expressed as a percentage of the old value. It is widely used in financial and economic analysis to track growth rates, inflation, and other time-series movements.

name: Percentage Change in Parameter Value
definitions: Percentage change in parameter value is a composite metric that measures the degree of change in a financial indicator relative to a benchmark value. It is calculated by comparing the analysis item amount with the analysis benchmark amount, and is commonly used in financial analysis, trend comparison, and factor change assessment.

Percentage change in parameter value is an indicator that measures the relative change of a financial or economic parameter between two different points in time or states. It is calculated by dividing the change amount by the base value, and is commonly used in sensitivity analysis, trend analysis, and financial forecasting.

name: Percentage Change in Profit
definitions: Percentage change in profit is a relative metric that measures the growth or decline of a company's profit across different periods. It is typically calculated by dividing the change in profit by the base period profit. It can also be derived from relationships with other financial metrics (such as the rate of change in earnings per share, the degree of operating leverage, etc.) and serves as a crucial foundation for sensitivity analysis (e.g., calculating sensitivity coefficients).

name: Percentage Change in Quantity Demanded
definitions: Percentage change in quantity demanded is an indicator measuring the magnitude of change in the quantity demanded of a good or service relative to its original quantity, typically expressed as a percentage. It is used to analyze the sensitivity of quantity demanded to changes in price, income, or other factors, and serves as the basis for calculating price elasticity of demand.

name: Percentage Change of the Factor
definitions: Percentage change of the factor refers to the magnitude of change in the value of a specific factor (such as sales volume, unit price, cost, etc.) over a given period relative to its original value, typically expressed as a percentage. It is used to measure the degree and rate of change of that factor.

name: Percentage Decline
definitions: Percentage decline is a relative metric that measures the extent of decrease from an initial state to the current state, commonly used to describe the decline proportion of stock prices, asset values, or financial data (such as turnover). Its core concept is to calculate the percentage of the decrease relative to the original value.

Percentage decline measures the proportional decrease in value from an initial amount to a final amount, expressed as a percentage. It is commonly used to assess market downturns or individual security price drops, such as identifying bear market conditions (typically a 20% or greater decline).

name: Percentage Depletion
definitions: Percentage depletion is an accounting and tax method for recognizing depletion expense on natural resource properties by applying a fixed statutory percentage to gross revenue from resource sales, subject to regulatory limits, industry-specific rates, and caps.

name: Percentage Increase
definitions: Percentage increase is an indicator measuring the extent to which a stock, asset, or price rises over a period, typically expressed as a percentage, calculated as (Current Price - Initial Price) / Initial Price × 100%.

name: Percentage Price Change
definitions: Percentage price change is a common metric for measuring the magnitude of price movement of a commodity, service, or asset over a period of time. It is calculated by comparing the new price with the old price and serves as a foundation for analyzing price volatility and calculating price elasticity of demand.

name: Percentage Reporting No Change
definitions: Percentage Reporting No Change is a composite economic survey indicator that refers to the percentage of enterprises or entities reporting no change in business conditions or key metrics in surveys such as the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) or other data surveys. It is calculated through formulas and is used to reflect the stability of economic activity and the distribution of changes, typically serving as a component in the calculation of diffusion indices.

name: Percentage Spread
definitions: Percentage spread measures the bid-ask spread expressed as a percentage of the stock price, serving as an indicator of trading cost and market liquidity.

name: Percentage Variance
definitions: Percentage variance expresses the variance as a percentage of the budgeted value, indicating the magnitude of deviation from expectations and enabling comparability across items or periods.

name: Percentage of Completion
definitions: Percentage of Completion is a composite metric measuring the degree of completion of a project, service, or product. It is typically calculated as the ratio of actual incurred costs, work performed, or value achieved to the estimated total amount, and is widely applied in cost accounting and financial management areas such as the Percentage of Completion (POC) method and the Equivalent Units of Production method.

Percentage of completion is an accounting method primarily used for long-term construction contracts or long-term service contracts, which recognizes current period revenue and expenses based on the progress of contract completion. It reflects the proportion of the project completed at a specific point in time relative to the total project.

name: Percentage of Completion Method
definitions: The percentage-of-completion method recognizes revenue and expenses for long-term contracts proportionally to the project's progress. Under the cost-to-cost approach, the degree of completion is measured by comparing costs incurred to date with the total estimated cost, and this percentage is applied to contract amounts for revenue and expense recognition.

The Percentage of Completion Method is a revenue recognition approach for long-term contracts that recognizes revenue proportionally to the project's progress. Progress is commonly measured using inputs (e.g., cost-to-cost) or outputs (e.g., milestones). The method matches revenue with the degree of completion in each period, ensuring faithful representation of performance under IFRS 15/ASC 606.

name: Percentage of Debt Market Value to Face Value
definitions: The percentage of debt market value to face value refers to the ratio between the trading price of bonds or debt instruments issued by a company in the financial market and their par value (face value), usually expressed as a percentage. It reflects the impact of factors such as market interest rate changes and the company's credit risk on the value of the debt.

name: Percentage of Reported Deterioration
definitions: Percentage of Reported Deterioration refers to the proportion by which a key financial indicator worsens relative to a benchmark value during a financial reporting period, used to quantify the extent of performance decline. It is typically calculated based on fundamental data such as net profit and operating revenue, representing a specific case in variance analysis that focuses on negative changes.

name: Percentage of Reports Showing Improvement
definitions: The Percentage of Reports Showing Improvement is a composite metric used to measure the proportion of improved reports within the total number of reports. It is typically calculated based on the number of reports showing improvement and the total number of reports, expressed as a percentage. This metric is commonly used to assess improvements in auditing, quality control, or management reporting and is referenced in economic indicators such as the Purchasing Managers' Index.

name: Performance Fee
definitions: A performance fee is a compensation charged by an asset manager or hedge fund based on a percentage of profits generated over a period, aligning manager incentives with investor returns and often subject to benchmarks, hurdles, or high-water marks.

A performance fee is compensation paid to an investment manager, commonly in hedge funds, based on a percentage of profits generated over a period. It is often subject to mechanisms such as a high watermark to ensure fees are only charged on new gains beyond the fund’s prior peak net asset value.

name: Performance Fee (Two and Twenty)
definitions: Under the Two and Twenty fee structure, the performance fee is typically 20% of positive gains and is payable only when the fund’s Assets Under Management (AUM) exceed the investor’s high-watermark, ensuring fees are not charged on previously lost capital.

name: Performance Score
definitions: Performance Score is a quantitative performance metric calculated through a weighted average method, integrating evaluation results from multiple dimensions such as Key Performance Indicators, 360-degree assessments, and personal behavior appraisals, used to measure the overall performance of employees or departments.

name: Period Cash Flow
definitions: Period cash flow refers to the net increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents of an enterprise during a specific accounting period. It is a core indicator in the cash flow statement, reflecting the final outcome of cash inflows and outflows generated from operating, investing, and financing activities during that period.

Period cash flow refers to the total net inflow or outflow of cash and cash equivalents generated by a company through operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It reflects the company's ability to generate and utilize cash during that period and is a key indicator for assessing liquidity, financial health, and operating performance.

name: Period Cash Receipts
definitions: Period cash receipts refer to the actual cash received by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as sales of goods and provision of services, during a specific accounting period. It is a core component of cash flows from operating activities in the cash flow statement and reflects the cash collection capability of the enterprise's main business.

name: Period Days
definitions: Period days refer to the number of days used to measure the length of a specific time interval in financial calculations. It typically serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating interest, discounting, turnover rates, etc. Its determination can be directly specified or agreed upon based on specific calendar conventions (e.g., a year calculated as 360 days, 365 days, or actual days).

name: Period Demand
definitions: Period demand refers to the quantity of products, materials, or funds required within each independent time segment, obtained by dividing the total future demand over a specified period into specific time cycles (such as years, quarters, or months) in financial, production, or inventory management.

name: Period Discount Factor
definitions: The period discount factor is a core concept in financial management and financial analysis, used to discount a unit of cash flow at a specific future point in time to its present value. It is a composite indicator whose value is determined jointly by the discount rate and the number of periods, serving as the foundation for pricing and valuation of financial products such as interest rate swaps.

name: Period Expense Ratio
definitions: The Period Expense Ratio is a key financial metric for measuring a company's operational efficiency. It refers to the percentage of total period expenses incurred during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year) relative to the operating revenue for the same period. Period expenses typically include administrative expenses, selling expenses, and financial expenses. These costs are not directly associated with the production of specific products or services but are necessary for maintaining overall business operations. A lower ratio generally indicates stronger expense control capabilities and higher operational efficiency.

name: Period Expenses
definitions: Period expenses refer to costs incurred by an enterprise for organizing and managing production and operating activities. These expenses are not directly associated with the production of specific products, cannot be directly allocated to product costs, occur over time irrespective of changes in production volume, and are entirely borne by the current period's profit and loss. They primarily include administrative expenses, selling expenses, and financial expenses.

name: Period Revenue
definitions: Period revenue refers to the total income earned by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during a specific accounting period (e.g., a quarter or a year). It is a fundamental primary account on the income statement.

name: Period Tax Payable
definitions: Period Tax Payable refers to the amount of income tax that a taxpayer is required to pay to the tax authority for a specific tax period (such as a month, quarter, or year), calculated in accordance with tax laws and regulations. It is typically derived from the taxable income for that period and the applicable tax rate.

name: Period n Return
definitions: Period n return refers to the ratio of the return earned on an investment during a specific nth period (e.g., the nth month, the nth year) to the initial investment cost, used to measure the investment performance for that specific period.

name: Period t
definitions: Period t refers to the specific time interval or number of periods from the present point in time at which a future cash flow occurs in financial and financial calculations. It is commonly used in discounting calculations to determine the present value of future cash flows.

name: Periodic Amortization Expense
definitions: Periodic amortization expense refers to the amount of cost allocated to each accounting period for long-term assets (such as intangible assets and long-term prepaid expenses) or financial assets (such as bond investments), spread over their estimated useful lives or benefit periods according to a specific method.

name: Periodic Annuity Amount
definitions: The periodic annuity amount is the fixed sum paid or received in each period of an annuity cash flow. It can be calculated using financial metrics such as present value, interest rate, and number of periods, and is widely applied in time value analysis scenarios such as loan amortization and pension payments.

name: Periodic Annuity Payment
