It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, indicating demand elasticity for pricing and revenue management decisions.

name: Price Target
definitions: Price target is an analyst’s estimated fair value for a stock based on fundamental inputs. Using the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio method, the price target is calculated by multiplying an appropriate P/E ratio by the company’s earnings for a specified period (e.g., trailing twelve months), serving as a benchmark for valuation and investment decisions.

name: Price Value of a Basis Point
definitions: Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP) is the dollar change in a bond’s price resulting from a 1 basis point (0.01%) change in yield. It quantifies interest rate sensitivity and is calculated as modified duration times the bond’s dirty price times 0.0001.

name: Price Variance
definitions: Price variance refers to the cost difference resulting from the discrepancy between actual price and standard price under standard costing. It is a component of variable cost variance in cost variance analysis and is commonly used in analyzing direct materials, direct labor, and variable manufacturing overhead.

name: Price at the End of the Restriction Period
definitions: Price at the end of the restriction period refers to the market price of a stock at the specific point in time (typically the lock-up expiration date) when the share lock-up period concludes and the relevant shares become freely tradable on the market. This price is a direct market-derived or contractually agreed-upon base figure used for assessing share value or calculating related financial derivatives, rather than a composite value computed through other financial formulas.

name: Price of Complementary Goods
definitions: The price of complementary goods refers to the price of goods that must be used together with another product to satisfy the same consumer need. Examples include cars and gasoline, household appliances and electricity. Generally, the demand for a product moves inversely with the price of its complementary goods; that is, when the price of a complementary good rises, the demand for the product decreases.

name: Price per Square Foot
definitions: Price per square foot is a valuation metric calculated by dividing the total price of an asset by its area in square feet, commonly used in real estate to compare property values on a standardized basis.

name: Price to Free Cash Flow
definitions: Price to Free Cash Flow (P/FCF) is a valuation ratio that compares a company's market capitalization to its free cash flow. It indicates how much investors are willing to pay for each unit of free cash flow and is used to assess equity valuation relative to cash generation capacity. Lower values may suggest undervaluation and higher values may suggest overvaluation, contingent on industry norms and company context.

name: Price to Tangible Book Value (PTBV)
definitions: Price to Tangible Book Value (PTBV) is a valuation ratio that compares a company’s market price per share to its tangible book value per share, indicating how the market values the firm’s tangible net assets. It is particularly relevant for asset-intensive industries where tangible assets comprise a significant portion of total value.

name: Price-Earnings Ratio
definitions: The Price-Earnings (P/E) ratio measures the price investors are willing to pay for each dollar of a company's earnings, serving as a key indicator of market expectations and stock valuation.

The price-earnings (P/E) ratio is a market valuation multiple that compares a company's current stock price to its earnings per share (EPS). It indicates how much investors are willing to pay per unit of earnings and is commonly used to assess whether a stock is overvalued or undervalued relative to peers or historical levels.

name: Price-Weighted Index
definitions: A price-weighted index is a type of stock market index calculated by summing the current market prices of all its constituent stocks and then dividing by a divisor (or adjustment factor). The level of the index is directly dependent on the stock prices of its constituents, with higher-priced stocks exerting a greater influence on the index. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a classic example of a price-weighted index.

name: Price-to-Book Ratio
definitions: The Price-to-Book Ratio is the ratio of a stock's price to the company's book value per share (or net assets), reflecting the market's valuation level of the company's net assets and used to measure whether a stock is overvalued or undervalued.

Price-to-Book (P/B) ratio compares a company's current market price per share to its book value per share, indicating whether a stock is potentially overvalued or undervalued relative to its net asset value.

Price-to-Book (P/B) ratio is a financial valuation metric that compares a company's current market price per share to its book value per share, commonly used to identify potentially undervalued stocks.

name: Price-to-Book Ratio (P/B Ratio)
definitions: The Price-to-Book (P/B) ratio compares a company’s market price per share to its book value per share, indicating how the market values the company’s net assets. A lower P/B may suggest undervaluation relative to the firm’s book value, while a higher P/B may reflect growth expectations or asset-light business models. This implementation uses an adjusted book value per share that excludes intangible assets.

name: Price-to-Book Ratio Multiple
definitions: The Price-to-Book Ratio Multiple is a valuation metric that measures a stock's market value relative to its book value (net assets), reflecting the price multiple investors are willing to pay for each unit of the company's net assets per share.

name: Price-to-Cash Flow Ratio
definitions: The Price-to-Cash Flow (P/CF) ratio measures a company's valuation relative to the cash it generates from operations. It is calculated either on a per-share basis as the market price per share divided by operating cash flow per share, or on a company-wide basis as market capitalization divided by total operating cash flow. The ratio helps assess valuation using cash flows, which are less susceptible to accounting adjustments than earnings.

name: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio
definitions: The Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay per dollar of a company's earnings. It is calculated by dividing the market price per share by the earnings per share (EPS) and is widely used in equity valuation and comparative analysis.

The Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of a company's earnings by comparing the market price per share to earnings per share (EPS). It is a core relative valuation metric used to gauge whether a stock is overvalued or undervalued versus peers or industry benchmarks, and is less meaningful when EPS is zero or negative.

name: Price-to-Earnings Ratio
definitions: The price-to-earnings ratio is the ratio of a stock's market price to its earnings per share, used to assess stock valuation levels. It is a key metric in valuation techniques and comparable company analysis, reflecting the price investors pay per unit of earnings.

The Price-to-Earnings Ratio, commonly referred to as the P/E ratio, is a financial metric that measures a stock's price relative to the company's earnings per share, used to assess the investment value or valuation level of a stock.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is a valuation metric that measures a company's current share price relative to its earnings per share, indicating how much investors are willing to pay per unit of earnings.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay per dollar of a company's earnings. It is a valuation metric used to assess whether a stock is overvalued or undervalued relative to its earnings performance.

The Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio is a valuation metric that compares a company's current stock price to its earnings per share (EPS), indicating how much investors are willing to pay per dollar of earnings and helping assess whether a stock is overvalued or undervalued.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is a valuation metric that compares a company's current share price to its earnings per share (EPS), indicating how much investors are willing to pay per dollar of earnings.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio measures the market's valuation of a company's equity relative to its earnings. It is calculated as Market Capitalization divided by Net Income (equivalently, Price per Share divided by Earnings per Share) and is widely used in relative valuation and market multiple analysis. Interpretation depends on industry norms and economic context; a valid P/E requires positive earnings.

The price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio measures a company's equity valuation by comparing the market price per share to its earnings per share (EPS), indicating how much investors are willing to pay for one unit of current earnings.

name: Price-to-Earnings Ratio (P/E Ratio)
definitions: The Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio is a valuation multiple that measures the market price per share relative to earnings per share (EPS), indicating how much investors are willing to pay for each unit of a company’s earnings. It is widely used to compare valuations across companies, industries, and market indexes, and is meaningful primarily when EPS is positive.

name: Price-to-Earnings Ratio at Issuance
definitions: The Price-to-Earnings Ratio at Issuance refers to the ratio of a company's stock offering price to its earnings per share (typically referring to the EPS of the last full fiscal year prior to issuance) during its initial public offering (IPO). It is a key metric for evaluating the reasonableness of new stock pricing and assessing the company's valuation level.

name: Price-to-NAV Ratio
definitions: The Price-to-NAV Ratio compares a fund's market price to its Net Asset Value (NAV) to indicate whether the fund trades at a premium (ratio > 1) or discount (ratio < 1) relative to its underlying net assets. It is commonly used for ETFs and closed-end funds to assess investor sentiment and potential pricing inefficiencies.

name: Price-to-Rent Ratio
definitions: The price-to-rent ratio measures the relationship between a property's purchase price and its annual rental income. It is calculated as the median home price divided by the median annual rent and is used to assess housing valuation, affordability, and whether buying or renting is more economical in a given market. Higher ratios generally indicate buying may be less favorable relative to renting, while lower ratios suggest potential buying attractiveness.

name: Price-to-Sales (P/S)
definitions: The Price-to-Sales (P/S) ratio is a valuation metric that measures how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of a company's sales. It is calculated by dividing the market value (price) per share by the sales per share, and is commonly used to compare relative valuation across companies, especially in sectors where earnings may be volatile or negative.

name: Price-to-Sales Ratio
definitions: The Price-to-Sales Ratio is a financial ratio used to evaluate stock valuation levels, reflecting the relationship between a stock's market value and the company's revenue. This metric is commonly used to value companies that are not yet profitable or have unstable earnings.

The Price-to-Sales Ratio, commonly referred to as the P/S ratio, is an indicator for evaluating a company's stock valuation level. It is calculated by dividing the company's total market capitalization by its sales revenue, or by dividing the stock price per share by the sales revenue per share. This ratio reflects the price the market pays for each unit of sales revenue.

The price-to-sales (P/S) ratio measures the value the market assigns to each dollar of a company's revenue by dividing market capitalization by total revenue. It is commonly used for assessing relative value, particularly for high-growth companies or those without positive earnings.

name: Price/Earnings to Growth (PEG) Ratio
definitions: The PEG ratio is a valuation metric that adjusts the Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio by the expected earnings growth rate to assess whether a stock’s price is reasonable relative to its growth prospects. Commonly used in GARP (Growth at a Reasonable Price) investing, a PEG near 1 is often interpreted as fair value, while values above or below 1 may indicate overvaluation or undervaluation relative to growth.

name: Price/Earnings-to-Growth (PEG) Ratio
definitions: The Price/Earnings-to-Growth (PEG) ratio measures a stock’s valuation adjusted for its expected earnings growth. It is calculated as the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio divided by the earnings growth rate, helping investors compare companies with different growth prospects. A PEG below 1.0 is often viewed as potentially undervalued, assuming the growth estimate is reliable and positive.

name: Prime Cost
definitions: Prime cost refers to the costs incurred in the production or provision of services that can be directly and clearly attributed to specific products or services, primarily including direct materials and direct labor—original expenditures that can be directly traced to the product. It represents the most fundamental cost data in accounting records and serves as the starting point for subsequent cost calculation and analysis.

name: Prime Rate
definitions: The prime rate, or base lending rate, is an interest rate used by banks, typically representing the rate at which they lend to their most creditworthy customers. This rate serves as a benchmark for various floating-rate financial products, such as adjustable-rate mortgages, credit cards, and home equity lines of credit.

name: Principal
definitions: Principal refers to the original amount of a loan, deposit, or investment before interest is calculated, serving as the basis for determining derived values such as interest and future value in financial calculations.

name: Principal Amount
definitions: Principal amount refers to the original sum of money initially invested or borrowed in financial calculations (such as calculating interest, future value, or present value). It serves as the basis for computing financial metrics like interest and future value, typically functioning as a known input variable rather than a calculated result.

The principal amount refers to the original sum of money initially invested or loaned in a financial transaction or borrowing, excluding any interest, earnings, or additional fees. It serves as the basis for calculating interest and evaluating returns.
Principal amount refers to the total original funds initially invested or lent in an investment or borrowing transaction, serving as the basis for calculating interest, returns, or future value.

name: Principal Component
definitions: Principal components are a small number of new, mutually uncorrelated variables obtained through linear combinations of multiple correlated original variables (indicators) using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). These new variables retain the maximum possible information from the original data and are used to simplify data structure and reduce dimensionality.

name: Principal Present Value
definitions: Principal Present Value refers to the value of the original capital invested at the beginning of an investment or financial calculation at the calculation point in time. When considering the time value of money, it typically refers to the discounted present value of the principal corresponding to a future series of cash flows, serving as the basis for calculating investment returns and future values.

name: Principal Repayment Amount
definitions: The principal repayment amount refers to the portion of the loan principal that a borrower repays in each installment. It is a key component of the total debt repayment, and its calculation depends on the loan principal, interest rate, repayment term, and repayment method (such as equal principal or equal principal and interest). It is a core concept in financial management and financial analysis.

name: Principal Repayment Portion
definitions: In the repayment process of debts such as loans or bonds, the portion of each periodic payment that is used to reduce the original principal amount (i.e., the initial debt amount). It does not include the interest portion.

name: Principal Terminal Value
definitions: Principal terminal value refers to the total value achieved by the initially invested principal at the end of a specific investment period, after appreciation over time (such as through interest, dividends, or capital gains). It reflects the final outcome of the principal after considering the time value of money and investment returns.

name: Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance (PITI)
definitions: PITI is the total monthly mortgage payment comprising principal and interest, plus the monthly portions of property taxes and homeowners insurance. It is used to evaluate housing affordability and underwriting metrics such as the debt-to-income ratio for fixed-rate mortgages.

name: Prior Period Accounting Profit
definitions: Prior period accounting profit refers to the total profit or net profit ultimately realized by an enterprise through operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities in the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It serves as a reference data for comparison when preparing the current period's income statement.

name: Prior Period Amount
definitions: The prior period amount is a benchmark figure directly entered in financial statements (such as the income statement or cash flow statement) for comparison with current period data. It represents the actual amount incurred for the corresponding item in the previous accounting period (e.g., the same period last year or the prior period). It is typically obtained directly from historical financial data by specifying an accounting period (e.g., 'Year-1' or 'Month-1'), rather than being derived through formula calculation.

Prior Period Amount refers to the financial data from the previous reporting period used for comparison with the current period amount in financial statements (such as the income statement). The specific period referenced depends on the type of statement: it typically refers to the previous month's amount in monthly statements, the previous quarter's amount in quarterly statements, and the year-ago period amount in annual statements. Its core function is to serve as a comparative benchmark, aiding in the analysis of trends in a company's financial position.

name: Prior Period Applicable Income Tax Rate
definitions: The prior period applicable income tax rate refers to the statutory corporate income tax rate actually applied to an enterprise's taxable income when calculating the income tax expense for the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter).

name: Prior Period Asset Impairment Loss
definitions: Prior period asset impairment loss refers to the loss recognized by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) due to the recoverable amount of an asset being lower than its carrying value. This loss reflects the decline in the economic value of the asset during the prior period and is deducted as an expense when calculating the total profit for the prior period.

name: Prior Period Cost of Sales
definitions: Prior Period Cost of Sales refers to the total direct costs incurred by an enterprise for its daily business operations, such as selling goods and providing services, during the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year or quarter). It is typically taken directly from the 'Cost of Sales' line item in the income statement of the prior period.

name: Prior Period Current Assets
definitions: Prior period current assets refer to the total amount of current assets presented on a company's balance sheet at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous quarter or fiscal year). It represents the aggregate of assets that the company owned at the end of the prior period and are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle. This is a fundamental data point directly obtained from historical financial statements.

name: Prior Period Current Income Tax
definitions: Prior period current income tax refers to the amount of income tax determined and payable to tax authorities, calculated in accordance with tax laws and regulations for transactions and events that occurred in the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter). It is one of the components used to calculate the prior period income tax expense.

name: Prior Period Current Liabilities
definitions: Prior period current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt that an enterprise is obligated to settle within one normal operating cycle or within one year from the balance sheet date, as recorded at the end of the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous fiscal year or quarter). Its calculation logic is the same as that for current period current liabilities, and it serves as fundamental data for calculating financial metrics such as changes in working capital and increases in liabilities.

name: Prior Period Deferred Tax
definitions: Prior period deferred tax refers to the net combined amount of deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities recognized according to accounting standards at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the prior year or prior quarter). It reflects the tax amounts from temporary differences in the prior period that are expected to affect income tax expense in future periods.

name: Prior Period Deferred Tax Asset
definitions: Prior period deferred tax asset refers to the amount of assets formed at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) due to deductible temporary differences between accounting treatment and tax regulations, which are expected to be used to reduce taxable income in future periods. It reflects the recognition of future tax benefits at the end of the prior period.

name: Prior Period Deferred Tax Liability
definitions: Prior period deferred tax liability refers to the amount of income tax calculated at the applicable tax rate, based on taxable temporary differences between the carrying amount of assets and their tax base at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the prior year or prior quarter), which is expected to be payable to tax authorities in future periods. It reflects the future tax obligation recognized in the previous period's financial statements.

name: Prior Period Dividend
definitions: Prior period dividend refers to the dividend that a company has actually paid or declared to its shareholders during a specific past accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the company's historical profit distribution and serves as an important reference for analyzing the company's dividend policy and forecasting future dividends.

name: Prior Period EBIT
definitions: Prior Period EBIT refers to the earnings before interest and taxes achieved by an enterprise in the previous accounting period, i.e., profit before deducting interest expenses and income tax expenses. It is a fundamental composite indicator in financial analysis used to evaluate business operating performance, financial leverage, and calculate financial ratios such as the EBIT change rate.

name: Prior Period Expenses
definitions: Prior period expenses refer to various costs incurred by an enterprise during the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) for organizing and managing production and operating activities, selling goods, or providing services, which cannot be directly attributed to the cost of a specific product or service. These expenses are generally directly recognized in the profit or loss of the period in which they occur and constitute a significant deduction item in calculating the total profit of the prior period.

name: Prior Period Fair Value Change Gains
definitions: Prior Period Fair Value Change Gains refer to the unrealized gains or losses arising from changes in the fair value of assets measured at fair value (such as trading financial assets, investment properties, etc.) held by an enterprise during the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year or quarter). These gains or losses are included in the total profit of the prior period, reflecting the changes in the book value of assets due to market price fluctuations during that period.

name: Prior Period Income Tax
definitions: Prior period income tax refers to the income tax expense calculated, actually paid, or accrued by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter) in accordance with tax laws and regulations. It is a historical actual amount, serving as fundamental raw data in financial statements, typically used for comparative analysis with current period data.

name: Prior Period Income Tax Expense
definitions: Prior period income tax expense refers to the income tax expense recognized by an enterprise in the previous accounting period, which is related to the total profit of that period. Its calculation logic is consistent with the current period income tax expense and it is an important component in calculating the prior period net profit.

name: Prior Period Indicator Value
definitions: Prior period indicator value refers to the numerical value of a specific financial or business metric from the previous comparable period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) used for comparison with current period data in financial or operational analysis. It serves as the baseline reference data for calculating changes such as growth amount and growth rate.

name: Prior Period Investment Income
definitions: Prior period investment income refers to the net income or return realized by an enterprise from external investment activities (such as purchasing stocks, bonds, funds, or other equity or debt investments) during the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year, quarter, or month).

name: Prior Period Net Income
definitions: Prior period net income refers to the final financial result generated from business operations in the previous accounting period (e.g., previous quarter, previous fiscal year), representing the profit amount after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes. It reflects the operating performance of the enterprise in the prior period.

name: Prior Period Net Operating Assets
definitions: Prior period net operating assets refer to the net value of a company's operating assets minus operating liabilities at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). It represents the net capital scale actually invested and occupied by the company in its operating activities during the prior period and serves as the basis for calculating dynamic indicators such as net investment in net operating assets for the current period.

name: Prior Period Net Profit
definitions: Prior period net profit refers to the net profit achieved by an enterprise in the previous accounting period. It is the historical value of net profit, a composite metric that can be calculated from income statement items, commonly used in financial comparative analysis and metric change calculations (such as change in earnings per common share).

name: Prior Period Non-current Liabilities
definitions: Prior period non-current liabilities refer to the total amount of liabilities with a repayment period exceeding one year or one normal operating cycle that an enterprise bears as of the balance sheet date of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). They are directly sourced from the financial statements of the prior period and serve as fundamental data for financial analysis and comparison.

name: Prior Period Non-operating Expenses
definitions: Prior period non-operating expenses refer to various losses or expenditures incurred by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter) that are not directly related to its daily production and operating activities. These expenses are typically incidental, such as losses from damage or scrapping of fixed assets, charitable donations, fines, extraordinary losses, etc.

name: Prior Period Non-operating Income
definitions: Prior period non-operating income refers to various revenues generated by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) that are not directly related to its daily production and operating activities.

name: Prior Period Operating Current Assets
definitions: Prior Period Operating Current Assets is a composite metric calculated based on prior period financial data, specifically the portion of total current assets excluding trading financial assets, used to measure the level of operating current assets in the prior period.

name: Prior Period Operating Current Liabilities
definitions: Prior period operating current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations that is expected to be repaid within a normal operating cycle (typically within one year), as of the closing date of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). They generally include short-term liability items directly related to core business operations, such as accounts payable, deferred revenue, accrued employee compensation, and taxes payable.

Prior period operating current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations that is expected to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle, as recorded at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the prior fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the extent of the enterprise's reliance on short-term operating funds in the prior period.

name: Prior Period Operating Long-term Liabilities
definitions: Prior period operating long-term liabilities refer to debts with a repayment term exceeding one year that an enterprise bears at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) to support its long-term operating activities. These liabilities are typically related to the core business operations of the enterprise, such as long-term borrowings and bonds payable, but exclude portions due within a short term (usually within one year).

name: Prior Period Operating Revenue Amount
definitions: Prior period operating revenue amount refers to the total revenue earned by an enterprise through its principal operating activities, such as sales of goods and provision of services, during the previous comparable accounting period (e.g., previous month, previous quarter, or previous fiscal year). In the income statement, it is typically presented as the 'prior period amount' column for comparison with the current period amount to analyze revenue trend changes.

name: Prior Period Other Comprehensive Income
definitions: Prior period other comprehensive income refers to the various gains or losses that were directly recorded in the changes of owners' equity but not included in the current period's net profit during the previous accounting period. It reflects changes in asset values or equity adjustments that occurred in the prior period but were not presented in the income statement.

name: Prior Period Other Current Liabilities
definitions: Prior Period Other Current Liabilities refer to various obligations of an enterprise at the balance sheet date of the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter) that are expected to be settled within one year or one normal operating cycle (whichever is longer), and are not separately presented under major current liability items (such as short-term borrowings, accounts payable, etc.).

name: Prior Period Permanent Differences
definitions: Prior period permanent differences refer to differences arising in the previous accounting period (such as the prior year or quarter) due to fundamental discrepancies between accounting standards and tax laws in the recognition of revenues and expenses, resulting in irreconcilable variances between pre-tax accounting profit and taxable income that cannot be reversed or eliminated in future periods. Such differences only affect the income tax expense of the period in which they occur and do not give rise to deferred tax assets or liabilities.

name: Prior Period Preferential Reduction Amount
definitions: The Prior Period Preferential Reduction Amount refers to the amount directly reduced or credited from the tax payable by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) according to applicable tax preferential policies. It reflects the actual scale of tax benefits enjoyed by the enterprise in the prior period and is one of the adjustment items to be considered when calculating the current period's actual tax burden.

name: Prior Period Preferred Stock Dividends
definitions: Prior period preferred stock dividends refer to the compensation distributed to preferred shareholders in the previous accounting period according to the provisions of the preferred stock issuance terms, based on the agreed dividend rate or amount. It is a non-leaf node indicator that must be deducted when calculating the change in earnings per common share.

name: Prior Period Price
definitions: Prior period price typically refers to the historical transaction price or cost of an asset, commodity, or service before a specific point in time or period. In financial analysis, it is often used as a benchmark for evaluating current price movements, calculating returns, or analyzing market trends.

name: Prior Period Reported Amount
definitions: The Prior Period Reported Amount refers to financial data from the previous comparable period used for comparison with current period amounts in financial statements. It is typically not raw data taken directly from the books, but rather derived through retrieval operations on specific accounting items for a designated period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year), fitting the definition of being calculable via formulas from other metrics.

name: Prior Period Reported Improvement Quantity
definitions: Prior Period Reported Improvement Quantity refers to the absolute change calculated by comparing the values of the same indicator in the current period and prior period financial statements, used to measure the degree of improvement in financial or operational performance, and typically serves as the basis for calculating derivative metrics such as the improvement percentage.

name: Prior Period Revenue
definitions: Prior period revenue refers to the total revenue recognized by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as sales of goods and provision of services, during the previous accounting period (e.g., previous month, quarter, or fiscal year). It is historical data directly obtained from the accounting records of the prior period and serves as the foundation for financial comparison and analysis.

Prior period revenue refers to the total operating revenue achieved by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or fiscal year). On the income statement, it is typically used as a comparative benchmark for analyzing changes in current period revenue.

name: Prior Period Sales
definitions: Prior period sales refers to the total revenue amount generated by a company from selling goods or providing services during a specific period preceding the current period (e.g., the previous fiscal year, quarter, or month). It is a fundamental historical financial data point, typically obtained directly from the company's accounting records or financial statements, and is used for comparative analysis with current period data.

name: Prior Period Shareholders' Equity
definitions: Prior period shareholders' equity refers to the total shareholders' equity of an enterprise in the previous accounting period, typically calculated based on balance sheet items using the formula: Shareholders' Equity = Total Assets - Total Liabilities. As a historical value, it is used in financial analysis and ratio calculations, such as the shareholders' equity growth rate, and is categorized as a non-leaf node concept.

name: Prior Period Taxes and Surcharges
definitions: Prior Period Taxes and Surcharges refer to the total amount of various related taxes and fees attributable to business activities, as presented in the income statement for the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter). These taxes and fees typically include Consumption Tax, Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, Education Surcharge, Resource Tax, Property Tax, Urban Land Use Tax, Vehicle and Vessel Tax, Stamp Duty, etc.

name: Prior Period Trading Financial Assets
definitions: Prior period trading financial assets refer to the carrying amount of trading financial assets presented on the balance sheet at the end of the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year or quarter). They reflect the fair value of financial assets (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.) held by the enterprise for short-term trading purposes at the end of the prior period.

name: Prior Period Value
definitions: Prior period value refers to the numerical value from the previous accounting period in financial reports, used for comparative analysis. It typically denotes the amount of line items from the preceding period in statements such as the income statement, which can be obtained or calculated through accounting ledger functions. In financial analysis, it is often used as a benchmark for calculating metrics such as growth rates.

name: Prior Probability
definitions: Prior probability refers to the initial estimated probability of an event occurring, based on prior experience, historical data, logical analysis, or theoretical deduction, before considering any new evidence or data.

name: Prior Year Amount
definitions: In accounting and financial reporting, 'Prior Year Amount' typically refers to the financial data as of the end of the last complete fiscal year. For example, when preparing the current year's income statement, the 'Prior Year Amount' column reflects the operating results for the same period of the previous year, used for year-over-year comparative analysis.

name: Prior Year Credit Sales Amount
definitions: Prior Year Credit Sales Amount refers to the total sales revenue from goods or services achieved through credit sales (i.e., allowing customers deferred payment) within the previous fiscal year. It is typically sourced directly from the company's sales records or income statement and serves as fundamental historical data for analyzing accounts receivable turnover and the effectiveness of credit policies.

name: Prior Year Dividend Per Share
definitions: Prior Year Dividend Per Share is a composite financial metric calculated using the prior fiscal year's financial data, representing the dividend amount received per common share. It reflects the company's dividend distribution level in the previous year and is commonly used in calculations such as the dividend growth rate.

name: Prior Year Operating Current Assets
definitions: Prior Year Operating Current Assets refers to the total amount of current assets used for daily business operations at the end of the previous fiscal year. It is typically calculated by combining operational items such as accounts receivable, inventory, and prepayments, and serves as a key foundational metric for calculating the prior year's operating working capital.

name: Prior Year Operating Current Liabilities
definitions: Prior Year Operating Current Liabilities refer to the debts related to daily business operations that are expected to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle at the end of the previous fiscal year. They are typically calculated by combining balance sheet items such as accounts payable, advances from customers, employee compensation payable, taxes payable, etc., and are a key component in calculating financial metrics like operating working capital.

name: Prior Year Operating Working Capital
definitions: Prior Year Operating Working Capital refers to the balance of operating working capital at the end of the previous accounting year, which is the difference between operating current assets and operating current liabilities. It is a composite metric commonly used in calculating financial analysis indicators such as the increase in operating working capital, reflecting the short-term operating fund status of the enterprise in the prior year.

name: Prior Year Revenue
definitions: Prior year revenue refers to the total revenue amount realized by an enterprise through its ordinary business activities, such as sales of goods, provision of services, and transfer of asset usage rights, during the previous complete fiscal year (typically from January 1 to December 31). It is an important historical data item in financial statements, used for comparative analysis with current year revenue.

name: Prior Year Sales
definitions: Prior year sales refers to the total revenue amount generated by a company from the sale of goods or provision of services during the previous complete fiscal year. It is a fundamental historical business data point that reflects the company's past operational scale and performance level.

Prior year sales refers to the total revenue generated by a company from its ordinary business operations, such as selling goods and providing services, during the previous complete fiscal year. It serves as a critical baseline for assessing historical business scale and calculating financial metrics like sales growth rate.

name: Prior Year Sales Revenue
definitions: Prior year sales revenue refers to the total revenue amount obtained by an enterprise through its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during the previous complete fiscal year. It reflects the company's past operating scale and performance level, serving as important historical data for financial analysis and forecasting.

Prior year sales revenue refers to the total income generated by an enterprise from its ordinary operating activities, such as selling goods, providing services, or transferring the right to use assets, during the last complete fiscal year. It is a key financial metric for measuring the business scale and performance of the enterprise in the previous year.

name: Prior Year Sales Volume
definitions: Prior year sales volume refers to the total quantity of products or services sold by an enterprise through the sale of goods or provision of services during the previous complete fiscal year. It serves as a critical foundational data point for conducting year-over-year sales comparisons, calculating sales growth rates, and performing related analyses.

name: Prior Year Stock Price per Share
definitions: Prior year stock price per share refers to the market price of a listed company's stock at the end of the previous complete fiscal year, typically based on the closing price on the last trading day of that year. It reflects the market's assessment of the company's value at a specific point in time and serves as fundamental data for calculating metrics such as stock returns and growth rates.

name: Private Equity
definitions: Private Equity (PE) refers to equity in non-publicly traded companies that is not issued to the general public but rather to specialized investment funds and limited partnerships, which actively participate in the management and structure of the enterprises. As a financial product, private equity funds utilize private capital to finance long-term investment strategies for illiquid companies, typically involving leveraged buyouts, operational restructuring, and value creation through revenue growth, margin improvement, debt repayment, and multiple expansion.

name: Private Equity Fund
definitions: A private equity fund is a collective investment vehicle used to invest in various equity (and, to a lesser extent, debt) securities according to investment strategies related to private equity. It typically takes the form of a limited partnership with a lifespan of 10 years (often extendable by one to two years), raised and managed by a private equity firm acting as the general partner.

name: Pro Rata
definitions: Pro rata refers to allocating amounts proportionally based on an entity's share of the total, commonly used to distribute costs, dividends, interest, payroll, or benefits according to applicable units relative to total units.

Pro rata refers to the proportional allocation of amounts based on each party's share of a total. It is commonly used for distributing dividends, bonuses, interest, fees, or costs. The pro rata distribution amount equals the product of the pro rata share (expressed as a proportion) and the total quantity of the related item.

Pro rata refers to the proportional allocation of amounts based on a defined ratio or time fraction. In fixed income, pro rata accrued interest is the interest owed to the bond seller for the elapsed portion of the coupon period, calculated proportionally to the number of days lapsed relative to the total days in the period.

name: Probability
definitions: Probability is a numerical measure of the likelihood of a random event occurring, with a value between 0 and 1. A value of 0 indicates the event is impossible, while 1 indicates the event is certain. In the field of finance and accounting, it is often used as a known weight or base data for calculating metrics such as expected rate of return.

name: Probability Corresponding to Each Market Return
definitions: In financial risk and return analysis, 'Probability Corresponding to Each Market Return' refers to the likelihood (i.e., probability) assigned to each possible outcome of market return (or portfolio return) when calculating the expected value, variance, and standard deviation of market returns. It serves as the fundamental data point for constructing the probability distribution of returns and measuring risk (such as standard deviation).

name: Probability Corresponding to the Expected Rate of Return
definitions: In calculating the expected rate of return on an investment, this concept refers to the likelihood of occurrence for each possible rate of return outcome (such as high return, low return, or loss) in the forecast, typically expressed as a percentage or decimal. It serves as the key weighting factor for calculating the weighted average of various possible return scenarios to derive the overall expected value.

name: Probability Density Function
definitions: The probability density function describes the density of the probability distribution of a continuous random variable around various possible value points. Its function value itself is not a probability, but its integral over a certain interval equals the probability that the random variable falls within that interval.

name: Probability Density Function Value
definitions: The probability density function (PDF) value refers to the output value of the probability density function for a continuous random variable corresponding to a specific input value (e.g., x). It describes the relative likelihood of the random variable taking values near that point. It is not a probability itself, but the probability over an interval can be obtained by integrating the PDF over that interval.

name: Probability Density Function of Random Variable X
definitions: The probability density function is a non-negative real-valued function that describes the distribution of a continuous random variable X. It is not a probability itself, but its integral over any interval equals the probability that random variable X falls within that interval.

name: Probability Distribution Function
definitions: The probability distribution function, typically referring to the cumulative distribution function, describes the probability that a random variable takes a value within a specific interval (usually less than or equal to a certain value). It fully characterizes the statistical regularity of the random variable.

name: Probability of Default
definitions: Probability of Default (PD) is a financial term used to describe the likelihood of a default occurring within a specific time frame. It provides an estimate of the possibility that a borrower will fail to fulfill its debt obligations.

name: Probability of Each Scenario
definitions: Probability of each scenario refers to the assignment of a numerical value to each possible future occurrence (or state) of an event in decision analysis, investment evaluation, or risk management, quantifying the likelihood of that scenario occurring. The sum of the probabilities of all possible scenarios equals 1.

name: Probability of Economic Scenarios
definitions: Probability of economic scenarios refers to the numerical estimation of the likelihood of different economic conditions (such as boom, recession, normal, etc.) occurring in the future, used in risk assessment and financial decision-making. These probabilities are fundamental input data, typically directly assigned based on historical statistics, expert judgment, or market expectations, and are used to calculate metrics such as expected return and risk.

name: Probability of Occurrence
definitions: Probability of occurrence is a numerical measure describing the likelihood of a random event happening in the future, with its value ranging between 0 and 1. A value of 0 indicates the event is impossible, while 1 indicates the event is certain. It serves as a fundamental input for risk assessment, financial modeling, and investment decision-making.

Probability of occurrence refers to the likelihood that a specific event or situation will actually happen under given conditions, typically represented by a numerical value between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates impossibility and 1 indicates certainty.

name: Probability of Occurrence of Each State
definitions: The probability of occurrence of each state refers to the measure of likelihood, derived through statistical or model analysis, that a specific event or business condition may occur in the future. It serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as the expected rate of return on assets, and is typically calculated based on historical data, sample statistics, or specific probability distribution models (e.g., binomial distribution).

name: Probability of Occurrence of Scenario i in Year t
definitions: In financial forecasting or risk assessment models, this refers to the likelihood of a specific scenario i (e.g., favorable, average, or poor market conditions) actually occurring in future year t. This probability is typically set directly based on historical statistical data, expert judgment, or model assumptions, and serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating derived metrics such as expected values.

name: Probability of Occurrence of the Return
definitions: In the field of finance and accounting, particularly when assessing investment risk and return, 'Probability of Occurrence of the Return' refers to the likelihood that a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) will achieve a particular level of return in the future under given market or economic conditions. It is one of the fundamental data points required for calculating an asset's expected return and measuring risk (e.g., variance).

name: Probability of Risk Event Occurrence
definitions: Probability of risk event occurrence refers to the likelihood that an adverse or uncertain event will actually occur in the future under specific conditions, and is one of the core elements for measuring risk severity.

name: Probability of the Value
definitions: Probability of the value refers to the likelihood that a random variable takes a specific value or falls within a specific interval, with its value ranging between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates an impossible event and 1 indicates a certain event.

name: Probability of the i-th Scenario
definitions: In probability theory and statistics, 'Probability of the i-th Scenario' refers to the likelihood of the occurrence of a specific i-th scenario or outcome among multiple possible scenarios or outcomes, typically represented by a numerical value between 0 and 1.

name: Proceeds from Disposal of Existing Fixed Assets
definitions: Proceeds from disposal of existing fixed assets refer to the cash income obtained by a company when disposing of its original, no longer used fixed assets (such as through sale, scrapping, or dismantling during renovation or replacement). This income represents a cash inflow item that must be considered when calculating the initial investment of a project or the cost of asset replacement.

name: Proceeds from Sale of Trading Financial Assets
definitions: Proceeds from sale of trading financial assets refer to the actual amount received by an enterprise from the buyer when selling financial assets held for short-term trading purposes (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.). This amount serves as the basis for calculating investment gains or losses arising from the disposal of such assets and typically equals the net amount of fair value at the time of sale minus relevant transaction taxes and fees.

name: Proceeds from Sale of Used Assets
definitions: Proceeds from the sale of used assets refer to the cash or cash equivalents obtained by an enterprise through the sale or disposal of assets such as used fixed assets, second-hand goods, or old properties. In accounting treatment, it is typically recorded as an original inflow and serves as the basis for calculating relevant taxes and fees (such as value-added tax and income tax).

name: Processing Time
definitions: Processing time refers to the time required to complete a specific processing operation for a product or component, serving as essential data for calculating production costs, scheduling production plans, and evaluating production efficiency.

name: Processing Weight
definitions: Processing weight refers to the total weight of raw materials or semi-finished products input for processing at the initial stage of a production or manufacturing process. It serves as fundamental data for calculating yield rates, loss rates, and conducting cost accounting.

name: Procurement
definitions: In the field of finance and accounting, procurement primarily refers to the total price actually paid or payable by an enterprise to acquire materials such as raw materials and goods for production or sales, as well as directly related expenses such as transportation, handling, insurance, and taxes. It forms the basis of the initial cost of inventory and directly impacts subsequent cost of sales and profit.

name: Procurement Cost
definitions: Procurement cost refers to all expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire raw materials, goods, or services, including the direct purchase price paid to obtain inventory as well as incidental costs such as related taxes, transportation, loading/unloading, and insurance. It is a core component of the initial measurement of inventory.

name: Procurement and Storage Fee Rate
definitions: The procurement and storage fee rate is a predetermined percentage rate set by an enterprise to compensate for various expenses incurred during material procurement, inspection, storage, and safekeeping (such as purchasing staff salaries, travel expenses, warehouse rent, and losses). It is typically determined directly based on historical data, industry practices, or contractual agreements and serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating the specific amount of procurement and storage fees.

The Procurement and Storage Fee Rate refers to a ratio used in finance, accounting, and construction cost engineering to calculate the total expenses incurred during the material procurement and storage process. These expenses typically include salaries, benefits, office expenses, travel costs, fixed asset usage fees, and other costs generated by the material supply department in organizing procurement, transportation, inspection, warehousing, and storage. This rate is a crucial component in calculating the actual unit price or budgeted price of materials.

name: Producer Price Index
definitions: The Producer Price Index is an index that measures the trend and degree of changes in the ex-factory prices of industrial enterprises' products. It is an important economic indicator reflecting price changes in the production sector during a specific period and serves as a key basis for calculating the inflation rate.

name: Producer Surplus
definitions: Producer surplus is the difference between the total revenue received from selling goods and the marginal cost of producing those goods, representing the benefit to producers from pricing above marginal cost.

name: Product Actual Labor Hours
definitions: Product actual labor hours refer to the direct labor working time actually consumed in the manufacturing process to produce specific products. It is fundamental data obtained through on-site recording, measurement, or estimation, primarily used to allocate direct labor costs and manufacturing overhead to individual products, serving as a crucial basis for cost accounting.

name: Product Cost
definitions: Product cost refers to the total expenses incurred by an enterprise from the input of raw materials to the completion and warehousing of a specific product throughout the entire production process. These expenses primarily include materials directly used for the product (direct materials), wages of workers directly involved in production (direct labor), and various indirect expenses incurred for organizing and managing production (manufacturing overhead, such as factory rent, equipment depreciation, etc.).

name: Product Output
definitions: Product output refers to the quantity of finished goods produced by an enterprise within a specific accounting period. It serves as a fundamental metric for measuring production scale, calculating costs, conducting break-even analysis, and formulating sales plans.

name: Product Quantity
definitions: Product quantity refers to the specific number of completed or unfinished products obtained through physical methods such as direct counting, weighing, or measurement during the production process. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting, production management, and inventory management.

name: Product Sales Mix Ratio
definitions: Product sales mix ratio refers to the percentage of a specific product's sales revenue within the enterprise's total sales revenue. It serves as key foundational data for measuring product portfolio structure, analyzing revenue source composition, and calculating composite metrics such as the weighted average contribution margin ratio.

name: Product Sales Revenue
definitions: Product sales revenue refers to the total income obtained by an enterprise through the sale of its manufactured or purchased products, serving as one of the core indicators for measuring the scale and performance of business operations. It is typically calculated directly based on the actual sales volume and unit price of the products.

Product sales revenue refers to the total revenue amount obtained by an enterprise from selling a specific product or commodity within a given period. It is typically calculated by multiplying the sales volume of the product by its unit selling price, and serves as a key financial indicator for measuring the product's market performance and contribution.

name: Product Sales Volume
definitions: Product sales volume refers to the specific unit quantity of a particular product sold by an enterprise within a specified period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It serves as fundamental data for calculating sales revenue, analyzing sales performance, and determining market share.

name: Production Capacity
definitions: Production capacity refers to the maximum quantity of a specific product or service that an enterprise's productive fixed assets can produce within a given period under established organizational and technological conditions. It is a key indicator for formulating production plans, making investment decisions, and evaluating operational efficiency.

Production capacity is a predetermined or estimated baseline capacity figure used in management accounting for cost control and variance analysis, typically representing the maximum production capability under ideal or budgeted conditions. It serves as a fundamental parameter, primarily used to calculate metrics such as fixed manufacturing overhead capacity variance.

name: Production Cost
definitions: Production cost refers to the various production expenses incurred by an enterprise for manufacturing products or providing services, which can be directly attributed to specific cost objects, and constitutes the core component of inventory cost.

name: Production Cost of Inventory Goods
definitions: Production cost of inventory goods refers to the total of all expenses incurred by an enterprise during the production process for manufacturing finished products or goods available for sale. It primarily includes directly consumed raw materials (direct materials), compensation for workers directly involved in production (direct labor), and indirect expenses incurred for organizing and managing production (manufacturing overhead). These costs are accumulated and recorded as part of the carrying value of inventory when the finished products are completed and accepted into the warehouse.

name: Production Costs
definitions: Production costs (product costs) are the costs incurred to manufacture goods, comprising direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. These costs are capitalized into inventory and recognized as cost of goods sold when the goods are sold, and exclude period costs such as selling, general, and administrative expenses.

name: Production Costs Incurred in Current Period
definitions: Production costs incurred in the current period refer to the various production expenditures, expressed in monetary terms, that are actually incurred by an enterprise during the current accounting period for producing goods or providing services. They primarily include expenses such as direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead.

name: Production Costs Incurred in the Current Month
definitions: Production costs incurred in the current month refer to the total of all expenses actually incurred by an enterprise within the current accounting month for producing goods or providing services. It is directly aggregated from source documents such as material requisition forms, payroll sheets, and depreciation calculation tables, and serves as the foundational data for subsequent allocation in cost accounting.

name: Production Efficiency
definitions: Production efficiency is a productivity metric that measures the actual output rate relative to the standard output rate, expressed as a percentage. It indicates how effectively a production process utilizes resources to achieve expected performance under normal operating conditions.

name: Production Expenses Incurred in Current Period
definitions: Production expenses incurred in the current period refer to the total of various actual expenditures made by an enterprise during the current accounting period for producing goods or providing services. It reflects the value of resources invested in production activities during the period and serves as an important basis for calculating product costs and evaluating current operational efficiency.

name: Production Preparation Costs
definitions: Production preparation costs refer to the expenses incurred for production preparation activities, such as training maintenance personnel and familiarizing with process flows and equipment performance, before a project or new production line is officially put into operation.

name: Production Quota
definitions: Production quota refers to the standard quantity of qualified products that a worker or work team should complete per unit of time (such as a workday or an hour) under normal technical conditions, reasonable use of production tools, and correct labor organization. It is an important indicator for measuring labor efficiency and production capacity.

name: Production Requirement
definitions: Production requirement refers to the total quantity of raw materials or components required to be consumed within a given period to fulfill a specific production plan. It is a core intermediate variable in production planning and material management, typically calculated based on the planned production output and the material consumption quota per unit product. It serves as the foundation for preparing procurement budgets and determining estimated purchase quantities.

name: Production Subsidy
definitions: Production subsidy refers to economic assistance or financial support provided directly by the government or relevant institutions to enterprises to support specific production activities or industries. It is typically used to reduce production costs, encourage the production of specific goods, or achieve specific socio-economic objectives.

name: Production Tax
definitions: Production tax refers to the collective term for various taxes, surcharges, and fees levied by the government on production units for their production, sales, and business activities, as well as for the use of certain factors of production (such as land, labor, capital) in these activities. It is a primary data item directly generated from production and operating activities and serves as the basis for calculating net production tax.

name: Production Volume
definitions: Production volume refers to the quantity of products actually manufactured and completed by an enterprise or production unit within a specific period, which is available for sale or use. It is the most fundamental raw data in the production process, typically obtained directly through production records, statistical reports, etc., rather than being calculated from other financial or efficiency indicators.

name: Production Worker Wage Allocation Rate
definitions: The production worker wage allocation rate is the ratio used to allocate the total wages of production workers proportionally based on the actual labor hours consumed by various products.

name: Production and Sales Volume Change Rate
definitions: Production and Sales Volume Change Rate is a composite indicator used to measure the degree of change in production volume and sales volume of an enterprise or industry. It is typically calculated by comparing current period data with base period data, serving as a crucial foundational variable for analyzing operating leverage effects.

name: Production or Procurement Cost
definitions: Production or procurement cost refers to all expenditures incurred by an enterprise from the start of production or procurement until the inspection and acceptance of products or goods into inventory. For purchased goods, it primarily includes purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, loading and unloading fees, and insurance premiums. For self-produced products, it mainly comprises direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. It is one of the fundamental components constituting the selling price of goods.

name: Production/Purchase Cost Price
definitions: Production/Purchase Cost Price refers to the direct and fundamental costs incurred by an enterprise for producing or purchasing a single unit of goods, excluding subsequent domestic expenses, freight, insurance, and profit. In trade terms, it serves as the foundational component constituting export prices such as FOB, CFR, and CIF.

name: Productivity
definitions: Productivity is an indicator measuring the efficiency ratio between the input of production factors (such as labor, capital) and the output of goods or services produced. It reflects the effectiveness of resource utilization and serves as a key foundation for evaluating economic or enterprise performance.

name: Products Received into Warehouse
definitions: Products Received into Warehouse refers to the physical quantity of finished goods or merchandise that an enterprise receives and stores in its warehouse within a specific period through means such as procurement or production completion. It is a core data point in inventory management, used to track inventory inflows.

name: Profit
definitions: Profit is the difference between total revenue earned from selling products or providing services and total costs over a specific period, reflecting the operating results of a business.

name: Profit Available for Distribution to Investors
definitions: Profit available for distribution to investors refers to the portion of profit that can actually be distributed to the owners of the enterprise (such as shareholders, partners, etc.) after a series of statutory and internal allocations (such as appropriation to surplus reserves) during a specific accounting period. It is a key stage in the profit distribution process, reflecting the ultimate return that owners can obtain from the enterprise's earnings.

name: Profit Available for Distribution to Shareholders
definitions: Profit available for distribution to shareholders refers to the portion of profit remaining after the company has appropriated necessary retained earnings such as statutory surplus reserve and discretionary surplus reserve. This remaining profit can be used to pay dividends to shareholders (including both preferred and common shareholders) or for other forms of distribution. It reflects the amount of profit, both current and accumulated, that can genuinely be returned to shareholders.

name: Profit Before Tax (PBT)
definitions: Profit before tax (PBT) is the earnings a company generates after operating profit is adjusted for net interest—subtracting interest expense and adding interest income—but before income tax expense. It indicates profitability prior to tax obligations.

name: Profit Change Rate
definitions: Profit change rate is a financial metric that measures the degree of change in a company's profit relative to a base period, commonly used to analyze the impact of operating leverage or financial leverage on profit fluctuations.

name: Profit Distributed to Investors in Current Period
definitions: Profit distributed to investors in the current period refers to the amount of cash dividends determined to be distributed to shareholders (investors) after calculating net profit, appropriating statutory surplus reserves, etc., in accordance with the profit distribution resolution of the board of directors or shareholders' meeting. It is the result of the profit distribution process, representing a decision-based or calculation-based composite metric that depends on distributable profit, distribution policy, and specific resolutions.

name: Profit Distributed to Shareholders
definitions: Profit distributed to shareholders refers to the portion allocated from the company's distributable profits, as resolved by the board of directors, and paid directly to shareholders in forms such as cash. This is the specific outcome of the company's profit distribution action, with its amount determined by corporate decisions rather than calculated through a fixed formula.

name: Profit Function
definitions: The profit function is a key financial function describing a company's profitability, typically referring to total profit or net profit. It is calculated from other financial indicators such as operating profit, non-operating income and expenses, and income tax expense through explicit formulas, serving as a core metric for measuring a company's financial performance over a specific period, rather than being a fundamental raw data point.

name: Profit Margin
definitions: Profit margin is a financial ratio used to measure the percentage of a company's profit relative to its revenue. Expressed as a percentage, it reflects the amount of profit a company earns per dollar of revenue generated.

name: Profit or Loss Value
definitions: Profit or loss value refers to the final numerical figure of profit or loss generated by a company's operating activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It reflects the difference between revenue and costs/expenses and is a core indicator for measuring a company's financial performance.

name: Profit or Loss from Tick Movements
definitions: Profit or loss from tick movements quantifies the monetary outcome resulting from price changes measured in ticks for a traded instrument. It is computed as the product of the number of ticks moved and the tick value (the currency amount per tick), and is widely used by traders in markets with defined tick size and contract specifications to estimate gains or losses.

name: Profit-Sharing Plan
definitions: A profit-sharing plan is an employee compensation arrangement in which a company distributes a portion of its profits to employees. Under the comp-to-comp method, each employee’s allocation is proportional to their compensation relative to the total compensation of all eligible employees, ensuring a fair and formula-driven distribution of profits.

name: Profitability Index
definitions: Profitability Index (PI) is a capital budgeting metric that equals the present value of expected future cash inflows divided by the initial investment. It measures the value created per unit of investment, where PI > 1 indicates an investment that is expected to generate value above its cost.

name: Profitability Ratios
definitions: Profitability ratios are financial metrics used to evaluate a company's ability to generate profit relative to its revenue, operating costs, balance sheet assets, or shareholders' equity. These ratios are essential in fundamental analysis to assess financial performance and efficiency in generating profits from operations and investments.

name: Progress Billings
definitions: Progress billings refer to invoicing a client for a portion of the contract value based on the percentage of completion of a long-term project. It aligns cash collection with project progress, commonly used in construction and other industries with long-duration contracts. The billed amount is typically calculated by multiplying the total contract amount by the verified percentage of completion, subject to contractual terms, retainage, and compliance with agreed measurement of progress.

Progress billings are interim invoices and related accounting entries that recognize revenue and profit based on the percentage of completion for long-term projects. Under the percentage-of-completion approach, realized profit to date is measured as the total expected profit multiplied by the percentage of completion, aiding in timely financial reporting and analysis of project performance.

name: Progressive Tax
definitions: Progressive tax is a taxation system in which the marginal tax rate increases as taxable income rises, resulting in higher-income taxpayers paying a larger proportion of their income in taxes. The total tax liability is computed by applying different marginal rates to successive portions of income defined by tax brackets.

name: Progressive Tax Liability
definitions: Progressive tax liability is the total tax owed under a progressive tax system where tax rates increase as income crosses successive bracket thresholds, ensuring vertical equity by imposing higher effective rates on higher income earners.

name: Project Beta Coefficient
definitions: The project beta coefficient is a measure of the systematic risk or volatility of a project relative to the overall market (typically represented by the market portfolio). It reflects the sensitivity of the project's returns to changes in the overall market returns. A beta coefficient greater than 1 indicates the project's risk is higher than the market average, while a beta less than 1 indicates risk lower than the market average.

name: Project Commissioning Year
definitions: The project commissioning year refers to the year in which an investment project completes construction and officially commences production operations, beginning to generate cash inflows. It marks the starting point of the operational period within the project's calculation period (typically including the construction period and the operational period), signifying the transition of the project from the capital investment phase to the revenue recovery phase.

name: Project Cost of Capital
definitions: Project cost of capital is a composite metric used to evaluate the feasibility of investment projects, typically referring to the discount rate used to discount project cash flows. It is calculated based on the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) or other methods, involving fundamental data such as debt cost, equity cost, and tax rate. It is a key parameter in capital budgeting and investment decision-making.

name: Project Duration
definitions: Project duration refers to the total time length required to complete an engineering project or specific work task, typically calculated from the project commencement date to the date when the project is fully completed and passes acceptance inspection. It is a core metric for measuring progress and efficiency in project management.

name: Project Expected Value
definitions: Project Expected Value is the weighted average of all possible outcomes calculated by their respective probabilities of occurrence in uncertain decision-making, used to measure the anticipated economic value of a project.

name: Project Life
definitions: Project life, also known as the project calculation period, refers to the entire time span from the construction start point to the end of the production and operation phase. It is derived by adding the construction period and the production and operation period, serving as a key parameter for cash flow estimation and analysis in project investment decisions.

name: Project Quantity Growth Rate
definitions: The Project Quantity Growth Rate is an indicator that measures the degree of change in the number of projects over a specific period (e.g., one year, one quarter). It is commonly used to assess the activity level of business expansion, market development, or investment activities. Its core calculation logic is the ratio of the increase in the number of projects in the current period relative to the base period (previous period) to the number of projects in the base period.

name: Project Required Rate of Return
definitions: The project required rate of return refers to the minimum rate of return required by investors or a company for a specific investment project. It is commonly used as the discount rate in capital budgeting to evaluate the net present value of a project. It is a composite metric, typically calculated based on methods such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) or the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC).

name: Project Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate
