It consists of Social Security tax up to the annual wage base, Medicare tax on all net earnings, and an additional Medicare tax on earnings above filing-status-specific thresholds.

name: Self-manufactured Semi-finished Goods
definitions: Self-manufactured semi-finished goods refer to intermediate products that are produced in-house, have undergone partial processing stages, but are not yet finalized as finished goods and require further processing. In accounting, they are classified as a type of inventory, and their cost typically includes raw materials consumed, direct labor, and allocated manufacturing overhead.

name: Self-operated Transportation Cost
definitions: Self-operated transportation cost refers to the expenses incurred by an enterprise when using its own transportation vehicles for goods transportation. It typically consists of basic cost items such as fuel costs, depreciation expenses, and labor costs. As a mixed cost, it includes both fixed and variable cost components. It is a constituent part of total transportation cost and is used in logistics cost analysis and control to account for internal transportation expenditures.

name: Seller's Profit (Wrap-Around Loan)
definitions: Seller's profit in a wrap-around loan is the interest income the seller earns by extending a new loan that encompasses an existing mortgage. The profit arises from interest on the incremental principal financed beyond the existing mortgage and the interest rate spread applied to the existing mortgage balance, reflecting the seller's margin from the wrap-around structure.

name: Selling Expenses
definitions: Selling expenses refer to various direct costs incurred by an enterprise during the process of selling goods and providing services, such as advertising and promotion expenses, sales personnel compensation, travel expenses, business entertainment expenses, transportation costs, exhibition fees, etc. These expenses are directly related to the enterprise's marketing and sales activities, aiming to promote product sales and expand market share.

name: Selling Price
definitions: Selling price refers to the actual transaction amount agreed upon by buyers and sellers for goods, services, or assets when a specific transaction occurs. It serves as fundamental transactional data and is typically used as a given condition for subsequent financial calculations or analyses.

Selling price refers to the actual or expected amount received by the seller for disposing of an asset (such as commodities, stocks, fund shares, etc.) in a transaction. It is the original transaction data and serves as the fundamental input for calculating financial metrics such as profit and return.

Selling price is the amount charged by a company to customers for the sale of products or services. It serves as the basis for revenue recognition and is a key variable in calculating financial metrics such as capital gains and gross profit margin.

Selling price refers to the monetary amount charged by an enterprise or individual to purchasers when selling goods or providing services. It is the monetary representation of the value of goods or services, typically determined based on factors such as cost, expected profit, and market supply and demand.
Selling price refers to the price charged by an enterprise when selling goods to end consumers or downstream buyers, representing the market transaction value of the goods.

name: Selling Price per Unit
definitions: Selling price per unit is the sales price of each unit of product. It is a fundamental element for calculating sales revenue, implementing cost-plus pricing, and conducting cost-volume-profit analysis. In financial management, it is used for pricing decisions and profit planning.

name: Semiannual Compound Interest
definitions: Semiannual compound interest is the interest accrued when interest is compounded twice per year. The compounded interest equals the difference between the future value under semiannual compounding and the original principal, reflecting the time value of money with semiannual compounding frequency.

name: Senkou Span A
definitions: Senkou Span A is a forward-looking component of the Ichimoku Kinko Hyo indicator, calculated as the average of the Tenkan-sen and Kijun-sen, and plotted 26 periods ahead to form one boundary of the Ichimoku cloud for identifying potential future support and resistance areas.

name: Senkou Span B
definitions: Senkou Span B is a component of the Ichimoku Kinko Hyo indicator calculated as the average of the highest high and lowest low over a specified period (typically 52), plotted 26 periods ahead to form one edge of the Ichimoku cloud for identifying future support and resistance areas.

name: Sensitivity Analysis
definitions: Sensitivity analysis is a risk assessment technique in financial modeling that measures how changes in a key input affect a model’s output. It adjusts a base value by specified percentage changes and evaluates the resulting outcomes to gauge robustness and identify critical value drivers.

Sensitivity analysis evaluates how variations in one or more input assumptions (independent variables) affect a target financial metric (dependent variable). In this implementation, the adjusted value is derived by scaling the base value by the percentage change in the independent variable, moderated by a sensitivity factor under a linear response assumption. It is widely used in financial modeling, valuation, capital budgeting, and risk assessment to quantify exposure to input uncertainty and assess the robustness of results.

name: Sensitivity Coefficient
definitions: The sensitivity coefficient is a composite metric used in financial sensitivity analysis, representing the ratio of the percentage change in a target value (e.g., profit) to the percentage change in a specific factor. It measures the sensitivity of the target value to changes in that factor, with a larger absolute value indicating a higher degree of sensitivity.

name: Serial Correlations
definitions: The Durbin-Watson statistic is a regression diagnostic used to detect first-order serial correlation (autocorrelation at lag 1) in regression residuals. It ranges from 0 to 4, where approximately 2 indicates no autocorrelation, values near 0 indicate positive autocorrelation, and values near 4 indicate negative autocorrelation.

name: Series EE Bond Maturity Value
definitions: Series EE Bond maturity value is the future value of the bond at its maturity date, calculated by compounding the initial investment at a fixed annual interest rate with semi-annual compounding over the holding period.

name: Service Fee
definitions: Service fee refers to the remuneration earned by individuals independently engaging in various service activities outside of an employment relationship, such as income from providing consulting, design, performance, video recording, translation, and other services.

name: Service Price
definitions: Service price refers to the direct fee amount charged by an enterprise or individual to a client for providing specific services, as stipulated in contracts or according to market conventions. It is typically determined based on service content, time, percentage, or fixed rates, and serves as the fundamental pricing data in service transactions.

name: Service Revenue
definitions: Service revenue refers to the income recognized by an enterprise from payments received from customers, based on contractual agreements or service completion, during the process of providing labor or services (such as consulting, management, technical services, etc.). It is a significant component of an enterprise's operating revenue and is typically recognized directly upon the provision of services.

name: Service Volume
definitions: Service volume refers to the total sum of the original measurement units of services provided by an enterprise or institution to its customers within a specific period. It serves as fundamental data for measuring the scale of business operations. It is typically quantified in specific units such as number of times, duration, or person-times, rather than being a composite indicator derived from financial calculations.

name: Settlement Cash
definitions: Settlement cash refers to the cash that creditors agree to accept as consideration for full or partial debt repayment during corporate debt restructuring. This cash payment is used to offset or reduce the carrying value of the restructured debt and represents the cash outflow component to be considered when determining the fair value or market value of the restructured debt.

name: Setup Time
definitions: Setup time is a crucial component of standard time, referring to the time consumed by non-direct production activities such as equipment adjustment, tool installation, and material preparation for executing specific tasks or batch production. It is typically estimated based on empirical formulas or functions related to processing parameters (e.g., diameter, length, weight) and is classified as a composite calculation metric.

name: Severance Pay
definitions: Severance pay is compensation provided to an employee upon termination of employment, often determined by years of service and salary level. In jurisdictions or policies where the benefit is set as one month's salary per year of service, severance pay equals the monthly salary multiplied by total years of service. From an accounting perspective, severance obligations are recognized as an expense and a liability when the obligation is incurred under applicable standards.

name: Severity of Risk Event
definitions: Severity of risk event refers to the magnitude or depth of negative consequences caused by an occurred risk event or potential hazardous situation in risk management. It is typically combined with the likelihood of the risk event's occurrence to assess the overall risk level.

name: Share Capital
definitions: Share capital refers to the total funds raised by a company from shareholders through the issuance of shares, representing the permanent investment of shareholders in the company and constituting a significant component of the company's equity capital.

name: Share Change Ratio
definitions: The Share Change Ratio refers to the percentage change in the total number of shares resulting from corporate actions such as new share issuances or share repurchases, measured relative to the total number of shares before the change. It is a key parameter for calculating indicators like the ex-rights/ex-dividends reference price.

name: Share Float Period
definitions: The share float period refers to the specific time frame or status during which shares issued by a company can be freely bought, sold, and transferred on public markets (such as stock exchanges) without restrictions. It serves as the fundamental condition for calculating metrics such as time-weighted average shares outstanding.

name: Share Price
definitions: Share price refers to the real-time trading price of a listed company's stock in the securities market, reflecting the market's valuation of the company and the supply-demand relationship. It serves as fundamental data for calculating financial metrics such as dividend yield.

name: Share Repurchase
definitions: Share repurchase, also known as stock buyback, refers to a company's action of reacquiring its own shares. It serves as an alternative method of returning capital to shareholders, often offering tax advantages compared to dividend distributions, and can enhance earnings per share by reducing the number of shares outstanding.

name: Share Repurchase Cost
definitions: Share repurchase cost refers to the total cash amount actually paid by a listed company to repurchase its own issued shares, including the purchase price of the shares and related direct expenses such as transaction fees and taxes.

name: Share Repurchase Price
definitions: Share repurchase price refers to the actual price paid by a listed company for each share of its outstanding stock repurchased in a share buyback transaction. It is typically based on market price or a specific price set by the company and serves as the core raw data in share repurchase transactions.

name: Share Repurchase Reduces Share Capital
definitions: Share repurchase reduces share capital refers to the financial action where a listed company uses its own funds to buy back a portion of its issued shares from the open market and subsequently cancels these shares, leading to a direct reduction in the company's registered capital (i.e., share capital). This is a method for companies to adjust their capital structure or return cash to shareholders.

name: Shareholder
definitions: A shareholder refers to an individual or legal entity legally registered as the owner of equity shares in a public or private company. Shareholders may be referred to as members of the company, whose legal status is separate from the company itself, and who are generally liable only to the extent of the unpaid amount on their shares, unless otherwise guaranteed.

name: Shareholder Equity Ratio
definitions: The shareholder equity ratio measures the proportion of a company's total assets financed by shareholders' equity. It indicates the firm's capital structure, financial stability, and reliance on equity versus debt financing.

name: Shareholder Value Added (SVA)
definitions: Shareholder Value Added (SVA) measures the value created for shareholders by comparing net operating profit after tax to the cost of capital; a positive SVA indicates operating returns exceed the required return on capital.

name: Shareholders' Equity
definitions: Shareholders' equity refers to the residual portion of a company's total assets after deducting total liabilities, representing the net claim of shareholders on the company's assets. It is a composite metric, typically comprising components such as share capital, capital reserves, surplus reserves, and retained earnings.

Shareholders' equity represents the residual interest in a company's assets after deducting liabilities. It equals total assets minus total liabilities and reflects the company's net worth, comprising paid-in capital and retained earnings. It is reported on the balance sheet and is used to assess financial health, solvency, and value to shareholders.

Shareholders' equity is the residual interest in a company's assets after deducting total liabilities. It represents owners' claims on the business and appears in the equity section of the balance sheet. Positive shareholders' equity indicates that assets exceed liabilities, supporting solvency and financial stability, while negative equity may signal distress or insolvency.

name: Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate
definitions: Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate is a financial metric that measures the growth degree of a company's shareholders' equity over a specific period, usually expressed as a percentage. It reflects the company's ability to expand its net assets through operational accumulation or financing activities, and is used to assess the company's growth potential and financial sustainability. It often serves as the basis for calculating the sustainable growth rate.

name: Shareholding Ratio
definitions: Shareholding ratio refers to the proportion of a shareholder's (or investor's) capital contribution to the total registered capital of a company, used to measure the size of their equity stake in the company.

Shareholding ratio refers to the proportion of a company's total share capital held by a shareholder (or a group of related shareholders), typically used to measure their ownership stake and influence within the company.

name: Shares Outstanding
definitions: Shares outstanding refers to the actual number of common shares circulating in the market during a specific reporting period. The calculation must consider share issuance, repurchases, and their respective time-weighting to reflect the average number of shares during the reporting period, which is used to determine key financial metrics such as earnings per share and net asset value per share.

Shares outstanding refers to the number of common shares actually available for trading in the market, commonly used to calculate financial metrics such as earnings per share and net asset value per share. Depending on the calculation purpose, it can be categorized into basic shares outstanding and weighted average shares outstanding, with the latter incorporating the time-weighting of share count changes during the calculation period.

Shares outstanding typically refers to the total number of a company's issued common shares held by public investors, excluding treasury shares repurchased and held by the company itself. It is fundamental data for a company's capital structure and is usually obtained directly from the company's share register or notes to the financial statements.

Shares outstanding refers to the total number of common shares issued by a company and held by investors (including the public and insiders) at a specific point in time (such as the financial statement date), excluding treasury shares repurchased and held by the company. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating metrics such as market capitalization and earnings per share.

Shares outstanding refers to the total number of shares issued by a publicly listed company that are freely tradable on a stock exchange. It excludes shares that are subject to long-term lock-up or restricted from sale by company management, controlling shareholders, etc.

name: Sharpe Ratio
definitions: In finance, the Sharpe ratio is used to measure the risk-adjusted performance of an investment (such as a security or portfolio) relative to a risk-free asset. Its calculation formula is: the difference between the investment return rate and the risk-free return rate divided by the standard deviation of the investment return rate. This ratio indicates the excess return an investor can obtain per unit of additional risk assumed.

The Sharpe ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure that calculates the excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation) of an investment asset or portfolio, indicating how much additional return an investor receives for each unit of increased risk.

The Sharpe ratio is a risk-adjusted performance metric that measures excess return per unit of total risk. It is calculated as the difference between a portfolio's return and the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of the portfolio's returns, indicating how effectively an investment compensates for the risk taken.

The Sharpe ratio quantifies risk-adjusted performance by measuring the excess return of an investment over the risk-free rate per unit of total risk (volatility), helping compare the efficiency of different portfolios or assets.

The Sharpe ratio is a risk-adjusted performance measure that quantifies excess return per unit of total risk. It is calculated as the investment’s expected return minus the risk-free rate, divided by the standard deviation of returns.

The Sharpe ratio measures the risk-adjusted performance of an investment by comparing its excess return over the risk-free rate to the volatility of its returns. It indicates how much excess return is earned per unit of risk, with higher values signifying more attractive risk-adjusted returns.

The Sharpe Ratio measures risk-adjusted performance by quantifying the excess return earned per unit of total risk, where risk is represented by the standard deviation (volatility) of returns. It compares an investment’s return to a risk-free benchmark to evaluate efficiency in converting risk into return.

name: Shipment Value
definitions: Shipment value refers to the total value of goods or products actually sold and delivered to customers by an enterprise within a specific period. It reflects the direct results of sales activities and serves as fundamental data for business operations and financial analysis.

name: Short Butterfly Spread
definitions: A short butterfly spread is an options strategy that involves selling one lower-strike option, buying two middle-strike options, and selling one upper-strike option, resulting in limited profit potential equal to the net premium received and limited loss potential equal to the difference between strikes minus the premium received.

name: Short Call
definitions: A short call is an options strategy in which an investor writes (sells) a call option and receives a premium, profiting if the underlying asset's price remains at or below the strike price at expiration. The maximum profit is limited to the premium received, while potential losses are theoretically unlimited if the underlying price rises significantly. The net profit or loss per contract equals the premium received minus the option's intrinsic value, multiplied by the contract size.

name: Short Call Net Profit/Loss
definitions: The net profit or loss of a short call option equals its expiration date value plus the option premium.

name: Short Call Option Value at Expiration
definitions: Short call option value at expiration refers to the net income received or payment obligation assumed by the option seller upon expiration due to the potential exercise of the call option. Its value depends on the relationship between the stock market price and the strike price, calculated as the negative of the greater of the difference between the stock market price and the strike price and zero.

name: Short Covering Profit or Loss
definitions: Short covering profit or loss measures the monetary outcome realized when closing a short position by buying back previously shorted shares. A profit occurs if the buy-to-cover price is lower than the original short sale price; a loss occurs if it is higher. This measure typically excludes transaction costs, financing costs, and taxes unless otherwise specified.

name: Short Float Percentage
definitions: Short float percentage measures the proportion of a company’s public float that has been sold short, indicating bearish sentiment and potential short-squeeze risk. It is calculated as shares sold short divided by float shares, expressed as a percentage.

name: Short Interest Percentage
definitions: Short interest percentage measures the proportion of a company's shares outstanding that have been sold short, expressed as a percentage. It indicates the scale of short-selling activity relative to total shares outstanding and is commonly used as a market sentiment indicator.

Short interest percentage measures the proportion of a company's outstanding shares that have been sold short, indicating the degree of bearish sentiment among market participants. It is calculated by dividing shares sold short by total outstanding shares and multiplying by 100; the denominator must be greater than zero.

name: Short Interest Ratio
definitions: The Short Interest Ratio (SIR), also known as Days to Cover, is calculated as total shares sold short divided by the stock's average daily trading volume. It estimates the number of trading days required for short sellers to cover their positions, and a higher SIR can indicate increased short squeeze risk and lower near-term liquidity.

Short interest ratio measures the number of days required for all shorted shares to be covered based on the stock's average daily trading volume. It is used to assess market sentiment, liquidity pressure on short positions, and potential for a short squeeze.

Short Interest Ratio is a market sentiment indicator that measures the number of shares sold short relative to the stock's average daily trading volume. It approximates the number of days it would take short sellers to cover their positions based on typical trading activity, with higher values indicating heavier shorting pressure and potentially greater sensitivity to changes in liquidity or market news.

Short Interest Ratio (Days to Cover) measures how many trading days it would take for short sellers to cover all short positions, given the stock’s average daily trading volume. It is used to assess the potential vulnerability of a stock to a short squeeze and short-interest risk.

name: Short Put
definitions: A short put is an options strategy where the investor writes (sells) a put option, receiving a premium upfront and assuming the obligation to buy the underlying asset at the strike price if exercised. The maximum profit is limited to the premium received, while potential loss increases as the underlying price falls below the strike price, typically scaled by the contract size (commonly 100 shares per contract).

name: Short Put Break-even Price
definitions: The Short Put Break-even Price is the underlying asset price at which a short put position realizes zero profit. It equals the strike price minus the premium received per share. Under a standard equity option contract (100 shares), the premium per share is the total premium divided by 100. This measure excludes transaction costs, taxes, and other fees.

name: Short Put Maximum Loss
definitions: Short put maximum loss is the worst-case loss an option writer can incur on a short put position if the underlying asset's price falls to zero. It equals the cost to purchase the underlying at the strike price for the contract size, minus the premium received.

name: Short Put Option Expiration Value
definitions: The value of a short put option at expiration is equal to the maximum of the difference between the strike price and the stock market price, otherwise zero.

name: Short Put Option Net Profit/Loss
definitions: The net profit/loss of a short put option equals its expiration date value plus the option price.

name: Short Sale
definitions: A short sale is the sale of borrowed securities with the expectation that their price will decline, allowing the seller to repurchase them at a lower price and return them to the lender. To mitigate credit risk, regulators and brokers require margin to be posted; under common rules (e.g., Regulation T in the U.S.), the initial margin requirement is set at 150% of the market value of the securities sold short.

name: Short Sale Profit
definitions: Short sale profit represents the gain or loss realized from closing a short position by repurchasing the borrowed shares at a price different from the original short sale price, multiplied by the number of shares involved.

Short sale profit is the gain realized when securities borrowed and sold short are repurchased (covered) at a lower price than the initial short sale price. It is calculated as the difference between the short sale price and the cover price, multiplied by the number of shares, typically stated before commissions, borrow fees, taxes, and dividends paid on borrowed shares.

name: Short Selling
definitions: Short selling is a trading strategy in which an investor borrows and sells securities with the expectation that their price will decline, allowing repurchase at a lower price to realize a gain. Short sale profit equals the difference between the initial selling price and the repurchase (cover) price, multiplied by the number of shares, excluding transaction costs, borrowing fees, and dividends.

name: Short Selling Profit
definitions: Short selling profit is the gain realized from selling borrowed shares at a higher initial price and repurchasing them at a lower final price, calculated as the price difference multiplied by the number of shares.

name: Short-term Borrowings
definitions: Short-term borrowings refer to various loans obtained by an enterprise from banks or other financial institutions with a repayment period of one year or less. They are a significant source of short-term financing for enterprises and are directly recorded as liability items on the balance sheet.

name: Short-term Borrowings Ending Balance
definitions: Short-term borrowings ending balance refers to the total book value of short-term borrowings that have not been repaid by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the enterprise's short-term liabilities to banks or other financial institutions at a specific point in time.

name: Short-term Borrowings Opening Balance
definitions: Short-term borrowings opening balance refers to the book value of short-term borrowings that have not been repaid at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is typically reflected under the 'Short-term Borrowings' account on the liability side of the balance sheet and serves as important baseline data for calculating changes in borrowings during the period and for cash flow analysis.

name: Short-term Debt
definitions: Short-term debt refers to financial obligations that are due within one year or one operating cycle (whichever is longer). It includes commercial paper, treasury bills, certificates of deposit, and other money market instruments with an original maturity of one year or less.

name: Short-term Debt Investments
definitions: Short-term debt investments refer to debt-based investments held by an enterprise that are expected to mature within one year (or one operating cycle) or are intended to be liquidated within one year, such as short-term government bonds and corporate short-term financing bills, with the objective of earning interest income while maintaining liquidity.

name: Short-term Equity Investment
definitions: Short-term equity investment refers to shares or equity interests in other companies purchased by an enterprise with the intention of obtaining returns through price differences in the short term (typically within one year). Such investments generally do not aim to control or exert significant influence over the investee, and changes in their value are recognized in current period profit or loss.

name: Short-term Growth Rate
definitions: Short-term growth rate is a percentage metric that measures the growth of a company's core financial indicators (such as revenue or profit) in a specific short-term period (typically one accounting period, e.g., a quarter or year) relative to the previous period. It is a key dynamic indicator for assessing short-term operating performance and market performance.

name: Short-term Investments
definitions: Short-term investments refer to investments made by an enterprise to utilize temporarily idle funds, purchasing securities that can be readily converted into cash and are not intended to be held for more than one year (including one year), primarily including various marketable securities such as stocks and bonds.

name: Short-term Treasury Bill Face Value
definitions: Short-term Treasury bill face value refers to the principal amount stated on the bill at issuance (typically for government bonds with maturities of one year or less) and promised by the government to repay to the holder at maturity. It serves as the basis for calculating the issue price, discount rate, and yield of the Treasury bill.

name: Short-term Treasury Bill Yield
definitions: Short-term Treasury bill yield refers to the annualized return an investor can obtain by holding a short-term Treasury bill until its maturity date. It serves as a key benchmark interest rate in the money market and is generally regarded as the risk-free rate. Its calculation methods vary, including bank discount yield, holding period yield, bond equivalent yield, etc., depending on market conventions and calculation purposes.

name: Shrinkage
definitions: Shrinkage refers to the loss of inventory that occurs when the recorded (book) inventory exceeds the actual (physical) inventory on hand, typically due to theft, damage, spoilage, miscounts, or administrative errors. It is used in retail and inventory accounting to assess discrepancies and inform internal controls and loss prevention measures.

name: Shutdown Point
definitions: The shutdown point is the short-run operating threshold at which a firm should cease production because producing an additional unit does not create economic value. Under this decision rule, the firm shuts down when marginal revenue is less than or equal to marginal cost, ignoring fixed costs, indicating that continuing operations would not increase contribution or reduce losses.

name: Simple Interest
definitions: Simple interest is the interest calculated solely on the principal for a specified period at a stated annual rate, commonly used for term deposits when compounding is not applied.

Simple interest is the interest calculated only on the original principal of a loan or investment, without compounding, typically computed as the product of the principal, the annual interest rate, and the time in years.

Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal, not on accumulated interest. Under simple interest, the total accrued amount equals the principal plus interest computed as Principal × Annual Interest Rate × Term in Years. This method is commonly used for short-term loans and investments where interest does not compound.

name: Simple Linear Regression (OLS)
definitions: Simple linear regression (OLS) estimates a linear relationship between one independent variable (X) and a dependent variable (Y) by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, yielding the regression slope (a) and intercept (b) for the line Y = aX + b. In finance and accounting, it is used for beta estimation, factor sensitivity, forecasting, and trend analysis.

name: Simple Moving Average
definitions: A Simple Moving Average (SMA) is the arithmetic mean of a sequence of prices or index values over a specified number of periods. It is used to smooth short-term fluctuations and highlight underlying trends in financial time series for technical analysis and risk monitoring.

Simple Moving Average (SMA) is the arithmetic mean of a specified number of consecutive observations in a time series, commonly applied to security prices to smooth short-term volatility and highlight underlying trends.

name: Simple Moving Average (SMA)
definitions: The Simple Moving Average (SMA) is the arithmetic mean of a specified number of sequential observations (e.g., closing prices) in a time series, used to smooth short-term volatility and highlight underlying trends for technical and quantitative analysis.

The Simple Moving Average (SMA) is a technical analysis indicator that calculates the arithmetic mean of an asset’s prices over a specified number of periods. It smooths short-term fluctuations to help identify the underlying price trend, giving equal weight to each observation within the chosen window.

name: Simple Random Sample
definitions: Simple random sampling is a probability sampling method in which each unit in the population has an equal chance of selection. In financial auditing and analytics, SRS is used to select transactions, accounts, or securities without bias for substantive testing, compliance testing, or estimation, ensuring representative evidence and unbiased inference.

name: Simple Return
definitions: Simple return measures the percentage change in investment value from initial cost to final value without accounting for compounding or time period, reflecting the basic gain or loss on an investment.

Simple return measures the percentage change in an investment's value over a holding period, calculated as the gain or loss relative to the starting price. It does not account for compounding or annualization, and is suitable for quick, non-time-adjusted performance assessments.

name: Simpson's Rule
definitions: Simpson's Rule is a numerical integration method that approximates the value of a definite integral by approximating the integrand with a quadratic parabola. It is commonly used in financial calculations to approximate complex integrals such as the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution.

name: Single Asset Return
definitions: Single asset return refers to the total return an investor obtains from a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) over a given holding period. It typically consists of two components: interest or dividend income received during the holding period, and capital gains (or losses) resulting from price changes in the asset itself.

name: Single Asset Return Rate
definitions: Single asset return rate refers to the total rate of return obtained from an asset over a specific holding period (typically one period, such as a year), usually consisting of two components: interest or dividend income received during the period, and capital gains (or losses) resulting from price changes of the asset itself.

name: Single Investment Return Rate
definitions: The single investment return rate refers to the total rate of return obtained by an investor from an independent investment (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) over a specific period. It typically consists of two components: the return rate from interest or dividend income received during the holding period, and the return rate from asset price changes (capital gains or losses).

name: Single Order Shortage Quantity
definitions: Single order shortage quantity refers to the quantity of goods that cannot be satisfied within one order cycle due to demand exceeding available inventory in an Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model that allows stockouts. It is a key variable for calculating stockout costs, and its value depends on ordering policies, demand levels, and inventory status, typically calculated through probabilistic models or deterministic formulas.

name: Single-Period Return on Assets
definitions: Single-period return on assets is an indicator that measures the total return of an asset over a specific holding period (such as one year or one month). It consists of two components: the interest or dividend income earned during the period, and the capital gain (or loss) resulting from price changes in the asset itself.

name: Single-Trial Success Probability
definitions: Single-trial success probability refers to the likelihood of a specific event (typically termed 'success') occurring in a single independent random trial. It is a numerical value between 0 and 1, commonly used to describe the probability of success per trial in Bernoulli trials or the binomial distribution.

name: Sinking Fund Factor
definitions: The sinking fund factor is a ratio coefficient used to calculate the equal periodic deposit amount required to accumulate a specific future sum (e.g., for debt repayment) by a designated future date. Its value equals the reciprocal of the ordinary annuity future value factor.

The sinking fund factor is a coefficient used in financial management to calculate the equal annual deposit required to repay a future debt or accumulate a fund. It is the reciprocal of the ordinary annuity future value factor, denoted as (A/F,i,n), where i is the interest rate and n is the number of periods.

name: Sinking Fund Payment
definitions: A sinking fund payment refers to the equal periodic payment amount that must be deposited into a sinking fund to retire a specific debt at a specified future date, calculated based on the future debt amount, interest rate, and number of periods. It is a key compound metric in debt repayment planning.

A sinking fund payment is the fixed annual contribution set aside to accumulate sufficient funds to retire a specified amount of debt over a defined period. In this simplified approach, the payment is calculated by evenly distributing the total debt across the number of years, assuming no investment returns, inflation, or changes in economic conditions.

name: Site Preparation and Temporary Facilities Cost
definitions: Site preparation and temporary facilities cost refers to the expenses incurred before the commencement of a construction project, including site leveling, removal and clearance of obstacles to make the construction site ready for work, as well as the costs associated with the construction, maintenance, demolition, and restoration of temporary buildings, structures, and other temporary facilities required to meet construction needs.

name: Skewness
definitions: Pearson's first coefficient of skewness quantifies the asymmetry of a distribution by comparing the mean to the mode and scaling by the standard deviation. Positive values indicate right-skewness (long right tail), while negative values indicate left-skewness (long left tail). In finance, it is used to assess asymmetry in return distributions and risk profiles.

Skewness is a statistical measure of the asymmetry of a return distribution around its mean. Pearson's second coefficient of skewness estimates skewness by comparing the mean and median relative to the standard deviation and is commonly used when the mode is weak or undefined.

name: Slope
definitions: Slope is a measure of the inclination of a line (or the tangent of a curve) relative to the horizontal axis. Mathematically, it is typically defined as the ratio of the change in the vertical coordinate to the change in the horizontal coordinate. In financial and economic analysis, it is commonly used in linear regression models to measure the marginal relationship between variables.

name: Slope (Rate of Change)
definitions: Slope (rate of change) measures the incremental change in a financial metric per unit change in an independent variable (commonly time), and is used in trend analysis, linear forecasting, and sensitivity assessment across financial and managerial accounting applications.

name: Slope of the Demand Curve
definitions: The slope of the demand curve measures the ratio between the change in price and the change in quantity demanded along the curve. It is typically negative, indicating an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: as price increases, quantity demanded decreases, and as price decreases, quantity demanded increases.

name: Social Security
definitions: Social security is a system established by the state through legislation, funded by mandatory social insurance contributions, which provides material assistance to workers in circumstances such as old age, illness, work-related injury, unemployment, and childbirth. The contribution amount is calculated based on the contribution base and contribution rate, and it serves as a significant source of funds for government transfer payments.

name: Solvency Ratio
definitions: The solvency ratio measures a company's ability to meet its long-term obligations by comparing cash-flow-like earnings (net income plus non-cash charges such as depreciation and amortization) to total liabilities. Higher values indicate greater long-term debt-paying capacity.

name: Solvency Ratios
definitions: Solvency ratios are financial metrics that measure a company's ability to meet its long-term debt obligations and assess its financial stability and leverage.

name: Sorted Numerical Sequence
definitions: A sorted numerical sequence refers to a new data sequence obtained by rearranging a set of original numerical data according to ascending or descending order rules. It is not a composite indicator calculated through mathematical formulas, but rather a common data processing and presentation method for underlying data, with its results entirely dependent on the values of the original data.

name: Sortino Ratio
definitions: The Sortino Ratio measures the excess return of an investment over a benchmark per unit of downside risk. Unlike the Sharpe Ratio, it penalizes only harmful volatility by using downside deviation. In this implementation, excess return is measured relative to the risk-free rate.

name: Southbound Stock Connect Market Capitalization
definitions: Southbound Stock Connect market capitalization refers to the total market value of all issued shares of Hong Kong-listed companies eligible for the Southbound Stock Connect program. It is calculated by multiplying the total number of the company's issued shares by the current market trading price of the stock, directly reflecting the overall market valuation size of the company.

name: Sovereign Default Compensation Amount
definitions: Sovereign default compensation amount refers to the compensation payment required due to a sovereign state or its institutions failing to fulfill contractual obligations (such as debt repayment). It is typically calculated based on the total amount involved in the default, the agreed penalty rate, and the duration of the default, and serves as a key consideration in the assessment of country risk premium.

name: Spare Parts and Components Cost
definitions: Spare parts and components cost refers to the procurement cost incurred for replacing and repairing equipment, parts, materials, and components, which is calculated and reserved based on a certain percentage of equipment cost or installation engineering cost to maintain the normal operation of production equipment.

name: Special Additional Deductions
definitions: Special Additional Deductions refer to specific itemized amounts stipulated by China's Individual Income Tax Law that taxpayers are permitted to subtract from their comprehensive income when calculating taxable income. These items include social insurance premiums such as basic pension insurance, basic medical insurance, unemployment insurance, and housing provident fund contributions. They serve as crucial raw input data for individual income tax calculation, requiring taxpayers to declare based on their actual circumstances, and cannot be derived through formulas.

Special Additional Deductions are a provision in China's Individual Income Tax system that allows taxpayers to deduct additional specified amounts from their comprehensive income when calculating taxable income, based on their actual specific personal and family expenditures (such as children's education, continuing education, serious illness medical expenses, housing loan interest, housing rent, and elderly support). This aims to reduce taxpayers' burden and enhance the fairness of the tax system.

name: Special Drawing Rights (SDR)
definitions: Special Drawing Rights (SDR) are an international reserve asset created by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The SDR’s value is determined by a weighted basket of major currencies and is used as a unit of account and to supplement member countries’ official reserves. The SDR value in USD is computed by multiplying the fixed currency units in the basket by their respective USD exchange rates and summing the results.

name: Special Payables
definitions: Special payables refer to funds received by an enterprise from the government or other sources, designated for specific or special purposes, typically used for designated engineering projects or capital expenditures, and classified as non-current liabilities of the enterprise.

name: Specific Consumption Tax
definitions: Specific consumption tax is a method of calculating consumption tax based on the sales quantity of taxable consumer goods (such as weight, volume, number of units, etc.) and a predetermined fixed unit tax amount, rather than on the price or sales revenue of the goods. This method is typically applicable to specific commodities such as beer, yellow wine, and refined oil products.

name: Specific Financial Metrics
definitions: Specific financial metrics refer to quantitative standards or ratios used to measure and evaluate a company's financial condition, operating results, and cash flows, serving as core tools for financial analysis.

name: Specific Item Amount
definitions: Specific item amount refers to the monetary value accounted for or recorded for a particular, independent project, account, or cost center in finance, accounting, or project management. It is typically used to reflect specific figures such as investment, cost, revenue, or budget for an individual project, serving as fundamental data for project analysis, budgeting, and financial consolidation.

name: Specific Overhead Costs
definitions: Specific overhead costs refer to the aggregate of various expense items incurred by an enterprise in its production and operating activities that are not directly associated with the production of specific products or provision of services but are necessary for maintaining overall organizational operations. These costs typically cannot be directly attributed to a particular product or service and must be allocated to different cost objects using certain allocation bases (such as labor hours, machine hours, direct costs, etc.).

name: Speed of Sound
definitions: The speed of sound refers to the velocity at which sound propagates through a specific medium (such as air, water, or solids), and its magnitude depends on the properties and state of the medium (such as temperature, density, and pressure). In standard atmospheric pressure and air at 15°C, the speed of sound is approximately 340 meters per second.

name: Spending Amount Threshold
definitions: The spending amount threshold is a composite indicator calculated based on IC card internal parameters, merchant-set transaction limits, and relevant business rules. It is used to control the maximum allowable amount for a single spending transaction and serves as a key parameter in risk management and transaction authorization processes.

name: Spending Variance
definitions: Spending variance is a component of fixed manufacturing overhead cost variance under standard costing. It refers to the difference between the actual fixed manufacturing overhead incurred and the budgeted (or standard) fixed manufacturing overhead, used to measure the budgetary control level of fixed manufacturing overhead.

name: Spot Asset Value
definitions: Spot asset value refers to the value of an asset at the current point in time, calculated by discounting and summing all future expected cash flows generated by the asset using a discount rate that reflects its risk and time value.

name: Spot Exchange Rate on Balance Sheet Date
definitions: The spot exchange rate on the balance sheet date refers to the exchange rate used for immediate conversion between two currencies on the day when an enterprise prepares its balance sheet (i.e., the financial reporting cutoff date). In the translation of foreign currency financial statements, it is typically used to translate monetary items in the balance sheet (such as cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable, etc.) to reflect the true value of these items on the reporting date.

name: Spot Price
definitions: Spot price refers to the transaction price for the immediate delivery and settlement of an underlying asset (such as stocks, commodities, foreign exchange, etc.) at the current moment in financial or commodity markets. It is directly determined by the immediate market supply and demand and represents raw market data reflecting the current value of the asset.

name: Spot Price Volatility
definitions: Spot price volatility refers to the phenomenon where the immediate transaction prices of commodities, securities, or financial assets in the spot market fluctuate upward and downward over time. This fluctuation results from the combined effects of various complex factors such as market supply and demand, macroeconomic conditions, policy adjustments, and unexpected events, and serves as fundamental market observation data.

name: Spot Rate
definitions: The spot rate is the yield to maturity of a zero-coupon security at a given point in time, representing the current market's required annualized yield for a zero-coupon bond of a specific maturity. It is commonly used in bond pricing, cash flow discounting, and the construction of the term structure of interest rates.

name: Spread Betting Position Value
definitions: Position value in spread betting represents the notional monetary exposure of a position, computed as the stake per point multiplied by the instrument's opening price. It is used to assess leverage, margin requirements, and potential profit or loss sensitivity to price movements.

name: Spread Betting Profit or Loss
definitions: Spread betting profit or loss is the monetary outcome of a spread bet, calculated by multiplying the stake per point by the difference between the opening price and the closing price of the underlying instrument. It reflects leveraged exposure to price movements, where profits and losses can exceed the initial margin, and a positive value indicates a gain while a negative value indicates a loss.

name: Spread Commission
definitions: Spread commission represents the monetary impact of a specified point (pip) difference across a given transaction size. It quantifies the commission or cost attributable to the bid–ask spread and point value, commonly used in foreign exchange and other point-based markets.

name: Square Root
definitions: The square root is a mathematical operation function used to calculate the square root of a non-negative value, i.e., a number that, when multiplied by itself, equals the original number. In financial and financial analysis, it is commonly used to calculate derived metrics such as volatility (e.g., standard deviation in Rho value calculations).

name: Stable Growth Rate
definitions: The stable growth rate is the sustainable compound growth rate that a company can maintain over the long term after entering a phase of long-term equilibrium development. It is commonly used to calculate the terminal value (continuing value) in business valuation. In financial analysis, the stable growth rate is typically estimated or assumed based on theoretical models such as the sustainable growth rate model or the potential output growth rate of the macroeconomy.

name: Stamp Duty
definitions: Stamp duty is a tax levied on the execution or receipt of legally effective taxable documents (such as contracts, property transfer deeds, business account books, etc.) in economic activities and transactions. The tax amount is directly calculated based on the recorded amount, fees, revenue, or number of documents, according to statutory proportional rates or fixed rates.

name: Standard Activity Allocation Rate
definitions: The Standard Activity Allocation Rate is a predetermined fixed allocation rate calculated based on budgeted or normal activity costs and activity volumes in Activity-Based Costing. It is used to allocate activity costs to cost objects (such as products or services), which can avoid the impact of fluctuations in actual activity costs on product costing and facilitates the provision of stable cost information for decision-making.

name: Standard Activity Level
definitions: Standard Activity Level refers to the predetermined level of operational activity or output quantity expected to be achieved under normal production conditions, used for establishing cost standards or allocating manufacturing overhead in standard costing or activity-based costing. It serves as a crucial benchmark for measuring efficiency, calculating cost variances, and implementing cost control.

name: Standard Activity-Based Costing
definitions: Standard Activity-Based Costing is a cost management method that integrates the concepts of standard costing and activity-based costing. It first establishes standard cost consumption rates for various activities (such as standard labor hours, standard material usage, etc.), then calculates the standard cost that should have been incurred based on actual activity volumes (such as actual production batches, actual service instances, etc.). This calculated standard cost is compared with the actual activity costs incurred to analyze cost variances, perform cost control, and evaluate performance.

name: Standard Allocation Rate
definitions: The standard allocation rate is a predetermined rate used under standard costing to allocate manufacturing overhead to products or cost centers. It is typically calculated based on budgeted data and serves as the foundation for cost variance analysis, such as fixed manufacturing overhead cost variance analysis.

name: Standard Base Freight
definitions: Standard base freight refers to the fundamental freight component in cargo transportation, calculated solely based on core billing parameters such as transportation distance, cargo weight, or volume, excluding surcharges, service fees, or other special charges. It constitutes the core component of the total freight cost.

name: Standard Base Salary
definitions: Standard base salary refers to the fixed foundational wage standard established by an enterprise according to its internal compensation system or industry practices for a specific position, job grade, or role, before considering factors such as performance, allowances, or overtime. It typically serves as the benchmark for calculating total labor costs, overtime pay, social insurance contribution bases, etc.

name: Standard Consumption per Unit
definitions: Standard consumption per unit refers to the predetermined quantity standard of resources, such as raw materials, labor hours, or energy, allowed for producing one qualified product under standard production conditions. It is a preset target value, not a calculated figure, primarily used for cost control and efficiency measurement.

name: Standard Cost
definitions: Standard cost is the total cost calculated based on actual output and standard cost per unit, used for comparison with actual costs.

name: Standard Cost Driver Rate
definitions: Standard Cost Driver Rate refers to a predetermined allocation rate used in Activity-Based Costing to assign costs from activity centers to cost objects (such as products or services). It is typically based on budgeted or standard costs, calculated by dividing the estimated total cost of an activity center by the estimated total quantity of the cost driver, and is used for cost control and variance analysis.

name: Standard Cost at Actual Output
definitions: Standard cost at actual output refers to the total cost calculated based on the actual quantity of products completed during a specific period, using predetermined standard consumption per unit (e.g., materials, labor hours) and standard prices (e.g., material price per unit, wage rate). It serves as one of the benchmarks for measuring variances between actual costs and standard costs (such as price variances and efficiency variances).

name: Standard Cost per Unit
definitions: Standard cost per unit refers to the predetermined cost standard for various production factors (direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead) required to produce one unit of qualified product under normal production efficiency. It is a composite expected cost indicator and serves as a benchmark for cost control, budget preparation, and variance analysis.

name: Standard Deviation
definitions: Standard deviation is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of individual observations from the mean within a dataset, reflecting the volatility or spread of the data. In financial management and finance, standard deviation is commonly used to quantify the risk or stability of investment returns and serves as a core parameter in risk assessment and asset pricing models.
Standard deviation is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion or spread of a set of data points around their mean, widely used in finance to assess the volatility or risk of returns.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance, measuring the dispersion of a dataset relative to its mean. In finance, it quantifies the volatility or risk of investment returns.
Standard deviation is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of a set of data points around their mean, commonly used in finance to gauge the volatility or risk of asset returns.

Standard deviation quantifies the dispersion of investment returns around their mean, serving as a core risk measure (volatility) in portfolio management and performance analysis. A higher standard deviation indicates greater variability in returns and higher risk.

Standard deviation is a statistical measure of dispersion that quantifies how widely observations are distributed around their mean. It is defined as the square root of variance and, in finance, is commonly used to measure the volatility of returns, informing risk assessment, portfolio construction, and performance analysis. Unlike variance, standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the underlying data.

name: Standard Deviation (Sample)
definitions: Sample standard deviation quantifies the dispersion of prices around their mean, using Bessel's correction (n − 1) to estimate population variance from a sample. It is a core volatility measure and is commonly applied in mean-reversion analytics, including normalization via Z-scores.

name: Standard Deviation of Asset A Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of Asset A returns is a composite metric calculated through statistical analysis of Asset A's historical return data. It measures the dispersion or volatility of Asset A's returns relative to its average return, serving as a core indicator in risk assessment and portfolio management.

The standard deviation of Asset A returns is a statistical measure of the volatility or risk of Asset A's returns. It indicates the dispersion of Asset A's actual returns around its average return (expected return). A larger standard deviation suggests more volatile returns and higher risk for Asset A, while a smaller standard deviation indicates more stable returns and relatively lower risk.

name: Standard Deviation of Asset B Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of Asset B returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion or volatility of Asset B's returns. It is calculated by measuring the deviation of its historical or expected returns from the average return, serving as a key parameter for assessing asset risk.

The standard deviation of Asset B returns is a statistical measure of the volatility or risk of Asset B's returns. It indicates the dispersion of Asset B's actual returns relative to its expected return (mean). A larger standard deviation suggests more volatile returns and higher risk for Asset B, while a smaller standard deviation indicates more stable returns and relatively lower risk.

name: Standard Deviation of Asset Excess Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of asset excess returns is a risk metric that measures the volatility of an asset's or portfolio's returns relative to a benchmark (such as the market portfolio or the risk-free rate). It represents the dispersion of excess returns from their mean and is a key input for calculating risk-adjusted return metrics such as the Sharpe Ratio.

name: Standard Deviation of Asset Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of asset returns is a statistical metric calculated from other financial data, used to measure the dispersion of returns and reflect the risk level of asset returns.

name: Standard Deviation of Benchmark Returns
definitions: Standard deviation of benchmark returns is a statistical measure used to quantify the volatility of benchmark returns, reflecting the dispersion of benchmark return rates relative to their mean. It is commonly used in asset risk analysis and investment decision-making.

name: Standard Deviation of Demand During Lead Time
definitions: The standard deviation of demand during lead time is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility of customer demand throughout the entire period from order placement to goods receipt. It is typically calculated based on historical daily (or weekly) demand data and the lead time, serving as a key parameter for determining safety stock levels, calculating reorder points, and assessing stockout risk.

name: Standard Deviation of Expected Daily Cash Balance Changes
definitions: The standard deviation of expected daily cash balance changes is a statistical measure of the volatility of daily cash balance fluctuations, calculated from historical data or forecasting models. It is used in cash management models (such as the Miller-Orr model) to determine the cash return line and is a non-leaf composite indicator.

name: Standard Deviation of Market Portfolio Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of market portfolio returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility or risk of the market portfolio's rate of return. It is calculated using historical data or the probability distribution of returns from the assets within the market portfolio. This measure serves as a key parameter for quantifying systematic risk in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

name: Standard Deviation of Market Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of market returns is a statistical measure calculated from historical market return data, used to quantify the volatility of market returns. It serves as an important tool for measuring market risk, was first introduced by Markowitz in portfolio theory, and plays a key role in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and beta coefficient calculations.

name: Standard Deviation of Random Variable X
definitions: The standard deviation of random variable X is a statistic that measures the dispersion of its values, defined as the positive square root of the variance, reflecting the average deviation of the random variable's values from its mathematical expectation.

name: Standard Deviation of Random Variable Y
definitions: The standard deviation of random variable Y is the arithmetic square root of its variance, used to measure the dispersion of the random variable's values from its expected value. It is a core indicator in risk assessment and statistical analysis.

name: Standard Deviation of Return on Assets
definitions: Standard Deviation of Return on Assets is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of an asset's (or portfolio's) returns around its expected return (mean return). It reflects the uncertainty or risk level of asset returns; a larger standard deviation indicates more volatile returns and higher risk.

The standard deviation of return on assets is a statistical measure of the volatility or risk of an asset's returns. It reflects the degree of dispersion of the asset's various possible return outcomes relative to its average return (expected return). A larger standard deviation indicates greater return volatility and higher asset risk.

name: Standard Deviation of Returns
definitions: Standard deviation of returns is a measure of the volatility of stock returns, estimating its risk level through the dispersion of historical continuously compounded returns.

Standard deviation of returns measures the dispersion of investment returns around their mean, serving as a core risk metric (volatility) in finance. Higher standard deviation indicates greater variability and market risk, and it is commonly used in portfolio analysis, performance evaluation, and risk management.

Standard deviation of returns measures the dispersion of periodic investment returns around their mean, quantifying volatility and risk. A higher standard deviation indicates greater variability and higher risk, while a lower standard deviation suggests more stable returns.

name: Standard Deviation of Returns for Security j
definitions: The standard deviation of returns for Security j is a statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of the investment returns of that security. It reflects the degree to which the actual returns of the security deviate from its average (expected) return. A larger standard deviation indicates greater volatility in the security's returns, which typically corresponds to higher risk.

name: Standard Deviation of Returns for Security k
definitions: The standard deviation of returns for Security k is a statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of the investment returns of that security. It reflects the degree to which the actual returns of the security deviate from its average return (expected return). A larger standard deviation indicates greater volatility in the security's returns, which typically corresponds to higher investment risk.

name: Standard Deviation of Security A Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of Security A returns is a statistic calculated based on historical return data, used to measure the volatility or risk of Security A returns. It can be derived from periodic return data and serves as a fundamental metric for portfolio risk analysis and the calculation of expected correlation coefficients.

name: Standard Deviation of Security B Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of Security B returns is a statistic calculated from historical return data, used to measure the volatility or risk of Security B returns, indicating the degree to which returns deviate from the average return. It is not a raw fundamental data item from financial statements but can be decomposed into operations of other metrics.

name: Standard Deviation of Security j
definitions: The standard deviation of Security j is a statistical measure of the dispersion of its historical returns relative to its average return, used to quantify the overall risk or volatility of the security. In portfolio theory, it serves as the basis for calculating covariance between securities.

name: Standard Deviation of Stock Returns
definitions: The standard deviation of stock returns is a statistical measure calculated from stock return data, used to gauge the volatility of stock returns and reflect stock investment risk. A larger standard deviation indicates greater return volatility and higher risk; conversely, a smaller standard deviation indicates lower volatility and lower risk.

name: Standard Deviation of the k-th Security
definitions: The standard deviation of the k-th security is a fundamental statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of that security's own rate of return. It is calculated based on the security's historical return data. A larger value indicates greater volatility in the security's returns, signifying higher risk. It serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating more complex risk metrics such as portfolio risk and covariance.

name: Standard Direct Labor Hours per Unit
definitions: Standard direct labor hours per unit refers to the predetermined, necessary working time for direct production workers to produce one qualified product under normal operating conditions in a standard costing system. It includes time for direct processing operations, necessary equipment adjustments, work breaks, and time consumed by normal scrap. It serves as the foundational data for calculating standard direct labor costs and standard variable and fixed manufacturing overhead costs.

name: Standard Error
definitions: Standard error is an indicator that measures the dispersion between a sample statistic (such as the sample mean) and the population parameter. It reflects the magnitude of sampling error, i.e., the average error that may occur when using a sample to estimate the population.

name: Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead
definitions: Standard fixed manufacturing overhead is the predetermined, allocable fixed manufacturing cost (such as factory rent, equipment depreciation, fixed salaries of management personnel, etc.) set for each unit of product in cost management, based on budgeting or standard costing. It is typically calculated by dividing the total budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead by the planned standard capacity (such as standard labor hours or standard output) to derive a standard allocation rate.

name: Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Rate per Hour
definitions: The standard fixed manufacturing overhead rate per hour is a predetermined rate used in cost accounting to allocate total fixed manufacturing overhead costs (such as factory rent, equipment depreciation, and other costs that do not vary directly with production volume) to each unit of product based on the budgeted standard labor hours. It is a budgeted figure used to calculate the standard cost of a product, rather than being based on actual incurred costs.

name: Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Charges
definitions: Standard freight and miscellaneous charges refer to the predetermined standard cost or rate used in financial accounting or cost accounting for calculating and measuring transportation and related miscellaneous expenses associated with material procurement or goods transportation. It is typically based on historical data, industry standards, or contractual agreements, and is used for budgeting, cost control, and variance analysis. It is an essential component of the total standard procurement cost of materials.

name: Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Charges per Unit Material
definitions: Standard freight and miscellaneous charges per unit material refer to the predetermined standard rate or unit price set for each unit of material in cost accounting and budgeting, used to calculate its transportation and related miscellaneous expenses. It is typically determined based on historical data, contractual agreements, or market prices, serving as a benchmark input for cost control and budget preparation.

name: Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Rate Coefficient
definitions: The Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Rate Coefficient is a pre-determined ratio or multiplier used to calculate the total standard freight and miscellaneous charges. It is typically determined by logistics companies based on comprehensive factors such as market conditions, transportation distance, and cargo type, and can be adjusted according to the specific requirements of the shipper. It serves as a key parameter in the freight and miscellaneous charge calculation model.

name: Standard Hourly Wage Rate
definitions: Standard Hourly Wage Rate refers to the ratio of the total estimated direct labor wages to be paid for producing a unit of product to the standard total labor hours under a standard cost system, serving as the basis for calculating the standard direct labor cost.

name: Standard Hours
definitions: Standard hours refer to the labor time required to complete a specific task or process under standard working conditions, used for cost calculation, production planning, and efficiency evaluation. It is a non-leaf node concept that can be calculated from other time metrics and is often referenced in determining the standard cost per unit.

name: Standard Hours for Completed Products
definitions: Standard hours for completed products refer to the predetermined standard labor time allocated for producing one qualified product in manufacturing cost accounting. It is a standard time consumption benchmark established by enterprises based on production processes, equipment conditions, and historical experience, primarily used for cost calculation and efficiency evaluation.

name: Standard Hours of Work-in-Process at Month-End
definitions: Standard Hours of Work-in-Process at Month-End refers to the total standard hours calculated at the month-end point for work-in-process, based on the time quota of its respective production stage and its degree of completion (or an agreed conversion coefficient). It is a composite metric used under the standard cost method or the standard proportion method to allocate costs such as direct labor and manufacturing overhead between finished goods and work-in-process at month-end.

name: Standard Hours per Unit
definitions: Standard hours per unit refer to the direct labor hours that should be consumed to produce one unit of qualified product under standard production conditions. It is a fundamental metric for setting standard costs, preparing production budgets, and conducting efficiency analysis.

Standard hours per unit refer to the predetermined standard of direct labor time that must be consumed to produce one unit of qualified product under normal production technology and organizational conditions. It serves as the foundational data for establishing direct labor cost budgets and conducting efficiency variance analysis.

Standard hours per unit refer to the predetermined or planned standard working time that an enterprise is expected to consume to produce or complete one unit of qualified product under normal production or construction conditions. It serves as essential foundational data for measuring production efficiency, formulating production plans, and conducting cost accounting.

name: Standard Inventory Cost
definitions: Standard inventory cost refers to the predetermined unit cost standard established by an enterprise for internal accounting and control purposes regarding the production or holding of inventory (such as raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods) in financial and cost management. It is typically based on reasonable estimates of direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead, and is used to compare with actual incurred costs for variance analysis and performance evaluation.

name: Standard Labor Cost
definitions: Standard labor cost is a key component of the standard costing system, referring to the predetermined direct labor cost that should be incurred to complete a unit of product or a specific task under standard production conditions. It is typically calculated from basic data such as standard hours and standard wage rates, or aggregated from standard values of sub-items including basic wages, welfare expenses, taxes, and fees. It serves as a critical benchmark for cost control, budget preparation, and labor cost variance analysis.

name: Standard Labor Hours per Unit
definitions: Standard labor hours per unit refers to the predetermined or standardized necessary labor time consumption for producing one unit of qualified product under normal production or construction conditions. It serves as an important basis for production planning, labor cost accounting, and productivity measurement.

name: Standard Labor Time Allowance
definitions: The Standard Labor Time Allowance is a core component for calculating the standard direct labor cost, referring to the standard direct labor hours required to produce one unit of product under existing production technology conditions. It is typically established through industrial engineering methods such as method study and time study, and is a composite or derived standard rather than raw data directly obtained from accounting records.

name: Standard Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate
definitions: The standard manufacturing overhead allocation rate is a ratio calculated based on the total budgeted manufacturing overhead and the total budgeted allocation base. It is used to allocate manufacturing overhead to product unit costs in standard costing systems and is a key metric for establishing standard costs per unit of product.

name: Standard Material Consumption for Various Products
definitions: Standard material consumption for various products refers to the established quantity standard of raw materials or auxiliary materials that must be consumed to produce one qualified product under current production and technological conditions. This standard includes the net material usage that constitutes the product itself, as well as reasonable and unavoidable losses during the production process.

name: Standard Material Cost
definitions: Standard material cost refers to the predetermined direct material cost that should be incurred under normal production conditions for producing a unit of product under the standard costing method. It is typically calculated by multiplying the standard quantity of materials by the standard price of materials, and is used for cost control, budgeting, and performance evaluation.

name: Standard Material Cost of Finished Products
