definitions: Typical Price is the average of an asset's high, low, and close prices for a given period. It serves as a representative price level and is commonly used as an input in technical indicators such as the Money Flow Index (MFI).

name: U-1 Unemployment Rate
definitions: The U-1 unemployment rate measures the percentage of the civilian labor force that has been unemployed for 15 weeks or more, highlighting long-term unemployment within the labor market.

name: U-2 Unemployment Rate
definitions: The U-2 unemployment rate measures the share of the civilian labor force composed of job losers and persons who completed temporary jobs, expressed as a percentage. It highlights short-term job loss dynamics and turnover within the labor market.

name: U-3 Unemployment Rate
definitions: The U-3 unemployment rate measures the percentage of the civilian labor force that is unemployed and actively seeking work. It is the official unemployment rate reported by statistical agencies and reflects individuals without jobs who have looked for work within the reference period.

name: U-4 Unemployment Rate
definitions: The U-4 unemployment rate is a broader measure of labor underutilization that includes discouraged workers in addition to the unemployed. It is calculated as the share of the total labor force including discouraged workers that is either unemployed or discouraged, expressed as a percentage.

The U-4 unemployment rate measures the percentage of the labor market that is unemployed when discouraged workers are included. It is calculated as the number of unemployed individuals plus discouraged workers divided by the labor force plus discouraged workers, expressed as a percentage. This broader measure captures job seekers who have stopped looking due to economic conditions but excludes other marginally attached and part-time-for-economic-reasons workers.

name: U-6 (Unemployment) Rate
definitions: The U-6 unemployment rate is a broad measure of labor underutilization reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It includes unemployed persons actively seeking work, individuals marginally attached to the labor force, and those working part-time for economic reasons (underemployed). It is calculated as the sum of unemployed, marginally attached, and underemployed persons divided by the labor force plus marginally attached persons, expressed as a percentage.

name: U-6 Unemployment Rate
definitions: The U-6 unemployment rate is the broadest measure of labor underutilization. It includes the unemployed, individuals marginally attached to the labor force, and those employed part-time for economic reasons, expressed as a percentage of the expanded labor force (civilian labor force plus marginally attached).

name: U.S. Dollar Index (USDX)
definitions: The U.S. Dollar Index (USDX) is a geometrically weighted index that measures the value of the U.S. dollar against a basket of six major foreign currencies (EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD, SEK, CHF). It is calculated by multiplying an indexing factor by the currency pair exchange rates raised to fixed weights, reflecting the relative importance of each currency in the basket. The index is normalized using an indexing factor so that the base period aligns with historical reference levels.

name: USD to KYD Conversion
definitions: Converts an amount in U.S. dollars (USD) to Cayman Islands dollars (KYD) using a fixed exchange rate.

name: Ulcer Index
definitions: The Ulcer Index is a technical analysis downside risk indicator that measures the depth and duration of price declines from recent highs. It is computed as the square root of the average of squared percentage drawdowns over a specified look-back period, emphasizing downside volatility only. In this implementation, the average is obtained by dividing the sum of squared percentage drawdowns by the look-back period.

name: Ultimate Net Loss
definitions: Ultimate net loss is the final amount of loss borne by the insurer after reducing the gross loss by the deductible, salvage value, and other recoveries, and capping the result at the policy limit. It represents the insurer’s net liability for a claim and is commonly used in claims settlement and excess-of-loss reinsurance.

name: Ultimate Oscillator
definitions: The Ultimate Oscillator is a weighted momentum oscillator that combines three timeframes (7, 14, and 28 periods) of buying pressure relative to true range to reduce false signals from typical oscillators. It scales between 0 and 100, with higher values indicating stronger upward momentum and lower values indicating stronger downward momentum, and is often used to identify divergences and potential overbought/oversold conditions.

name: Unadjusted Basis
definitions: Unadjusted basis is the initial cost basis of an asset at acquisition, equal to the cash consideration paid plus liabilities assumed and capitalizable property-related taxes and closing costs, prior to any subsequent adjustments such as improvements, depreciation, amortization, or impairments.

name: Unamortized Bond Discount
definitions: Unamortized bond discount refers to the remaining portion of the difference between a bond's face value and its lower issuance price that has not yet been allocated to interest expense through amortization (i.e., periodic recognition) over the bond's life. It is a contra account to the carrying value of bonds payable.

name: Unamortized Bond Issuance Costs
definitions: Unamortized bond issuance costs refer to the expenses incurred by an enterprise when issuing bonds that have not yet been allocated to the profit or loss of each period over the bond's term. These costs are initially recognized as part of the bond's carrying amount, as an adjustment to an asset or liability, and are subsequently amortized using the effective interest method to reflect the true cost of financing of the bond.

name: Unamortized Bond Premium
definitions: Unamortized bond premium refers to the portion of the premium arising from issuing bonds at a price above their face value that has not yet been amortized into interest expense over the bond's life. This remaining premium must be amortized in each accounting period until maturity to adjust the actual interest expense.

name: Unappropriated Retained Earnings
definitions: Unappropriated retained earnings represent the portion of retained earnings not restricted or set aside for specific purposes (such as legal reserves or capital commitments), and therefore available for dividends or other discretionary uses. They are reported within shareholders' equity on the balance sheet or the statement of changes in equity.

name: Unbiased Predictor
definitions: Under the Unbiased Expectations Hypothesis (Expectations Theory), the forward rate implied by current spot rates is an unbiased predictor of future short-term interest rates. This measure estimates the future one-year spot rate from the current one-year and two-year spot rates, assuming rates are expressed in decimals and there is no term premium.

name: Uncovered Interest Arbitrage
definitions: Uncovered interest arbitrage is a strategy that involves investing in a foreign currency money market instrument without hedging the foreign exchange exposure. The total return is determined by the foreign interest rate differential combined with the subsequent change in the foreign exchange rate relative to the domestic currency.

name: Uncovered Interest Rate Parity (UIP)
definitions: Uncovered Interest Rate Parity (UIP) posits that, without hedging exchange rate risk, the expected return on domestic deposits equals the expected return on foreign deposits after accounting for expected exchange rate movements. Under UIP, the expected future spot (or the UIP-implied forward rate) is the current spot exchange rate scaled by the ratio of the two countries' gross interest factors.

name: Undated Issue
definitions: An undated issue (perpetual bond) is a fixed-income security with no maturity date. Its present value equals the constant periodic coupon divided by the investor's required rate of return (discount rate), assuming coupons continue indefinitely and the discount rate remains positive.

name: Underapplied Overhead
definitions: Underapplied overhead is the condition where actual manufacturing overhead exceeds budgeted or applied overhead, yielding a positive overhead variance. It indicates that overhead costs were underestimated or insufficiently applied to production and typically requires period-end adjustment to cost of goods sold or inventory. In this context, a positive Overhead Variance (Actual Overhead − Budgeted Overhead) signals underapplied overhead, while a negative variance signals overapplied overhead.

name: Undercast
definitions: Undercast refers to the amount by which an estimate or recorded figure is lower than the actual realized amount. In budgeting and forecasting, it quantifies conservative estimates or understatements relative to actual outcomes, helping evaluate forecast accuracy and variance against actual performance.

name: Underemployment Rate
definitions: Underemployment rate measures the percentage of the labor force that is employed below their capacity in terms of hours, skills, or experience. It indicates the extent to which available labor resources are underutilized within an economy.

name: Underfunded Pension Plan
definitions: An underfunded pension plan, often referred to as an at-risk plan, is a defined benefit pension plan whose funding target attainment percentage falls below prescribed regulatory thresholds, indicating insufficient assets relative to the funding target. Under common standards (e.g., U.S. PPA/ERISA guidance), a plan is considered at risk when the current year funding target attainment percentage is below 80% and the previous year percentage is below 70%, which may trigger higher minimum required contributions and additional compliance measures.

name: Underlying Asset Current Price
definitions: Underlying asset current price refers to the real-time trading price or observable market quotation of an asset (such as stocks, commodities, indices, etc.) that serves as the basis for derivative contracts (e.g., options, futures) in financial markets at a specific point in time. It is the fundamental data for financial product pricing and trading decisions.

Underlying asset current price refers to the real-time market trading price of the underlying asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) corresponding to a financial derivative contract (e.g., options, futures). It is fundamental market data for determining derivative value, typically obtained directly from exchanges or quotation systems rather than calculated through formulas.

Underlying asset current price refers to the immediate market trading price of the asset serving as the contract subject for financial derivatives (such as options, futures) at a specific point in time.

name: Underlying Asset Downside Price
definitions: The Underlying Asset Downside Price is a derivative concept referring to the estimated or calculated future price of an underlying asset under a specific downside scenario assumption, derived through probabilistic models or valuation methods. It is not an original accounting data point but a scenario analysis value computed based on parameters such as the underlying asset price, volatility, and downside threshold, commonly used to evaluate the value of derivative instruments like downside options.

name: Underlying Asset Market Price
definitions: Underlying asset market price refers to the immediate transaction price agreed upon for a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) in an open, active trading market where buyers and sellers engage in voluntary and fair transactions. It is raw price data directly observed and obtained from the market, serving as fundamental input information for asset valuation, financial derivative pricing, and investment decision-making.

Underlying asset market price refers to the price agreed upon in a fair transaction between willing buyers and sellers in an open, active, and orderly market at a specific point in time. It reflects the consensus of market participants on the value of the asset and serves as a crucial reference for asset valuation, financial derivative pricing (e.g., options), and financial analysis.

name: Underlying Asset Price
definitions: Underlying asset price refers to the value representation of a specific asset at the current or a future point in time. In financial derivatives trading, the underlying asset typically refers to tradable assets such as stocks, bonds, commodities, currencies, and indices.

name: Underlying Asset Price Appreciation Rate
definitions: The underlying asset price appreciation rate refers to the percentage increase in the value of the underlying asset from the beginning to the end of a period, used to measure the degree of change in asset price. It is a key composite indicator for calculating investment returns, evaluating investment performance, and option pricing.

name: Underlying Asset Price Change
definitions: Underlying Asset Price Change refers to the difference in the price of the underlying asset, upon which financial derivatives (such as options, futures) depend, between two distinct observation points. This metric is a key intermediate variable for calculating the value of financial derivatives, risk exposure (e.g., Delta), and profit and loss, and is classified as a composite indicator derived from underlying market prices.

Underlying asset price change refers to the fluctuation in the market price of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, indices, etc.) that serves as the basis or reference for a financial derivative contract (e.g., options, futures) over a period of time. This change is a direct result of market trading and constitutes a critical external input data required for financial analysis and derivative pricing.

name: Underlying Asset Price During Stock Price Decline
definitions: Refers to the market price of the underlying asset (such as stocks, indices, etc.) that serves as the basis for financial derivative contracts (e.g., options) during specific periods or scenarios when stock market prices are falling.

name: Underlying Asset Price Volatility
definitions: Underlying asset price volatility is an indicator used to measure the uncertainty or degree of risk of future price movements of an underlying asset (such as stocks, commodities, etc.), typically expressed as a percentage. Higher volatility indicates that the asset price may experience larger upward or downward movements over a future period, implying greater uncertainty.

name: Underlying Asset Price at Expiration
definitions: The underlying asset price at expiration refers to the actual market trading price of the underlying asset (such as stocks, indices, etc.) specified in the option contract on its expiration date. It is the key market data determining the option's value at expiration, which cannot be calculated through models and must be obtained directly from real-time market quotes.

name: Underlying Asset Volatility
definitions: Underlying asset volatility is a quantitative measure of the uncertainty or risk associated with future price movements of the underlying asset, typically expressed as the standard deviation of asset returns. It can be calculated from historical price data and holds significant reference value in option pricing, risk management, and investment decision-making.

name: Underlying Profit
definitions: Underlying profit is a non-GAAP profitability measure that adjusts accounting profit to exclude non-recurring or unusual items, aiming to reflect the core, recurring performance of a company's standard operations.

name: Underpayment Penalty
definitions: Underpayment penalty is a tax penalty assessed for failing to pay the full amount of tax due on time. It is typically calculated monthly as a percentage of the underpaid tax amount for each month or partial month the balance remains unpaid, and may be subject to a statutory cap.

Underpayment penalty interest is the interest assessed on an underpaid tax amount for the period it remains outstanding. It is typically calculated using the applicable annual interest rate, compounded monthly, reflecting the cost of delayed payment imposed by tax authorities or financial institutions.

name: Underpayment Penalty Safe Harbor Threshold
definitions: The Underpayment Penalty Safe Harbor Threshold is the minimum tax payment amount required under IRS safe harbor rules to avoid an underpayment penalty. Taxpayers can avoid penalties by paying the lesser of 90% of the current year's tax or a specified percentage of the prior year's tax, with the percentage depending on Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).

name: Underpricing
definitions: Underpricing refers to the phenomenon where a stock's first-day closing price exceeds its IPO offer price, indicating the issuer priced the shares below the level set by market demand. The underpricing amount measures the absolute price difference between the first-day closing price and the IPO offer price; a positive amount indicates underpricing.

name: Underwater
definitions: Underwater refers to a condition where the outstanding loan balance on an asset exceeds its current market value, resulting in negative equity for the asset holder and potentially constraining financial flexibility.

name: Underwater Mortgage
definitions: An underwater mortgage refers to a situation where the current market value of a property is less than the outstanding mortgage principal, resulting in negative home equity and potentially constraining refinancing or sale options.

name: Underweight
definitions: Underweight refers to holding a smaller portfolio weight in a security relative to its benchmark. Underweight percentage quantifies the extent to which the portfolio weight is below the benchmark weight, calculated as the benchmark weight minus the portfolio weight. A positive result indicates an underweight position, while a negative result indicates an overweight position.

name: Underwriting Expense Ratio
definitions: The underwriting expense ratio measures the proportion of insurance premiums consumed by underwriting-related operating expenses over a period, indicating an insurer's cost efficiency in writing and servicing policies. A lower ratio generally signifies better operating efficiency and stronger underwriting performance.

name: Underwriting Fee
definitions: Underwriting fee is the compensation charged by investment banks or securities firms for providing underwriting services to companies issuing securities (such as stocks or bonds). This fee represents a core cost paid by the issuer to obtain the underwriter's professional services in areas such as securities pricing, sales, and distribution.

name: Underwriting Income
definitions: Underwriting income is the profit (or loss) generated from an insurer's core underwriting operations, calculated as premiums from insurance policies minus claims and underwriting-related expenses. It excludes investment income and reflects the insurer's operating performance in pricing risk, managing claims, and controlling expenses.

name: Underwriting Spread
definitions: Underwriting spread is the per-share difference between the public offering price and the price paid by underwriters to the issuer, representing the gross compensation to underwriters for distribution, pricing, and risk-bearing services in primary market offerings such as IPOs and follow-on offerings.

name: Undistributed Profit at End of Q2
definitions: Undistributed profit at the end of the second quarter refers to the cumulative balance of net profit retained by the enterprise and not yet distributed after one quarter of operations (typically from April 1 to June 30), following the allocation of statutory surplus reserves, discretionary surplus reserves, and profit distributions to investors.

name: Unearned Discount
definitions: Unearned discount refers to the unrecognized portion of the precomputed finance charge on a loan. Under the Rule of 78 (sum-of-the-digits method), the remaining finance charge that has not yet been earned by the lender is determined based on the number of payments remaining relative to the total payment schedule.

name: Unearned Interest
definitions: Unearned interest refers to the portion of the precomputed finance charge that has not yet been earned by the lender at the time of early repayment. Under the Rule of 78 (Sum-of-the-Digits method), the unearned interest rebate is calculated based on the sum of the digits weighting of remaining payments relative to the original payment schedule, providing a standardized approach for consumer loans with precomputed finance charges.

name: Unearned Premium
definitions: Unearned premium is the portion of written premium received by an insurer that has not yet been recognized as revenue because the corresponding coverage period has not elapsed. It is recorded as a liability and amortized into earned premium over the policy term, typically on a time-proportion (pro rata) basis.

Unearned premium is the portion of the written premium that has not yet been recognized as revenue because coverage has not yet been provided. It represents a liability (often recorded as the unearned premium reserve) that will be earned over the remaining policy term on a pro rata basis. Earned premium equals total premium minus unearned premium.

name: Unearned Revenue
definitions: Unearned revenue (deferred revenue) is a liability representing cash received for goods or services not yet delivered. As performance obligations are satisfied over time, a portion of the liability is recognized as revenue and the remaining balance is adjusted downward accordingly.

name: Unemployment Insurance
definitions: Unemployment insurance is a social insurance system mandated by national legislation, funded through collective social contributions, which provides material assistance to workers who have temporarily lost their livelihood due to unemployment, ensuring their basic living standards and promoting their re-employment.

name: Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base
definitions: The unemployment insurance contribution base refers to the wage income benchmark used to calculate the amount of unemployment insurance premiums payable by employers and individuals. Typically, the employer's contribution base is the total wages of the unit in the previous year, while the individual's contribution base is the individual's total wages in the previous year. Specific upper and lower limits are determined by local governments based on factors such as the average social wage.

name: Unemployment Insurance Contribution Rate
definitions: The unemployment insurance contribution rate refers to the percentage rate determined by national regulations, under which employers and individual employees respectively contribute unemployment insurance premiums based on a specified percentage of the employer's total payroll or the employee's individual wage. Typically, employers contribute 2% of their total employee payroll, while individual employees contribute 1% of their own wages, though specific rates may be adjusted according to local policies.

name: Unemployment Insurance Individual Contribution Amount
definitions: The Unemployment Insurance Individual Contribution Amount refers to the unemployment insurance premium calculated and paid by individual workers participating in the urban employee unemployment insurance scheme, based on a specified percentage of their monthly wages as stipulated by national regulations. It constitutes a component of individual social security expenditures and is used to provide basic living security and employment assistance during periods of unemployment.

name: Unemployment Insurance Individual Contribution Rate
definitions: The unemployment insurance individual contribution rate refers to the percentage of an employee's monthly wage that must be contributed to unemployment insurance. According to current regulations, this rate is typically 1% of the employee's monthly wage and is withheld by the employer from the employee's salary.

name: Unemployment Insurance Premium
definitions: Unemployment insurance premium refers to the fee paid by employers and individual employees according to state regulations, calculated as a certain percentage of the employee's wage income, used to establish the unemployment insurance fund. It is one of the prerequisites for employees to claim unemployment insurance benefits after becoming unemployed.

name: Unemployment Rate
definitions: The unemployment rate measures the percentage of the labor force that is unemployed and actively seeking work. It is calculated by dividing the number of unemployed persons by the total labor force and expressing the result as a percentage.

name: Unemployment Rate (U-5)
definitions: The U-5 unemployment rate measures the percentage of the expanded labor force—defined as the civilian labor force plus marginally attached workers—that is not employed. It includes unemployed persons and marginally attached workers (including discouraged workers) relative to the expanded labor force.

name: Unfavorable Variance
definitions: Unfavorable variance is the positive difference by which actual costs or values exceed budgeted, standard, or projected amounts. It signals cost overruns, revenue shortfalls, or performance inefficiencies relative to plan and is central to budgeting and variance analysis in management accounting.

name: Unified Tax Credit
definitions: The Unified Tax Credit is a nonrefundable federal transfer tax credit that offsets gift and estate tax liabilities up to the applicable credit amount, which is derived from the basic exclusion amount. It reduces or eliminates estate tax payable after exemptions and prior taxable gifts are considered, and may be affected by portability and lifetime gift use.

name: Unissued Shares
definitions: Unissued shares are authorized by a company’s charter but have not yet been issued. They represent the difference between total authorized shares and total issued shares (the sum of outstanding shares and treasury stock), indicating the potential shares available for future issuance.

name: Unit Benefit Formula
definitions: The unit benefit formula is a defined benefit pension plan accrual method that calculates an employee’s annual retirement benefit as the product of credited years of service, an accrual rate expressed as a percentage of salary, and the employee’s career average salary, linking benefit accruals to both service and pay under plan provisions.

name: Unit Consumption
definitions: Unit consumption refers to the fixed quantity of a specific resource (such as raw materials, energy, or labor hours) required to complete one unit of work (e.g., producing one product, delivering one service) in production, manufacturing, or the execution of a specific task. It serves as a fundamental input data point for cost accounting, budget preparation, and resource requirement planning.

name: Unit Consumption Price Change
definitions: Unit consumption price change is a derivative indicator that represents the change in unit price, typically calculated by comparing unit consumption prices across different periods, such as the change amount or change rate, used to analyze consumption price fluctuations or cost change trends.

name: Unit Contribution Margin
definitions: Unit Contribution Margin refers to the balance of the selling price per unit minus its variable cost per unit. It is used to measure the contribution of each unit of product to fixed costs and profit, and is a core indicator in management accounting for analyzing cost behavior and profitability.

Unit contribution margin is the amount remaining from each unit's sales price after deducting the unit variable cost, representing the per-unit profit contribution toward covering fixed costs and generating profit.

name: Unit Contribution Margin by Product
definitions: Unit Contribution Margin by Product refers to the amount remaining when the selling price per unit of a specific product is subtracted by the corresponding variable cost per unit. This amount is used to cover the company's fixed costs and ultimately forms profit, serving as a key indicator for measuring the profitability of individual products.

name: Unit Cost
definitions: Unit cost refers to the total cost incurred to produce each unit of product, typically calculated by dividing the sum of the beginning work-in-process inventory cost and the production costs incurred during the current month by the total output.

name: Unit Cost of Auxiliary Production
definitions: Unit cost of auxiliary production refers to the average cost per unit of product or service, calculated by allocating the total expenses incurred by auxiliary production departments (such as maintenance, power supply, and water supply workshops) for providing services to primary production and other departments, averaged over the total quantity of products or services provided.

name: Unit Cost of Finished Goods
definitions: Unit cost of finished goods refers to the average cost allocated per unit of finished product, used to measure production efficiency and profitability.

name: Unit Cost of Inventory
definitions: Unit cost of inventory refers to the average cost value corresponding to each unit of inventory held by an enterprise (such as one piece, one kilogram, or one carton), used to measure the cost level of stock goods or materials.

name: Unit Cost of Inventory Prior to Current Shipment
definitions: Unit cost of inventory prior to current shipment refers to the average cost per unit (e.g., per piece, per kilogram) of a specific batch of inventory calculated before the enterprise dispatches (sells or withdraws) that batch. This cost is typically determined based on the inventory valuation method chosen by the enterprise (such as FIFO, weighted average method, etc.) and is used to ascertain the cost of goods issued and to carry forward the cost of sales.

name: Unit Count
definitions: Unit count is a measurement unit, typically used to quantify the specific number of equipment, machinery, vehicles, or particular products. In financial and operational management, it is commonly employed to measure the physical scale of production, sales, or inventory.

name: Unit Direct Labor Cost
definitions: Unit direct labor cost refers to the direct labor expenses incurred in producing a single unit of product. It serves as a crucial foundation for calculating product variable costs, cost control, and budget preparation. It reflects the efficiency and cost level of direct labor input in the production process.

name: Unit Direct Material Cost
definitions: Unit direct material cost refers to the total cost of raw materials, primary materials, auxiliary materials, spare parts and components, purchased semi-finished goods, packaging materials, and low-value consumables consumed in producing one unit of a product, which constitute the physical substance of the product. Under standard costing, it is a predetermined cost target based on material price standards and standard material usage per unit of product.

name: Unit Fixed Cost
definitions: Unit fixed cost refers to the fixed cost allocated to each unit of product produced or service provided within a certain period. Fixed costs are those that do not vary with changes in production volume or business activity within a relevant range, such as rent, equipment depreciation, administrative salaries, and insurance premiums. Unit fixed cost decreases as production volume increases and is a fundamental composite indicator in cost behavior analysis and management accounting.

name: Unit Holding Cost
definitions: Unit holding cost refers to the total of various expenses incurred by an enterprise to maintain one unit of inventory (such as one item of goods or one ton of raw materials) over a specific period (typically one year). These expenses primarily include warehouse rental or depreciation, labor costs for warehouse management, insurance premiums for inventory, interest losses or opportunity costs from capital tied up, and risk costs such as potential damage, obsolescence, or depreciation of inventory.

Unit holding cost refers to the average cost incurred by a company to store each unit of inventory (such as one item, one ton, or one batch) over a specific period (typically one year). These costs typically include warehousing fees, insurance, interest on capital tied up, inventory obsolescence and spoilage, as well as warehouse depreciation and administrative expenses related to storage activities.

name: Unit Inventory Cost
definitions: Unit inventory cost refers to the average cost incurred by an enterprise to acquire and hold each unit of inventory over a specific period. It is a core indicator for inventory cost management and accounting, with calculation methods including the weighted average method at month-end and the moving weighted average method.

name: Unit Manufacturing Cost
definitions: Unit manufacturing cost refers to the total production cost required to manufacture one unit of product, typically calculated by dividing the total manufacturing cost over a specific period by the total production volume during that period. It is a core metric for cost accounting, product pricing, and profitability analysis.

name: Unit Market Value
definitions: Unit market value refers to the trading price or fair value of a single financial asset (such as per share of stock, per fund unit) in the open market, which is the result of the equilibrium of market supply and demand. In financial analysis, it serves as fundamental data directly used to calculate valuation metrics such as total market capitalization, price-to-earnings ratio, and price-to-book ratio, and is not itself derived from specific financial formulas.

name: Unit Material Quota
definitions: Unit material quota refers to the predetermined standard quantity of material consumption for producing one unit of qualified product (or completing one unit of workload) under specific production technology and management conditions. It serves as essential foundational data for material cost accounting, cost control, and production planning in enterprises.

name: Unit Opportunity Cost
definitions: Unit opportunity cost refers to the potential maximum benefit foregone for each additional or reduced unit of activity (such as production, transaction, or investment) in a specific decision. It measures the value of the alternative that must be sacrificed to obtain one unit of current benefit.

name: Unit Period Cost
definitions: Unit period cost refers to the average period cost borne by an enterprise per unit of product produced or service provided during a specific accounting period. Period costs include administrative expenses, selling expenses, and financial expenses. This metric is used to measure the level of period costs consumed per unit of output.

name: Unit Price
definitions: Unit price is the selling price per unit of a good or service, used in financial management for pricing decisions, cost analysis, and profit planning. It can be calculated using financial metrics such as total price, quantity, cost, and profit.

Unit price refers to the price per unit of product or commodity at the time of sale, serving as a core indicator in financial management and cost accounting. It can be derived from unit cost, unit profit, and applicable tax rate, or calculated based on cost-plus pricing method, compounded from unit fixed cost, unit variable cost, and cost-plus rate.

Unit price refers to the price charged by an enterprise for selling a single product, serving as fundamental data for calculating sales revenue, profit, and conducting financial decisions such as break-even analysis.

name: Unit Price per Product
definitions: Unit price per product refers to the selling price of each individual product. In cost-volume-profit analysis, it can be calculated using financial metrics such as profit, fixed costs, sales volume, and unit variable cost, and is a key variable for calculating contribution margin and assessing profitability.

name: Unit Product Consumption
definitions: Unit product consumption refers to the average quantity of a specific raw material, energy, or other resource consumed in the production process to manufacture one unit (e.g., one piece, one set) of a particular product. It serves as a fundamental data point in cost accounting, material management, and production planning.

name: Unit Product Cost
definitions: Unit product cost refers to the average cost incurred to produce a single unit of product, reflecting the expense level of similar products. It is the cost allocated to each unit by distributing the total cost based on different consumption levels, typically calculated by dividing total cost by total output. It is a key metric in cost accounting and pricing decisions.

Unit product cost refers to the average total cost incurred by an enterprise to produce each unit of product (such as one piece, one set, or one ton). It is typically calculated by dividing the total cost of a specific product (including direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead) by the total output of that product. It serves as essential foundational data for measuring production efficiency and conducting product pricing and cost control.

Unit product cost refers to the average total cost incurred by an enterprise to produce or sell a single product. It is typically calculated by dividing the total costs associated with the product (such as production costs, administrative expenses, etc.) during a specific period by the number of units produced or sold during that period. It serves as crucial fundamental data for measuring enterprise cost control and conducting product pricing.

name: Unit Product Price
definitions: Unit product price refers to the amount charged to customers per unit of product, forming the basis of sales revenue. Its determination methods vary, commonly including cost-plus pricing based on costs, as well as pricing strategies that consider target profit, market competition, and customer value perception.

name: Unit Product Required Equipment Setup Time
definitions: Unit Product Required Equipment Setup Time refers to the average preparation and adjustment time necessary for equipment to switch from one product or state to another for the production of each unit of product during the manufacturing process. It is one of the factors to be considered when establishing labor time standards and calculating manufacturing overhead.

name: Unit Product Rest Time
definitions: Unit Product Rest Time refers to the non-working time reserved or accounted for in the production process for operators to rest per unit of product produced. It is one of the components constituting the total standard direct labor hours and reflects the humanization factors and reasonable intervals for labor efficiency considered in standard time setting.

name: Unit Product Selling Price
definitions: Unit product selling price refers to the amount charged to customers for the sale of a single product. It is typically determined by market supply and demand, competitive conditions, corporate pricing strategy, or negotiation with customers, and serves as the fundamental data for calculating sales revenue.

name: Unit Product Work Efficiency
definitions: Unit product work efficiency is an efficiency metric that measures the relationship between the workload required to complete a unit product and the standard time consumed during the production process, used to evaluate the utilization efficiency of production resources.

name: Unit Product Workload
definitions: Unit product workload refers to the total amount of work required to produce one qualified product, serving as a fundamental component for calculating productivity metrics such as standard hours per unit.

name: Unit Profit
definitions: Unit profit refers to the amount remaining after deducting all related costs (including direct costs and allocated indirect expenses) from the revenue generated by selling a single product or providing a single service. It is a core metric for measuring the profitability efficiency of a company's products or services.

name: Unit Quantity Cost
definitions: Unit quantity cost refers to the cost amount allocated to each unit of product, typically calculated by dividing total cost by total quantity, commonly used in cost calculation for joint products or by-products.

name: Unit Selling Price
definitions: Unit selling price refers to the price charged by an enterprise for selling a single product, typically calculated through financial methods such as cost-plus pricing and sales profit margin pricing. It is a key indicator for formulating sales strategies, conducting profitability analysis, and managing target costs.

Unit selling price refers to the price charged by an enterprise for selling a single product, service, or unit of measurement (e.g., per piece, per kilogram, per ton). It is fundamental data in market transactions, revenue recognition, and internal pricing decisions, typically determined by market supply and demand, cost-plus pricing, or negotiation between buyers and sellers, rather than being calculated through fixed financial formulas.

name: Unit Selling Price of the Product
definitions: The unit selling price of the product refers to the price charged to customers for each unit of a specific product sold by the enterprise in the market. It serves as the basis for calculating sales revenue, profit, and conducting market pricing analysis.

name: Unit Stockout Cost
definitions: Unit stockout cost refers to the average economic loss incurred per unit of inventory shortage (e.g., one piece, one kilogram) due to supply interruption. It is a key intermediate variable for calculating total stockout cost, determining economic order quantity, and setting safety stock levels, typically encompassing potential costs such as lost profit from missed sales opportunities, additional expenses for emergency procurement, and loss of goodwill.

name: Unit Time Step
definitions: Unit time step refers to a predefined, fundamental time interval unit used for calculation, accounting, or model simulation in finance, management accounting, or financial analysis. It is not a calculated result but a predetermined time scale, such as a month, a quarter, a day, or an hour, serving as the temporal benchmark for measuring and analyzing economic activities (e.g., revenue, cost, cash flow).

name: Unit Variable Cost
definitions: Unit variable cost refers to the variable cost incurred for producing or selling one unit of product within the relevant range, with its total amount changing in direct proportion to the level of activity. It is a core concept in cost-volume-profit analysis and variable costing.

Unit variable cost refers to the average variable cost allocated to each unit of product produced or sold by an enterprise, which is the ratio of total variable cost to total output or total sales volume. It changes in direct proportion to the level of business activity.

name: Unit Variable Cost of New Proposal
definitions: Unit variable cost of a new proposal refers to the cost per unit of production or sales that is expected to vary directly in proportion to the level of activity under a new business proposal being considered or implemented (such as launching a new product, adopting a new process, or entering a new market). It is a key parameter for evaluating the profitability of the new proposal and making related decisions (e.g., whether to increase fixed cost investments).

name: Unit Variable Cost per Product
definitions: Unit variable cost per product refers to the variable cost per unit of product, reflecting the portion of costs that vary with changes in production or sales volume. It can be calculated by dividing total variable costs by sales volume, or by summing up individual unit variable cost components. It is a core metric in management accounting used for contribution margin analysis, break-even analysis, and decision-making.

name: Unit Variable Manufacturing Overhead Budget
definitions: The unit variable manufacturing overhead budget refers to the pre-planned or set standard amount of variable manufacturing overhead for producing a single unit of product during the budget period. It serves as the foundation for preparing the total manufacturing overhead budget and is typically calculated based on the standard hours per unit and the standard variable manufacturing overhead allocation rate.

name: Unit Variable Selling and Administrative Expenses
definitions: Unit variable selling and administrative expenses refer to the amount of expenses directly related to product sales or daily management activities in cost behavior analysis, whose total amount varies in direct proportion to changes in business volume (such as sales volume), averaged per unit of product. It is an important component of unit variable cost and is typically estimated based on historical data or business drivers rather than calculated through formulas.

name: Unit Variable Storage Cost
definitions: Unit variable storage cost refers to the amount of various variable costs directly related to inventory quantity incurred by an enterprise due to holding inventory, allocated per unit of inventory. It typically includes accrued interest on inventory funds, inventory damage and deterioration losses, and inventory insurance expenses. This cost is a fundamental parameter that usually needs to be estimated or set based on the enterprise's specific cost data, rather than calculated through a universal formula.

name: Unit Variable Transportation Cost
definitions: Unit variable transportation cost refers to the cost in transportation operations that is directly related to and varies proportionally with cargo turnover (e.g., thousand-ton-kilometers). It is typically determined through statistical analysis of historical data and serves as one of the fundamental variables for calculating total transportation cost.

name: Unit-of-Production Depreciation Expense
definitions: Unit-of-Production depreciation allocates an asset’s depreciable base based on actual output or usage rather than time. The per-period depreciation expense equals the per-unit depreciation rate—computed as (Original Cost minus Salvage Value) divided by Estimated Production Capacity—multiplied by the units produced in the period. This method is appropriate for assets whose wear and tear is driven by production volume.

name: Units Per Transaction (UPT)
definitions: Units Per Transaction (UPT) measures the average number of items purchased per transaction over a given period. It is a retail sales KPI that indicates basket size, merchandising effectiveness, and customer purchasing behavior.

name: Unlevered Beta
definitions: Unlevered beta (asset beta) measures the systematic market risk of a company's assets independent of financial leverage, derived by removing the impact of debt from the levered beta. It is used to compare pure business risk across firms and to re-lever betas for target capital structures in valuation and CAPM applications.

name: Unlevered Cost of Capital
definitions: Unlevered cost of capital is the required return on a company's assets assuming no leverage, reflecting the risk of the underlying business independent of financing. It is commonly estimated via CAPM using the unlevered beta, the market risk premium, and the risk-free rate.

name: Unlevered Free Cash Flow
definitions: Unlevered Free Cash Flow represents the cash flow available to all providers of capital before interest payments and independent of the firm's capital structure. It reflects the operating cash generation after capital expenditures and changes in working capital, net of taxes, and is widely used in valuation analyses such as discounted cash flow (DCF).

name: Unlimited Risk
definitions: Unlimited risk refers to exposure to potentially unbounded losses, most notably in short (written) naked call positions where the underlying asset's price can rise without limit. The writer's maximum profit is limited to the option premium received, while losses can grow indefinitely as the underlying price increases. The provided calculation estimates the profit or loss per contract at expiry, assuming 100 shares per option contract.

name: Unplanned Downtime Lost Hours
definitions: Unplanned downtime lost hours refer to the direct labor hour losses caused by forced interruptions in production or work activities due to sudden, unforeseen factors (such as equipment failure, material shortages, safety incidents, etc.). This portion of hours constitutes non-productive, non-value-added lost time and is one of the key metrics for measuring production efficiency and safety management levels.

name: Unrealized Gain
definitions: Unrealized gain is the increase in an asset's current market value over its original purchase price while the asset is still held and not yet sold, representing potential profit that may be recognized through fair value measurement depending on the accounting framework.

Unrealized gain is the increase in an asset's current market value above its purchase price that has not yet been realized through sale. It represents potential profit on held positions and may be reported in other comprehensive income or earnings depending on the accounting classification but is not taxable until realized.

name: Unrealized Gain or Loss (Available-for-Sale Securities)
definitions: For available-for-sale securities under U.S. GAAP, unrealized gains or losses represent the difference between the current fair value and the original cost basis of a security. These changes in value are measured at each reporting date and recognized in other comprehensive income (OCI), accumulating in equity (AOCI) until the security is sold or otherwise disposed, at which time amounts are reclassified to earnings.

name: Unrealized Intercompany Transaction Gains and Losses
definitions: Unrealized intercompany transaction gains and losses refer to the portion of internal profit or loss embedded in the transaction price when goods, services, or assets are traded within a corporate group (e.g., between a parent company and its subsidiaries), before the subject matter of the transaction (such as inventory or fixed assets) is fully sold to or consumed by external third parties outside the group. These gains and losses must be eliminated in the preparation of consolidated financial statements to prevent overstatement of the group's overall profit or asset value.

name: Unrealized Loss
definitions: Unrealized loss is the decline in the fair value of an asset relative to its purchase price that has not been realized through a sale. It represents a paper loss on unsold positions and helps investors assess current portfolio performance. Depending on the classification of financial instruments under applicable accounting standards, unrealized losses may be recognized in profit or loss or in other comprehensive income.

name: Unreasonable Fund Occupation Amount
definitions: Unreasonable fund occupation amount refers to the amount of funds occupied by assets that are inefficient, idle, overstocked, or fail to generate expected returns (such as excess inventory, stagnant accounts receivable, idle fixed assets, etc.) during the enterprise's production and operation process. These funds do not effectively participate in value creation and are typically deducted from the total fund occupation amount when forecasting future funding requirements.

name: Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain
definitions: Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain is the portion of gain on the sale of depreciable real property attributable to previously allowed depreciation on Section 1250 property. Under U.S. tax law, this portion is taxed at a maximum rate of 25%, distinct from the regular long-term capital gains rate. The unrecaptured amount is limited to the lesser of total gain realized and cumulative depreciation claimed, with any excess gain taxed at regular long-term capital gains rates.

name: Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain Tax
definitions: Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain tax is the U.S. federal tax assessed on the portion of a real property disposition gain attributable to straight-line depreciation, taxed at a capped rate (up to 25%) under Internal Revenue Code Section 1250. It applies to the depreciation recapture element of real estate gains and is calculated by multiplying the depreciation allowed or allowable by the applicable tax rate.

name: Unrecovered Loss at the Beginning of the Year
definitions: Unrecovered loss at the beginning of the year refers to the cumulative loss amount in a company's profit distribution account (e.g., 'Profit Distribution - Undistributed Profit') that has not yet been offset by subsequent years' profits at the start of a given fiscal year. It reflects the historical operating losses that the company still needs to recover using future profits or surplus reserves as of the beginning of the year.

Unrecovered loss at the beginning of the year refers to the cumulative loss amount that has not been offset by profits from subsequent years at the start of a given fiscal year. This portion of loss typically originates from operating losses in prior years and can be deducted pre-tax from taxable income of future years within the statutory time limit (e.g., five years) prescribed by tax laws.

name: Unstated Interest Paid
definitions: Unstated interest paid refers to interest imputed on installment sales that do not specify an explicit interest rate. Using the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR), the imputed interest represents the financing cost attributable to deferred payments over their respective time periods, as recognized for tax and accounting purposes.

name: Unsystematic Risk
definitions: Unsystematic risk is the firm- or asset-specific, diversifiable portion of total investment risk that is not driven by market-wide factors. In variance terms, it is measured as the residual variance of returns after removing the systematic (market) variance, i.e., the difference between total risk variance and systematic risk variance.

name: Unusual Item
definitions: Unusual items are gains or losses that are infrequent or not related to a company's ordinary activities. Analysts often adjust reported financial metrics by removing the effects of unusual items to derive a normalized view of core operating performance.

name: Up Factor
definitions: The Up Factor is a financial metric used to calculate the relative magnitude of numerical growth. It quantifies the degree of growth by comparing the percentage change between the current value and the base period value. It is commonly applied in financial analysis, financial modeling, and derivative pricing, such as in the valuation of up-and-down options.

The up factor is a calculation parameter in the binomial option pricing model, representing the possible multiple by which the stock price may increase per unit time. It is typically derived from volatility and time step length, and is used to calculate option value or stock price movements.

name: Up Option Value
definitions: Up option value is an intermediate variable in the binomial option pricing model, representing the option's expiration date value when the underlying asset price moves upward in a single-period binomial model. It typically refers specifically to the intrinsic value of a call option, calculated based on the comparison between the up-state stock price and the strike price.

name: Up Percentage
definitions: In the binomial tree model, it represents the maximum upward movement of the underlying asset price within a single period, typically determined by volatility and the length of the time period.

Up Percentage is a composite indicator used to calculate expected return, representing the magnitude of increase in asset price or value expressed as a percentage. It is commonly used in financial models such as risk-neutral pricing as a key variable for calculating expected return.

name: Up Probability
definitions: Up probability, in option pricing, refers to the probability of the underlying asset price increasing under the risk-neutral valuation principle. As a composite indicator, it depends on variables such as the risk-free rate, up factor, and down factor.

name: Up-Front Mortgage Insurance (UFMI)
definitions: Up-front mortgage insurance is a one-time insurance premium charged at loan origination on FHA-insured mortgages, calculated as a percentage of the base loan amount to insure the lender against default. The premium may be paid at closing or financed into the mortgage.

name: Up-Market Capture Ratio
definitions: Up-market capture ratio measures the percentage of a benchmark's positive return that an investment manager captures during rising markets. It is calculated as the manager's return divided by the benchmark index's return during up-market periods, multiplied by 100. A value above 100% indicates outperformance relative to the benchmark in up markets, while below 100% indicates underperformance.

name: Up-Maturity Value
definitions: Up-maturity value is a concept in option pricing, specifically referring to the intrinsic value of a call option at expiration when the market price of the underlying asset (e.g., a stock) is above its strike price (i.e., in an 'up' state). Its value equals the up-state stock price minus the strike price. If the stock price at expiration is below or equal to the strike price, this value is zero.

name: Up-State Option Value
definitions: Up-state option value is a derivative metric in option pricing models (such as the binomial model), representing the intrinsic value of a call option in an upward stock price state. It is calculated from the up-state stock price and the strike price, and is used for estimating subsequent option values (e.g., option value after a down-then-up movement). It is not an original accounting statement item.

Up-state option value is a derived metric in the binomial option pricing model, representing the expected value of an option when the underlying stock price moves upward. It is typically calculated using parameters such as the post-up stock price, strike price, and risk-free rate through binomial model formulas. It is not a primary accounting line item and is commonly used to evaluate option value along specific price paths.

name: Up-and-Out Option
definitions: An up-and-out option is a barrier option that becomes void (knocks out) if the underlying asset’s price rises to or above a predetermined barrier level during the option’s life. Once knocked out, the contract ceases to exist and typically has no payoff, reflecting the embedded risk control and path-dependent nature of barrier options.

name: Up-and-Out Option Cost Savings
definitions: Up-and-Out Option Cost Savings measures the per-contract premium reduction achieved by selecting an up-and-out (barrier) option instead of a comparable vanilla option on the same underlying and expiration. A positive value indicates the barrier option is cheaper than the vanilla option, while a negative value indicates the barrier option is more expensive.

name: Upper Limit of Integration
definitions: The upper limit of integration is a concept in mathematical analysis, specifically referring to the upper bound value of the integration interval in a definite integral. When this upper limit is a variable, the resulting function is called the upper limit of integration function, which represents the correspondence between the integral value of the integrand over the interval from a fixed lower limit to a variable upper limit and that upper limit variable.

name: Upper Limit of Previous Tax Bracket
definitions: The Upper Limit of Previous Tax Bracket refers to the maximum taxable income threshold corresponding to the lower adjacent tax bracket in a progressive individual income tax rate schedule. It serves as a key parameter in calculating the quick deduction amount, simplifying the computation process under progressive marginal tax rates.

name: Upside Factor
definitions: The Upside Factor is an indicator used to measure the magnitude, ratio, or positive trend of increases in asset prices or portfolio value. In hedging, it serves as an input variable for calculating the optimal hedge ratio; in quantitative multi-factor models, it refers to those factors or composite factors that can positively predict an asset's future returns. It is typically derived from historical prices, financial data, or market conditions through specific formulas and belongs to derivative (non-leaf) node indicators.

name: Upside Gain
definitions: Upside gain typically refers to the portion of returns in financial investments resulting from the market price appreciation of assets (such as stocks), representing the return investors obtain from asset value appreciation between purchase and sale.

name: Upside Potential
definitions: Upside potential is the expected percentage increase from the current market price to a forecasted target price, indicating the potential gain an investor may realize if the price reaches the target. A positive value suggests potential appreciation, while a negative value implies downside risk.

name: Upside Probability
definitions: Upside probability refers to the likelihood that the price of a stock or asset will rise within a specified future period. It is a composite indicator calculated based on predictive models, historical data, or market metrics, commonly used in financial analysis, investment decision-making, and option pricing.

name: Upside Return
definitions: Upside return refers to the expected rate of return investors anticipate under market or asset price upward conditions, typically derived from scenario analysis, conditional probability, or derivative calculations, used to evaluate investment upside potential and risk management.

name: Upside Scenario P/E Ratio
definitions: The Upside Scenario P/E Ratio is a price-to-earnings ratio calculated based on optimistic future expectations (such as stock price appreciation and earnings growth). It is commonly used in valuation analysis, reflecting the price multiple investors are willing to pay per unit of expected earnings under an assumed positive market scenario.

name: Upside Scenario Price-to-Book Ratio
definitions: The Upside Scenario Price-to-Book Ratio refers to the price-to-book ratio calculated based on forecasts of future stock prices and net assets under a scenario where the stock market is rising or optimistic expectations prevail. It is typically used to assess the potential level of a stock's price relative to its net assets per share under favorable market conditions, serving as a scenario-based assumption indicator in investment analysis and valuation.

name: Upside Scenario Return
definitions: Upside scenario return refers to the rate of return obtained from an investment under specific conditions of favorable market movements. It is essentially the specific application or contextual calculation of the basic return metric in an upward market environment, reflecting the asset's profitability under favorable market conditions.

Upside scenario return refers to the investment return or potential gain realized when market conditions are favorable and asset prices (such as stock prices) rise in financial markets or investment analysis. It is commonly used in option pricing, risk management, and scenario analysis to describe the returns investors may achieve under optimistic or favorable market conditions.

name: Upside/Downside Ratio
definitions: The Upside/Downside Ratio is a market breadth indicator that measures momentum by comparing advancing volume (shares or contracts traded that close above the opening price) to declining volume (those that close below the opening price). A ratio greater than 1 indicates positive breadth and potential upward momentum, while a ratio less than 1 indicates negative breadth and potential downward momentum.

The Upside/Downside Ratio measures market breadth by comparing total trading volume in advancing issues to total trading volume in declining issues. A value above 1 indicates predominance of advancing volume (bullish breadth), while a value below 1 indicates predominance of declining volume (bearish breadth).

name: Uptrend
definitions: An uptrend is a technical analysis pattern characterized by successive higher highs and higher lows across rolling periods, reflecting sustained upward price momentum and dominant buying pressure.

name: Upward Multiplier
definitions: The upward multiplier is a key derivative metric in financial derivative pricing models (such as the binomial tree model), representing the potential multiple by which a stock price may increase within a given time step. It is typically calculated based on parameters such as volatility and time step length, and is used in financial analyses like option pricing.

name: Upward Price
definitions: Upward price typically refers to the expected or assumed price level that an underlying asset may rise to in financial analysis or option pricing models. It is commonly used to calculate upward probability, option value, or assess the potential returns of investment projects.

name: Upward Price Change Rate
definitions: The upward price change rate is a ratio that measures the magnitude or trend of price increases for assets or commodities over a specific period, commonly used to analyze positive price fluctuations in the market.

name: Upward Price Movement Range
definitions: Upward price movement range refers to the extent of change in a stock's price from a lower level to a higher level within a specific time period (e.g., one trading day), typically expressed as a percentage or an absolute amount. It is a fundamental market observation metric reflecting the strength of a stock price increase.

name: Upward Price Ratio
definitions: The upward price ratio is a core parameter in the binomial option pricing model, representing the multiplicative factor by which the underlying asset price may increase in a single-period binomial model. It is typically derived from parameters such as the volatility of the underlying asset and the time step, and is used to construct possible future asset price paths. It serves as the basis for calculating risk-neutral probabilities and option values.

name: Upward Project Value
definitions: Upward project value refers to the project value corresponding to the growth of future cash flows under favorable market conditions.

name: Upward Return
definitions: Upward return is a derivative calculation metric, typically derived from the relationship between the future upward price and the current price. It is used to measure the potential rate of return of an asset price in future upward scenarios and serves as one of the fundamental variables for calculating expected return and risk-neutral probability.

name: Upward Return Rate
definitions: The upward return rate is an indicator used in the binomial tree model in financial modeling, representing the expected rate of return when the value of an asset or project moves upward. It is calculated based on variables such as the upward multiplier and is commonly used in scenarios like option pricing and risk-neutral valuation.

name: Upward Stock Price
definitions: Upward stock price refers to the higher price that a stock price may rise to in the next period under an option pricing model.

name: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax
definitions: The Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax (UMCT) is a surtax levied by the state on entities and individuals engaged in industrial and commercial operations who pay Value-Added Tax (VAT) and Consumption Tax. The revenue is specifically earmarked for the maintenance and construction of urban public utilities and facilities.

name: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Payable
definitions: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Payable refers to the amount of Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax that should be paid by entities and individuals engaged in industrial and commercial operations who pay Value-Added Tax (VAT) and Consumption Tax. It is calculated based on the actual amount of VAT and Consumption Tax (and potentially the exempted or credited VAT amount) paid during a specific period, multiplied by the applicable prescribed tax rate.

Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Payable, abbreviated as UMC Tax, is a type of surtax levied specifically for the maintenance and construction of urban public utilities and facilities, based on the actual amount of Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by the taxpayer.

name: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Rate
definitions: The Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax rate refers to the statutory percentage applied when calculating the tax payable for Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, which varies according to the administrative division of the taxpayer's location (e.g., urban area, county town, designated town, etc.). This rate is one of the key parameters for calculating the Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, and its tax base is the actual amount of Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by the taxpayer.

name: Useful Life
definitions: Useful life refers to the estimated period during which an asset is expected to provide services or generate economic benefits for an enterprise. It serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating depreciation of fixed assets or amortization of intangible assets, typically determined based on the nature of the asset, technological obsolescence rate, company policy, or relevant contractual agreements, rather than being derived through a formula.

Useful life refers to the length of time a fixed asset (such as equipment or plant) is expected to provide economic benefits to the enterprise, typically measured in years. It serves as a crucial parameter for calculating asset depreciation and amortization, as well as for assessing its economic value.

name: Useful Life (Months)
definitions: Useful life (months) refers to the length of time over which an intangible asset is expected to generate economic benefits for the enterprise, typically measured in months. It is a key parameter for calculating the monthly amortization amount of an intangible asset, determining the speed and amount of cost allocation over accounting periods.

name: Useful Life of Fixed Assets
definitions: The useful life of a fixed asset refers to the period over which an enterprise expects the asset to generate economic benefits, serving as a crucial basis for calculating fixed asset depreciation. It is typically determined by considering factors such as the asset's technical characteristics, operating environment, maintenance condition, and industry practices.

name: Useful Life of an Asset
definitions: The useful life of an asset refers to the period over which an enterprise expects to use a fixed asset, or the number of production or similar units of output it expects to obtain from the asset's use. It is a fundamental estimated parameter for calculating fixed asset depreciation, typically determined through professional judgment based on experience, technical characteristics, operating environment, and other factors, or by reference to industry standards.

name: Usury Rate
definitions: The usury rate is the maximum legally permissible interest rate under state or jurisdictional usury laws. It is commonly defined as a benchmark base rate plus a statutory additional rate and is used by lenders to ensure loan pricing complies with legal interest rate ceilings and avoids usury violations.

Usury rate refers to the maximum permissible interest rate on loans under applicable law or policy. A loan may be flagged for predatory pricing or a potential usury violation when its charged interest rate exceeds the prevailing market rate by more than an allowed threshold or cap used for screening.

name: Utilization Fee
definitions: A utilization fee is a contractual charge assessed by a lender when a borrower's use of a credit facility exceeds a specified utilization threshold. It is typically calculated as a percentage of the outstanding balance and prorated over the assessment period.

name: Utilization Rate
definitions: Utilization rate is a ratio that measures the actual usage level of resources, assets, or capacity relative to their planned or maximum available level, typically expressed as a percentage. It is a key performance indicator for evaluating operational efficiency, resource allocation effectiveness, and capacity management.

name: Vacancy Rate
definitions: Vacancy rate is the percentage of all available units or positions that are unoccupied at a specific point in time, commonly used in real estate to evaluate rental property performance and in employment to measure unfilled positions.

name: Valid Probability Distribution
definitions: A valid probability distribution (discrete) is a set of non-negative probabilities for mutually exclusive outcomes whose total equals 1. In finance and risk modeling, validating probability distributions ensures integrity of scenario weights, transition matrices, and event likelihoods used in credit risk, portfolio analytics, and Monte Carlo simulations.

name: Valuation Multiple
definitions: A valuation multiple is a ratio that compares a company’s market value or enterprise value to a specific financial metric (such as earnings, sales, or book value) to assess relative value in comparable company analysis.

name: Valuation Ratios
definitions: Valuation ratios are financial metrics that compare a company's market value to its fundamental financial figures such as earnings, book value, sales, and dividends to assess whether a stock is under or overvalued.

name: Valuation Techniques
definitions: Valuation techniques refer to a comprehensive set of methods, models, and procedures used to estimate the fair value of assets, liabilities, or equity instruments. They are not raw data but rather computational processes that integrate observable and unobservable inputs through specific formulas or models to derive composite metrics (such as fair value), conceptually positioned as non-leaf nodes in the hierarchy. Primary technical approaches include the market approach, income approach, and cost approach.

name: Value
definitions: Value refers to the economic worth of an asset or enterprise in financial terms, typically estimated through methods such as discounting future cash flows.

name: Value Added
definitions: Value added refers to the sum of newly created value and the transferred value of fixed assets generated by a production unit during a specific period through production activities. It is a key indicator for measuring the final outcome of production activities and is commonly used in national economic accounting and enterprise value analysis.

Value added refers to the portion of an economic entity's (such as an enterprise or department) output value that exceeds the value of intermediate inputs consumed (such as raw materials and services) over a specific period through production or business activities. It measures the new value created by the entity and serves as the basis for calculating value-added tax, assessing enterprise contribution, and conducting economic analysis.

name: Value Added Monthly Index
definitions: Value Added Monthly Index (VAMI) is a performance measurement tool that tracks the growth of an initial investment over time by compounding monthly net returns, assuming reinvestment of earnings.

name: Value Added Ratio
definitions: The Value Added Ratio is a metric that measures the proportion of newly created value to total output value or the efficiency of capital input in the production process. In economic statistics, it represents the ratio of value added to gross output value, used to assess production efficiency; in value-based management, it represents the ratio of Economic Value Added to invested capital, used to evaluate capital return efficiency.

name: Value Added by Sector of Tertiary Industry
definitions: Value added by sector of the tertiary industry refers to the new value created and the value of fixed assets transferred by resident units in each sector of the tertiary industry during the production process. It reflects the final results of production and operation of each sector over a given period, serves as a fundamental indicator for calculating the total value added of the tertiary industry, and is typically derived through composite formulas such as the income approach or expenditure approach.

name: Value Added of Construction Industry
definitions: Value added of the construction industry refers to the final monetary result of production and operating activities of construction enterprises during the reporting period, reflecting the additional value created by construction production activities. It is an important component in calculating the value added of the secondary industry and is typically computed using the production approach or the income approach (distribution approach).

name: Value Added of Primary Industry
definitions: Value added of primary industry refers to the newly created value generated in the production process of agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry, and fishery (the primary sector). It is a composite indicator and a component of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), typically calculated using the income approach or production approach.

name: Value Added of Production and Supply of Electric Power, Heat, Gas and Water
definitions: Value Added of Production and Supply of Electric Power, Heat, Gas and Water refers to the final monetary outcome of production activities within this industry during the reporting period. It is the balance of the total output of all production activities minus the value of material products and services consumed or transferred during the production process, reflecting the newly created value of the industry. It is an important component of the secondary industry's value added in national economic accounting.

name: Value Added of Secondary Industry in Current Period
definitions: Value added of secondary industry in the current period refers to the final outcome of production activities by all resident units in the secondary industry within a specified accounting period (usually a year or a quarter). It is a core indicator for measuring the production scale, growth rate, and structural changes of the secondary industry. Its calculation follows the principles of the System of National Accounts (SNA) and can be derived through two equivalent approaches: the production approach or the income approach.

name: Value Added of Secondary Industry in Same Period Last Year
definitions: Value Added of Secondary Industry in Same Period Last Year refers to the value of total output minus intermediate inputs of the secondary industry during the same period of the previous year, calculated as a historical value of a composite indicator, commonly used for year-on-year analysis and macroeconomic indicator calculations.

name: Value Added of the Secondary Industry
definitions: Value added of the secondary industry refers to the total value added created by all resident units in the secondary industry production activities of a country or region.
