It is a key component of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), encompassing value added from sub-sectors such as mining, manufacturing, production and supply of electricity, heat, gas, and water, and construction. It is typically calculated by aggregating the value added of each sub-sector or by employing methods such as the production approach or the income approach.

name: Value Added of the Tertiary Industry
definitions: Value added of the tertiary industry is the sum of the final outcomes of production activities created by all resident units in the tertiary industry during the accounting period. It is a key component of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), typically calculated by aggregating the value added of each sector using the production approach or income approach, reflecting the economic contribution of the service sector to the national economy.

name: Value Averaging Contribution
definitions: Value averaging contribution is the amount of money that needs to be added to or withdrawn from an investment portfolio under the value averaging strategy to achieve a predetermined target portfolio value for the next period.

name: Value Line Composite Index Arithmetic Change
definitions: The daily percentage change in the Value Line Arithmetic Composite Index, computed as the arithmetic mean of the daily percent changes of all constituent stocks, assuming equal dollar holdings in each stock.

name: Value Line Geometric Composite Index Daily Change
definitions: The daily percentage change in the Value Line Geometric Composite Index, calculated as the geometric average of individual stock price changes, reflecting the performance of an equally weighted stock index.

name: Value Ratio
definitions: Value ratio is a quantitative measure in value engineering that expresses the relationship between a product's functional performance and its total life-cycle cost, used to assess cost-effectiveness and guide design optimization decisions.

name: Value Stock
definitions: A value stock is a security that appears underpriced relative to its intrinsic value, often identified by comparing expected earnings growth with current stock price.
A value stock is a security that trades at a price lower than its intrinsic value, often identified by comparing its valuation multiples (such as P/E ratio) to industry averages or historical levels.

name: Value at Risk
definitions: Value at Risk (VaR) is a metric that measures the risk of loss on an investment or capital. It estimates the maximum potential loss in value of a portfolio over a specific time period, under normal market conditions and assuming no trading activity, at a given confidence level.
Value at Risk (VaR) is a statistical measure that quantifies the maximum expected loss of a portfolio over a specified time horizon at a given confidence level, based on historical return data.
Value at Risk (VaR) is a statistical measure that quantifies the maximum expected loss on a portfolio over a specified time horizon under normal market conditions at a given confidence level.

Value at Risk (VaR) estimates the maximum expected loss of a portfolio over a specified time horizon at a given confidence level under normal market conditions, serving as a core market risk metric for risk management and regulatory capital purposes.

name: Value at Risk (VaR)
definitions: Value at Risk (VaR) is a statistical measure that quantifies the maximum expected loss of a portfolio over a specific time horizon at a given confidence level, assuming normal distribution of returns.

Value at Risk (VaR) is a statistical measure that quantifies the maximum expected loss of a portfolio over a specified time horizon at a given confidence level, based on Monte Carlo simulated return scenarios.

Value at Risk (VaR) is a risk metric that estimates the maximum expected loss of a portfolio over a specified time horizon at a given confidence level, typically computed from the distribution of historical returns. It is widely used in financial risk management to quantify market risk, although it may underestimate tail risk and assumes return distribution properties that may not hold in practice.

name: Value at Risk Coefficient
definitions: The Value at Risk Coefficient is a ratio that measures the additional return (risk premium rate) required per unit of risk (coefficient of variation), used to quantify risk and convert it into a component of the investor's required rate of return.

name: Value from Two Periods Ago
definitions: Value from two periods ago refers to the financial data or indicator values recorded two statistical cycles prior to the current period (e.g., the current period). For instance, when analyzing current period volatility, data from two periods ago may be referenced as a historical benchmark or for comparative purposes.

name: Value of Change in Self-produced Semi-finished Goods
definitions: The value of change in self-produced semi-finished goods refers to the difference between the inventory value of semi-finished goods (work-in-progress) produced by the enterprise itself at the end and the beginning of an accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). This difference reflects the net increase or decrease in the inventory value of semi-finished goods during the production activities of the enterprise in that period.

name: Value of Completed Industrial Work for External Clients in the Accounting Period
definitions: Refers to the total value of industrial work or services that an enterprise has completed and delivered to external clients within a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). Such work typically includes processing, repairing, assembling, testing, etc., of raw materials or semi-finished products provided by clients, and its value is included in the enterprise's total output.

name: Value of Finished Goods Produced in the Accounting Period
definitions: The value of finished goods produced in the accounting period refers to the total value, calculated based on production cost or market price, of finished goods that have been completed and reached a predetermined salable condition by an enterprise within a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a key metric for measuring the enterprise's production output during the current period and is commonly used in calculating total output.

name: Value of Finished Goods in Current Period
definitions: Value of finished goods in the current period refers to the total value of all industrial finished goods (including semi-finished goods) that have been completed, inspected, packaged, and stored in the warehouse within the current reporting period (e.g., month, quarter, or year), and will not undergo further processing within this period. It is one of the core components for calculating an enterprise's total output value or gross output.

name: Value of Finished Products Produced in Current Period
definitions: Value of finished products produced in the current period refers to the total value of all industrial finished products (including semi-finished products) that have been completed during the current reporting period, require no further processing within that period, and have passed inspection, completed packaging, and been placed in inventory. It serves as a fundamental data point for calculating gross industrial output value.

name: Value of Goods Imports
definitions: Value of goods imports refers to the total original transaction value of all goods purchased from abroad and brought into a country or enterprise during a specific period. It is typically based on customs statistics or the contract price declared by enterprises, determined according to international trade terms (such as CIF or FOB), and serves as fundamental data for calculating the trade balance, customs duties, and conducting macroeconomic analysis.

name: Value of Self-Produced Semi-Finished Goods Sold and Intended for Sale During the Accounting Period
definitions: Refers to the value corresponding to the portion of self-produced semi-finished goods, which have undergone certain production processes but are not yet final finished products, that have been sold externally or are intended for sale during a specific accounting period (e.g., an accounting period). It is an important indicator for measuring the value of intermediate products in the enterprise's production process.

name: Value of Standard Normal Random Variable
definitions: The value of a standard normal random variable refers to a specific numerical value of a random variable that follows a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. It is commonly used in probability and statistics as a fundamental input parameter for calculating the probability of specific events (such as default probability, Value at Risk).

name: Value-Added Activity Standard Output Quantity
definitions: Value-Added Activity Standard Output Quantity refers to the predetermined quantity standard of qualified products or services that should be produced under ideal efficiency conditions for performing a value-added activity within a standard costing system or budgeting framework. It serves as a fundamental variable for calculating value-added costs and non-value-added costs, belonging to the standard or budget data set for management analysis rather than raw transaction data directly obtained from accounting ledgers.

name: Value-Added Activity Unit Standard Cost
definitions: Value-Added Activity Unit Standard Cost refers to the predetermined standard cost per unit of activity output (e.g., per labor hour, per machine hour) that should be consumed to complete a value-added activity in Activity-Based Costing. It typically consists of standard unit variable cost and standard unit fixed cost, and is used for cost control and performance evaluation.

name: Value-Added Activity Unit Standard Hours
definitions: Value-Added Activity Unit Standard Hours refer to the predetermined, theoretically required standard time allocated for the value-added portion of an activity to complete one unit of product or service in activity-based cost management. It serves as a benchmark for measuring the efficiency of value-added activities and is used for cost calculation, budgeting, and performance evaluation.

name: Value-Added Tax (VAT)
definitions: Value-Added Tax (VAT) is a turnover tax levied on the incremental value of goods or services at each stage of production, circulation, and consumption. Its core calculation method is output tax minus input tax.

name: Value-Added Tax Actually Paid in Current Period
definitions: Value-Added Tax actually paid in the current period refers to the amount of Value-Added Tax that an enterprise actually pays to the tax authorities during the current accounting period (such as monthly or quarterly) in accordance with tax laws and regulations. It reflects the actual situation of the enterprise's fulfillment of its Value-Added Tax payment obligations during that period.

name: Value-Added Tax Input Tax
definitions: Value-Added Tax input tax refers to the VAT amount paid or borne by taxpayers when purchasing goods, labor services, services, intangible assets, or real estate. This portion of tax can be credited against output tax when calculating the VAT payable for the current period.

name: Value-Added Tax Paid
definitions: Value-Added Tax Paid refers to the amount of value-added tax calculated based on taxable activities during a specific tax filing period, which has been actually declared to and paid to the tax authorities. It reflects the actual cash outflow for value-added tax borne by the enterprise in the current period.

name: Value-Added Tax Payable
definitions: Value-Added Tax Payable refers to the balance of output VAT calculated based on the current period's taxable sales and applicable tax rate, after deducting the input VAT permitted for credit in the current period. It represents the actual VAT amount the taxpayer is required to pay to the tax authorities.

Value-Added Tax Payable refers to the amount of value-added tax that a taxpayer is required to pay to the tax authorities within a certain tax period, calculated based on their taxable activities. It is the balance after deducting the current input tax from the output tax, serving as a core indicator of a company's VAT burden and directly impacting its cash flow.

name: Value-Added Tax Payable (Tax Paid)
definitions: "Value-Added Tax Payable (Tax Paid)" is a subsidiary account under the "Taxes Payable - Value-Added Tax Payable" account, used to record the actual amount of Value-Added Tax (VAT) paid by general taxpayers in the current month. It primarily reflects the VAT payments already remitted by the enterprise to the tax authorities and is classified as an asset account (a debit entry indicates an increase, i.e., tax already paid).

name: Value-Added Tax Rate
definitions: The Value-Added Tax rate is the statutory percentage stipulated by national tax laws, used to calculate the amount of Value-Added Tax payable by taxpayers on the sale of goods, labor, services, intangible assets, or real estate. It serves as the fundamental raw data for VAT calculation and cannot be derived from other financial indicators.

name: Value-added Cost of Value-added Activities
definitions: Value-added cost of value-added activities refers to the sum of variable costs and fixed costs incurred to perform value-added activities (i.e., activities that increase product value and for which customers are willing to pay) under the current actual activity output, commonly used in cost analysis within activity-based cost management.

name: Value-added Tax Payable
definitions: Value-added Tax Payable refers to the amount of value-added tax that a taxpayer is required to pay within a certain tax period, calculated according to tax laws. It is the net amount after deducting input tax from output tax and making relevant adjustments, and is an important current liability item for enterprises.

name: Value-at-Risk
definitions: Value-at-Risk (VaR) quantifies the maximum expected loss of a portfolio over a specified horizon at a given confidence level, typically computed using the lower-tail quantile of historical returns and expressed as a positive loss amount.

name: Values of Random Variable X
definitions: The values of random variable X refer to the set of all possible specific numerical values or outcomes that X can take in a random experiment. For example, when rolling a die, the random variable X representing the number of dots that appear has values of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

name: Values of Random Variable Y
definitions: The values of random variable Y refer to all possible specific numerical outcomes that Y may take in a random experiment or statistical model. These values are random, and their likelihood of occurrence is determined by the probability distribution of Y.

name: Vanilla Option Profit/Loss
definitions: Vanilla option profit or loss represents the net gain or loss from holding a standard call or put option contract until expiry, calculated as the intrinsic value minus the premium paid.

name: Variable
definitions: In the field of finance and accounting, a variable refers to a quantity that can assume different values in models, formulas, or analyses, used to describe, measure, or predict financial phenomena. It can be known observed data (such as sales volume, cost) or latent factors to be estimated (such as risk factors, market sentiment).

name: Variable Annuity Future Value (L Share Class)
definitions: Variable Annuity Future Value (L Share Class) is the terminal account value of an L-share variable annuity after compounding annual investment returns and deducting annual fees (e.g., mortality and expense charges, administrative fees). The calculation assumes fees are applied annually to the account value, resulting in net growth each period equal to (1 + growth rate) × (1 - annual fees).

name: Variable Compensation
definitions: Variable compensation refers to the non-fixed portion of employee remuneration that fluctuates based on individual, team, or company performance (such as achieving sales targets, realizing profit growth, etc.), distinguishing it from the fixed base salary. Common examples include bonuses, sales commissions, and equity incentives.

name: Variable Cost
definitions: Variable cost refers to costs whose total amount changes in direct proportion to changes in business volume (such as production or sales volume) within the relevant range. It is not a primary account directly obtained from accounting ledgers but rather a management accounting concept derived through calculation or analysis.

Variable cost refers to costs that change in direct proportion to changes in a company's business volume (such as production volume, sales volume, or project volume). Examples include raw material expenses and direct labor costs required for production. In contrast to fixed costs, total variable costs increase when production volume increases and decrease when production volume decreases.

name: Variable Cost Ratio
definitions: The variable cost ratio is the percentage of variable costs in sales revenue. It is complementary to the contribution margin ratio, indicating the increase in variable costs for each additional unit of sales revenue, and is used for cost control and profit analysis.

name: Variable Cost per Order
definitions: Variable cost per order refers to the variable expenses directly associated with each instance of placing a purchase order for inventory. These costs increase with the number of orders placed but are independent of the quantity ordered per instance. Common expenses include order processing fees, travel expenses for procurement personnel, communication costs, and document postage fees.

Variable cost per order refers to the total of various expenses directly related to and varying with each order placement, such as travel expenses, postage, telephone and telegraph charges, and order processing fees. These costs increase with the number of orders placed and serve as key foundational data for calculating economic order quantity and other inventory management models.

name: Variable Cost per Product
definitions: Variable cost per product refers to the costs incurred for each product during the production process that vary with the level of output under variable costing. It is composed of basic cost items such as direct materials, direct labor, and variable manufacturing overhead, forming a decomposable composite metric used to calculate the contribution margin per product.

name: Variable Cost per Unit
definitions: Variable cost per unit refers to the average allocation of variable costs contained in each unit of product, i.e., the ratio of total variable costs to total output (or sales volume). It varies in direct proportion to the level of business activity and is a core indicator for cost-volume-profit analysis, break-even point calculation, and short-term operational decision-making.

Variable cost per unit refers to the average allocation of costs incurred by an enterprise in producing or selling a single product, which changes in direct proportion to the increase or decrease in product output or sales volume. It is the value obtained by dividing total variable costs by total output or total sales volume.

name: Variable Cost-Plus Pricing
definitions: Variable cost-plus pricing is a pricing strategy that sets the selling price by adding a markup to the variable costs per unit, which includes allocated fixed costs per unit and the desired profit per unit.

name: Variable Death Benefit
definitions: Variable death benefit is the total payout to beneficiaries from a variable life insurance policy, comprising the cash value accumulated through investment returns plus any guaranteed death benefit, reflecting both market performance and contractual guarantees.

name: Variable Expense Ratio
definitions: The variable expense ratio refers to the ratio between a company's total variable expenses and its total sales revenue. It reflects the amount of variable expenses corresponding to each unit of sales revenue earned and serves as a key indicator for measuring cost structure and profitability.

name: Variable Interest Rate
definitions: A variable interest rate is a floating lending rate set as the prime rate plus a borrower-specific margin. When indexed to the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) Prime Rate, the loan's interest rate adjusts as the prime rate changes, reflecting bank funding costs and borrower credit risk.

name: Variable Interest Rate Interest Payment
definitions: The interest payment calculated under a variable interest rate for a specified principal amount, interest rate, and number of periods, commonly used for loans or mortgages with variable rate agreements.

name: Variable Manufacturing Overhead
definitions: Variable manufacturing overhead refers to manufacturing costs whose total amount varies in direct proportion to changes in production volume or activity level. Examples include indirect materials, indirect labor, and utilities directly related to production output.

name: Variable Manufacturing Overhead Cost
definitions: Variable manufacturing overhead cost refers to indirect production expenses that vary in direct proportion to changes in business volume (such as production output or labor hours) during the manufacturing process, and is a component of product cost under variable costing.

name: Variable Manufacturing Overhead Cost Variance
definitions: Variable manufacturing overhead cost variance is the difference between actual variable manufacturing overhead and standard variable manufacturing overhead, used to evaluate the overall control effectiveness of variable manufacturing overhead.

name: Variable Manufacturing Overhead Standard Allocation Rate
definitions: The variable manufacturing overhead standard allocation rate is the ratio used to allocate the total budgeted variable manufacturing overhead based on the total standard direct labor hours.

name: Variable Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost
definitions: Variable manufacturing overhead standard cost is the amount of variable manufacturing overhead allocated per unit of product under standard hours.

name: Variable Manufacturing Overhead per Unit
definitions: Variable manufacturing overhead per unit refers to the variable manufacturing overhead allocated to each unit of product. Its total amount varies in direct proportion to the level of activity (such as production volume or labor hours) and is a key component of variable cost per unit. It can be separated from total manufacturing overhead using cost decomposition methods such as the high-low method or regression analysis.

name: Variable Non-Manufacturing Costs
definitions: Variable non-manufacturing costs refer to those non-manufacturing costs whose total amount changes in direct proportion to changes in business volume (e.g., sales volume). These costs are not directly included in product costs but are related to sales, management, and other operational activities, such as sales commissions, packaging fees, and transportation fees paid based on sales volume.

name: Variable Overhead Cost per Unit
definitions: Variable overhead cost per unit represents the portion of variable manufacturing overhead allocated to each unit of production, calculated by dividing total variable overhead by the number of units produced.

name: Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance
definitions: Variable overhead efficiency variance refers to the variance in variable overhead costs caused by the difference between actual hours worked and standard hours allowed, reflecting the level of production efficiency.

name: Variable Overhead Spending Variance
definitions: Variable overhead spending variance refers to the difference between the actual variable overhead incurred and the variable overhead that should have been incurred based on actual hours worked and the standard allocation rate, reflecting the efficiency of cost control.

name: Variable Overhead Standard Allocation Rate
definitions: The Variable Overhead Standard Allocation Rate refers to a predetermined benchmark ratio used under standard costing to allocate variable manufacturing overhead to a unit of activity (such as machine hours or labor hours). It is typically calculated based on the total budgeted variable overhead and the budgeted activity level, serving as a crucial tool for cost control and variance analysis.

name: Variable Ratio Write Breakeven Points
definitions: The upper and lower price levels at which a variable ratio write option strategy produces neither profit nor loss, calculated by adjusting the strike prices by the maximum profit points.

name: Variable Selling and Administrative Expenses
definitions: Variable selling and administrative expenses refer to those expenditures for selling and administrative activities whose total amount changes in direct proportion to changes in the company's sales volume. For example, sales commissions, shipping fees, and packaging costs increase as sales volume rises and decrease as sales volume falls.

name: Variable Storage Cost per Unit
definitions: Variable storage cost per unit refers to the portion of cost incurred by an enterprise for storing one unit of goods (e.g., one piece, one ton) that changes with variations in storage quantity or duration. Examples include warehouse occupancy fees, insurance premiums for inventory, potential spoilage or deterioration of goods in storage, and interest costs arising from capital tied up in inventory. This cost component fluctuates based on the volume and duration of storage, distinguishing it from fixed costs such as warehouse rent and management salaries.

name: Variable Transportation Cost
definitions: Variable transportation cost refers to the portion of transportation expenses that varies proportionally with the volume of goods transported. In accounting, it is typically not an original account but is derived from total transportation costs through cost decomposition methods (such as the high-low method), or calculated based on unit variable cost and transportation volume. It is a composite indicator.

name: Variable Values
definitions: In statistics and data analysis, 'variable values' refer to the specific numerical values corresponding to each individual or observation unit within a particular sample or population for a given variable. For example, when studying the return on assets of a group of companies, the specific ROA figure for each company represents one value of that variable.

name: Variable-Rate Certificate of Deposit
definitions: A Variable-Rate Certificate of Deposit is a time deposit whose interest rate is periodically adjusted by reference to a specified benchmark rate (such as the federal funds rate) plus or minus a fixed adjustment factor, allowing investors to benefit from rising market rates while maintaining principal protection.

name: Variable-Rate Certificate of Deposit Interest
definitions: Variable-Rate Certificate of Deposit Interest is the total interest earned on a deposit in a variable-rate CD where the annual percentage rate changes during the term, calculated by applying each rate to the corresponding time segment and compounding monthly.

name: Variance
definitions: Variance is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion or volatility of a dataset (such as asset returns). It is calculated as the average of the squared differences between each data point and the overall mean. A higher variance indicates greater data fluctuation and higher risk.
Variance is the difference between the budgeted amount and the actual amount incurred, used in financial analysis to identify discrepancies and guide cost control measures.

Variance is a statistical measure that quantifies the degree to which individual data points deviate from the mean of the dataset, calculated as the average of the squared differences from the mean; in finance it is widely used to assess risk and volatility.

Variance is a statistical measure that quantifies the degree of spread or dispersion of a set of data points around their mean value, calculated as the average of the squared differences from the mean.

Variance measures the dispersion of a set of observations around their mean. In finance and accounting analytics, variance is used to quantify volatility of returns and variability of financial metrics; for samples, Bessel's correction (n - 1) is applied to provide an unbiased estimator.

name: Variance Contribution Rate
definitions: Variance Contribution Rate is an indicator in statistics and data analysis, primarily used in Principal Component Analysis or Factor Analysis. It measures the proportion of the total variance in the original data that can be explained by a specific principal component or common factor. A higher value indicates that the principal component or factor contains more original information and has stronger comprehensive capability.

name: Variance Inflation Factor
definitions: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) quantifies the degree to which the variance of an estimated regression coefficient is increased due to multicollinearity among independent variables in a regression model.

Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) quantifies how much the variance of an estimated regression coefficient is inflated due to multicollinearity among the independent variables. It is defined as the reciprocal of tolerance and is commonly used in econometrics and financial modeling to diagnose multicollinearity; higher VIF values indicate stronger multicollinearity.

name: Variance Swap Payout
definitions: Variance Swap Payout is the monetary amount exchanged at settlement of a variance swap, calculated as the notional amount multiplied by the difference between the realized variance of the underlying asset and the pre-agreed strike variance.

name: Variance of Market Portfolio Returns
definitions: The variance of market portfolio returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility or risk of the overall return of the market portfolio. It is calculated using the return data of all constituent assets in the market portfolio, their respective weights, and the pairwise covariances between assets. It serves as a key input parameter for calculating systematic risk (Beta coefficient).

name: Variance of Market Returns
definitions: Variance of market returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility or dispersion of returns for the entire market, typically represented by a market index. It measures market risk by calculating the weighted average of the squared deviations of possible market returns from their expected value (mean return).

name: Variance of Random Variable X
definitions: The variance of random variable X is a measure of the dispersion between its values and its mathematical expectation (mean). It describes the spread or volatility of the data distribution. A larger variance indicates that data points are more dispersed, while a smaller variance indicates that data points are more concentrated around the mean.

name: Variance of Random Variable Y
definitions: The variance of random variable Y is a measure of the dispersion or volatility between the values of Y and its mathematical expectation (mean). A larger variance indicates that the values of Y are more dispersed and volatile; a smaller variance indicates that the values of Y are more concentrated around the expected value and less volatile.

name: Variance of Security B Returns
definitions: The variance of Security B returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of Security B's periodic returns relative to their average return, reflecting the volatility or risk level of the security's returns. It is calculated from periodic return data and serves as the basis for computing the standard deviation of Security B returns.

name: Variation Margin
definitions: Variation margin is the additional collateral required to bring a margin account up to the initial margin level after adverse price movements, ensuring the clearing house or broker is protected against potential losses.

name: Various Costs
definitions: Various Costs is a collective term referring to the total sum of all expenditures incurred by an enterprise during a specific period for producing goods or providing services, as well as for sales, management, and other activities. It can typically be broken down into specific cost items such as direct materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead, selling expenses, and administrative expenses. It serves as the basis for calculating weighted average cost and for cost analysis and decision-making.

name: Various Deductions
definitions: Various Deductions refer to the total sum of costs, expenses, taxes, losses, and other expenditures that are permitted to be subtracted from total revenue according to tax laws when calculating taxable income. In both Individual Income Tax and Corporate Income Tax, it is a collective concept composed of multiple specific deduction items, and its amount needs to be derived by aggregating other specific deduction items.

name: Various Expenses
definitions: Various expenses refer to the consumption of various economic resources incurred by an enterprise in its daily operations to generate revenue, excluding cost of sales, such as selling, administrative, and research and development expenses, which directly reduce the current period's profit.

name: Various Other Expense Items
definitions: Various other expense items refer to the aggregate of miscellaneous, secondary, or difficult-to-classify expense outlays in an enterprise's total costs and expenses, excluding major cost items (such as direct materials, direct labor, depreciation, amortization, interest expense, etc.). These items are typically consolidated as 'Total Other Expenses' in business operating costs, income statements, or specific expense calculations (e.g., super-deduction).

name: Vasicek Interest Rate Model
definitions: The Vasicek Interest Rate Model is a stochastic differential equation that describes the evolution of interest rates over time, incorporating mean reversion to a long-term equilibrium level and volatility-driven random shocks.

name: Vega
definitions: Vega is a sensitivity metric calculated through mathematical models (such as the Black-Scholes option pricing model), measuring the sensitivity of an option's price to changes in volatility. It is not a raw data item from financial statements.
Vega measures the sensitivity of an option's price to changes in the volatility of the underlying asset, representing the change in option price for a 1% change in implied volatility.

Vega measures the sensitivity of an option's premium to changes in implied volatility, indicating the change in the option price for a 1 percentage point change in implied volatility, ceteris paribus.

name: Vega-Based Option Price Change
definitions: Vega-based option price change quantifies the expected change in an option's price resulting from a specified change in implied volatility. It is calculated as the product of the option's vega (the sensitivity of the option price to volatility) and the change in implied volatility, assuming other factors remain constant.

name: Vehicle and Vessel Tax
definitions: Vehicle and Vessel Tax is a property tax levied by the government on the owners or managers of vehicles and vessels that are legally required to be registered within China, primarily used to compensate for public expenditures in transportation infrastructure construction, maintenance, and improvement.

name: Vehicle and Vessel Usage Tax
definitions: Vehicle and Vessel Usage Tax is a property tax levied by the state on entities and individuals who own and use vehicles and vessels within China. The tax paid by enterprises is typically recorded under the 'Business Taxes and Surcharges' account.

name: Velocity of Money
definitions: Velocity of money measures the rate at which money is exchanged in an economy, calculated by dividing gross domestic product (GDP) by the money supply, indicating how many times a unit of currency circulates within a given time period.

name: Vertical Analysis
definitions: Vertical analysis expresses each financial statement line item as a percentage of a base figure, enabling comparison of relative proportions within a single period.

Vertical analysis is a financial statement analysis technique that expresses each line item as a percentage of a base amount (typically total sales or total assets) to evaluate the relative proportion of each component within the statement.

Vertical analysis is a method of financial statement analysis that expresses each line item as a percentage of a base figure within the same statement, typically total assets for the balance sheet or total revenue for the income statement, to assess relative proportions and structural composition.

name: Vested
definitions: In legal and financial contexts, 'vested' refers to an individual's immediate and secured right to an asset or benefit (such as employer contributions in a retirement plan), which cannot be forfeited by any third party, even if actual possession or receipt is deferred to the future.

name: Vested Benefit Percentage
definitions: Vested benefit percentage represents the proportion of employer-provided benefits (such as pension or stock options) that an employee has earned the irrevocable right to receive, determined by the years of service and the company’s vesting schedule.

name: Vested Shares per Year
definitions: Vested shares per year represent the number of equity awards that become exercisable or owned by the employee in each year under a linear vesting schedule, calculated as the product of total granted shares and the annual vesting rate.

name: Vesting
definitions: In legal and financial contexts, vesting refers to the point in time when an individual gains an irrevocable right to a specific asset or benefit, such as employer contributions in a retirement plan or stock options. Once vested, this right cannot be forfeited by any third party, even if actual possession or distribution occurs in the future.

name: Vesting Period
definitions: The vesting period refers to a predetermined, fixed duration in agreements such as insurance or share-based payments, starting from the grant date and lasting until the beneficiary (e.g., an employee or policyholder) becomes eligible to exercise the right (e.g., to exercise options or receive insurance benefits). During this period, the beneficiary must continue to provide services or meet other conditions for the right to ultimately vest.

name: Viager Occupied Value
definitions: Viager occupied value is the present value of a property in a viager (life annuity) transaction, adjusted downward based on the seller’s age to reflect the buyer’s obligation to pay a life annuity and the uncertainty of occupancy duration.

name: Viager Total Value Paid
definitions: Viager Total Value Paid represents the aggregate amount a buyer commits to pay under a viager real-estate contract, comprising the initial down payment plus all scheduled cash installments expected over the seller’s statistical remaining lifetime.

name: Volatility
definitions: Volatility is a statistical measure of the magnitude of price fluctuations and risk of an asset (such as stocks, bonds), typically expressed as the standard deviation of price returns. It reflects the intensity of price movements; higher volatility indicates greater price instability and higher risk.

name: Volatility Change
definitions: Volatility change refers to the absolute change or percentage change in volatility metrics across different periods, reflecting variations in the volatility of financial data or asset prices. It is a composite indicator calculated based on volatility, not a leaf node, and is commonly used in financial analyses such as option value changes.

name: Volatility Ratio
definitions: Volatility Ratio is a technical analysis measure that compares the current day's true range to the average true range (ATR), indicating how current price volatility relates to historical volatility and helping identify potential breakouts or patterns.

Volatility ratio is a technical indicator that measures the current day's true range relative to the exponential moving average (EMA) of past true ranges, indicating how volatile the current price movement is compared to recent historical volatility.

The volatility ratio measures the magnitude of the current day's true range relative to the prevailing Average True Range (ATR). It is commonly used in technical analysis to identify wide-ranging days when the ratio exceeds a preset threshold (e.g., 2.0).

name: Volatility Smile
definitions: Volatility smile is the U-shaped pattern formed by plotting implied volatilities of options with the same expiration and underlying asset against their strike prices, indicating higher implied volatility for deep in-the-money and out-of-the-money options relative to at-the-money options.

name: Volatility Swap Payoff
definitions: Volatility swap payoff is the monetary amount received or paid at settlement of a volatility swap contract, calculated as the notional value multiplied by the difference between realized volatility and the pre-agreed volatility strike.

name: Volume Discount
definitions: Volume discount is a pricing strategy where the unit price decreases as the purchase quantity increases, typically structured in tiers to incentivize larger orders.

name: Volume Index
definitions: A volume index is a relative number that measures the change in the quantity or physical volume of a group of goods or services between two different periods (e.g., the reporting period and the base period) after eliminating the effects of price changes. It reflects changes in the actual output of economic activities and is commonly used in constant price accounting, such as calculating the gross fixed capital formation at constant prices.

name: Volume Price Trend Indicator
definitions: Volume Price Trend (VPT) is a cumulative technical indicator that combines price movement and volume to assess the strength of price trends and confirm price direction.

name: Volume Variance
definitions: Volume variance is a component of fixed manufacturing overhead cost variance, reflecting the impact of the difference between actual output and budgeted output on the allocation of fixed manufacturing overhead. It is calculated by subtracting the standard cost of fixed manufacturing overhead from the budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead, and is classified as a composite indicator.

name: Volume Weighted Average Price
definitions: Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP) is a technical indicator that measures the average price a security has traded at throughout the day, weighted by volume. It reflects both price and volume activity, providing a benchmark for traders to assess price trends and execution quality within a single trading session.

name: Volume-Weighted Average Price
definitions: Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) is a trading benchmark that represents the average price a security has traded at throughout the day, weighted by the volume of shares traded at each price level.

name: Voluntary Reserve
definitions: Voluntary reserve refers to the amount of cash or assets that an insurance company chooses to hold beyond the minimum regulatory reserve requirements, typically expressed as a percentage of total revenue, to enhance financial stability and risk management.

name: Vomma
definitions: Vomma is the second-order partial derivative of an option's value with respect to the volatility of the underlying asset, measuring the rate of change of vega as volatility changes. It captures the convexity of vega and is crucial for understanding how an option's sensitivity to volatility itself shifts when implied volatility moves.

name: Vortex Indicator
definitions: The Vortex Indicator (VI) is a technical analysis tool used to identify trend reversals by comparing the current period’s high and low to the previous period’s high and low, producing two oscillating lines: VI+ and VI-.

name: Wage Allocation Rate
definitions: The wage (expense) allocation rate is a proportional coefficient used to allocate labor costs between finished goods and work-in-process at month-end, calculated based on standard labor hours.

name: Wage Cost Allocated to a Specific Product
definitions: Wage cost allocated to a specific product is the result of multiplying the actual labor hours used for that product by the wage allocation rate for production workers.

name: Wage Expense
definitions: Wage expense represents the total compensation incurred by an entity for hourly labor within a reporting period. It typically includes regular pay for standard hours and additional overtime pay for hours worked beyond the standard workweek, measured on a gross basis before payroll taxes, deductions, and benefits.

Wage expense is the amount of compensation for employees' hourly wages recognized as an operating expense within a reporting period. It appears on the income statement and may be recorded on a cash or accrual basis. In a monthly context, wage expense can be computed by aggregating the weekly wage amounts recorded for each week of the month.

name: Wage Income
definitions: Wage income refers to the basic monetary compensation received by an individual for providing labor services through employment or engagement with a specific entity or organization. It typically includes wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increments, labor dividends, allowances, subsidies, and other earnings related to employment or engagement, constituting a significant component of an individual's disposable income.

name: Wage Indexing Factor
definitions: The wage indexing factor is the ratio used by the Social Security Administration to adjust an individual's past earnings to the wage level of the year they turn age 60. It is calculated as the National Average Wage Index (NAWI) in the age-60 year divided by the NAWI in the specific prior year being indexed, and is applied when computing Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME).

name: Wage and Salary Income Amount
definitions: Wage and salary income amount refers to the total sum of all monetary income received by an individual due to employment or appointment, including wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increases, labor dividends, allowances, subsidies, and other income related to employment or appointment. It serves as the original starting point data for calculating the taxable income for individual income tax.

name: Wages
definitions: Wages refer to the labor compensation directly paid by an employer to an employee based on the employment contract, considering factors such as attendance records and performance results. It serves as the fundamental raw data for payroll accounting and is typically recorded as an expense account in accounting treatment.

name: Wages Allocable to Finished Goods
definitions: Wages allocable to finished goods refers to the portion of total labor costs allocated to completed products based on the wage allocation rate (typically based on standard labor hours), used for accurate product costing in cost accounting.

name: Wages Allocable to Work-in-Process at Month-End
definitions: Wages allocable to work-in-process at month-end refer to the portion of total labor costs allocated to unfinished products based on the wage allocation rate.

name: Wages Payable
definitions: Wages payable refers to the total amount of wages, including various salaries, bonuses, and allowances, that an enterprise owes to its employees based on wage rates, attendance, performance, and other fundamental data but has not yet actually paid. It constitutes a current liability of the enterprise.

name: Wages and Benefits Charged Against Profits
definitions: Refers to expense items in enterprise accounting where a portion of profits is directly used to pay employees or provide employee benefits. It is typically not directly included in operating costs or period expenses, but rather treated as a profit distribution or expense under specific management decisions, directly affecting the enterprise's final distributable profits or retained earnings.

name: Wages and Salaries Income
definitions: Wages and salaries income refers to all forms of labor remuneration received by an individual due to holding an office or being employed by a specific unit or organization. This typically includes basic wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increases, labor dividends, various allowances, subsidies, and all other income related to the office held or employment. It is one of the taxable items stipulated under China's Individual Income Tax Law, and the tax payable is usually calculated based on monthly income.

name: Wages and Welfare Expenses
definitions: Wages and welfare expenses refer to various welfare expenditures provided by an enterprise to its employees beyond direct compensation such as wages, bonuses, and allowances. They are typically accrued at a certain percentage (e.g., 14%) of the total payroll and are used to cover employee medical expenses, living hardship subsidies, expenditures for collective welfare facilities (such as canteens and bathrooms) and related personnel salaries, aiming to improve employees' living and working conditions.

name: Warrant Premium
definitions: Warrant premium is the amount by which a warrant's market price exceeds its intrinsic value (the in-the-money component). It reflects time value, implied volatility, and other market factors affecting the warrant's pricing.

Warrant premium (percentage) measures the relative extra cost of acquiring a share through a warrant versus purchasing the share directly in the market. It is computed as the difference between the warrant price plus the exercise price and the current share price, divided by the current share price, expressed as a percentage. A higher premium indicates a less cost-effective warrant compared to buying the underlying shares outright.

name: Wastage
definitions: Wastage refers to the quantity of raw materials, products, or goods that is reduced due to unavoidable scrap, defects, evaporation, breakage, or other causes during production, storage, or transportation. It is typically calculated as the original total quantity minus the final usable or remaining quantity.

name: Wastage Rate
definitions: Wastage rate is a key performance indicator that measures the extent of material loss during production, warehousing, or construction processes. It is typically expressed as a percentage and is used for cost control, budgeting, and material consumption quota management.

name: Waste Rate
definitions: Waste rate is a ratio that measures the actual consumption of materials or resources exceeding the planned or theoretical net usage in production or operational processes. It is a key indicator for cost control and efficiency analysis, commonly used in variance analysis under standard costing.

name: Waterfall Payment
definitions: Waterfall payment refers to the priority-based allocation of available cash to creditors, where interest obligations are satisfied before principal and higher-priority claims are paid before lower-priority claims. It is commonly used in structured finance to govern the order of cash distribution among tranches or creditors.

name: Wealth Added Index
definitions: The Wealth Added Index measures shareholder value creation by comparing total equity returns (share price gains plus dividends) against the company's cost of equity. A positive WAI indicates value creation for shareholders, while a negative WAI indicates value destruction.

name: Wealth Tax
definitions: Wealth tax is a levy imposed on an individual's net worth (total assets minus liabilities). The wealth tax liability is calculated by applying a tax rate to net worth and may be adjusted by a residency factor to reflect jurisdictional rules on taxable assets. This measure is typically used in systems employing a flat rate on net wealth.

Wealth tax is a levy on an individual's net worth (total assets minus liabilities). In a progressive system, successive portions of net worth are taxed at increasing bracket rates, and the final liability may be adjusted by a residency factor to reflect jurisdictional residency rules.

name: Weather Futures Payout
definitions: Weather futures payout is the monetary amount owed under a weather derivative or futures contract, calculated by multiplying the deviation of the observed temperature from a preset benchmark by a contractual multiplier. It is commonly applied in heating degree day (HDD) or cooling degree day (CDD) structures to hedge temperature-related revenue and cost exposures.

name: Wei
definitions: Wei is the smallest denomination of Ether (ETH), equal to 10^(-18) ETH. It is used to express precise monetary amounts in Ethereum-based transactions, smart contracts, and on-chain accounting. The conversion expresses Wei as Ether multiplied by 10^18.

name: Wei (Gwei to Ether Conversion)
definitions: Wei is the smallest denomination of Ether (ETH) on the Ethereum blockchain. Gwei equals 10^9 Wei and is commonly used to quote gas prices. This entry specifies the conversion from Gwei to Ether using the fixed conversion factor where 1 Ether = 10^9 Gwei.

name: Wei to Ether Conversion
definitions: Wei to Ether Conversion refers to converting an amount denominated in Wei, the smallest denomination of Ether (ETH), into Ether by dividing by the conversion factor of 10^18. This unit conversion is used for valuation, pricing gas, and precise accounting of Ethereum transactions and balances.

name: Weight
definitions: Weight is a relative concept for a specific indicator, representing its relative importance in overall evaluation or calculation. In statistics and finance, weight is commonly used to calculate weighted averages, where its value depends not only on the values of individual units but also on their frequency of occurrence or assigned importance proportion.

Weight refers to the numerical value assigned to each data item or indicator in the calculation of a weighted average or comprehensive evaluation to reflect its relative importance. A larger value indicates a greater influence of that data item in the overall calculation.

name: Weight of Asset A
definitions: The weight of Asset A refers to a predetermined proportion or coefficient assigned to a specific Asset A when calculating portfolio risk (e.g., standard deviation) or regulatory capital requirements (e.g., credit risk-weighted assets). It reflects the relative importance of that asset within the overall portfolio or risk exposure, typically set directly based on regulatory provisions, internal policies, or investment strategies, rather than derived from a formula.

name: Weight of Asset in Market Portfolio
definitions: The weight of an asset in the market portfolio refers to the proportion or share of a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) in the total value of the entire market portfolio (typically a theoretical portfolio comprising all tradable risky assets). It measures the importance of that asset relative to the entire market and serves as the basis for calculating metrics such as the expected return of the market portfolio.

name: Weight of Each Asset in the Market Portfolio
definitions: The weight of each asset in the market portfolio refers to the proportion of an individual asset's market value (e.g., stocks, bonds) to the total market value of all assets within the market portfolio, which represents the entire market. This proportion directly reflects the relative size and importance of that asset in the overall market and serves as a fundamental input parameter for financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

name: Weight of Individual Asset in Portfolio
definitions: The weight of an individual asset in a portfolio refers to the proportion of the market value of a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) to the total value of the entire investment portfolio composed of multiple assets. It reflects the relative importance and capital allocation of that asset within the portfolio.

name: Weight of Individual Assets in a Portfolio
definitions: The weight of individual assets in a portfolio refers to the proportion or percentage of the market value of each asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) relative to the total value of the entire portfolio. It measures the degree to which that asset influences the overall performance and risk of the portfolio, serving as key foundational data for asset allocation and risk management.

name: Weight of Security j
definitions: The weight of security j refers to the proportion of the total portfolio value allocated to security j (such as a specific stock or bond) when constructing an investment portfolio. It reflects the relative importance and investment share of that security within the portfolio.

name: Weight of the k-th Security
definitions: The weight of the k-th security refers to the proportion of its value within an investment portfolio, typically determined by its market value relative to the total market value of the portfolio, or derived through mathematical models such as mean-variance optimization. It serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating portfolio risk and return.

name: Weighted Alpha
definitions: Weighted Alpha is a time-weighted measure of a security's benchmark-relative performance (alpha) over a defined period, typically one year. It emphasizes recent returns by assigning higher weights to more recent observations and summarizes the weighted excess returns per day over the period.

name: Weighted Average
definitions: Weighted average is an average calculated by summing the products of each value multiplied by its corresponding weight, then dividing by the total weight. Its magnitude depends not only on the values themselves but also on their respective weights. In finance, it serves as a fundamental mathematical tool for calculating metrics such as Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) and inventory costs.

Weighted average is a statistical and financial calculation method that computes the mean value by assigning a weight to each data item based on its importance. In finance, it is commonly used to calculate inventory costs, cost of capital, etc., allowing more significant or larger-quantity data to exert greater influence on the average.

Weighted average is an averaging method where each observation is multiplied by a specified weight reflecting its relative importance. In finance and accounting, it is used to compute measures such as weighted average cost, weighted average shares outstanding, and portfolio returns by proportionally emphasizing more significant components.

Weighted average is a measure of central tendency where each value is multiplied by a specified weight and then summed, reflecting the relative importance or proportion of each component. In finance and accounting, it is widely used for portfolio expected returns, weighted average cost of capital (WACC), index construction, and inventory valuation under the weighted-average method. For proportional weighting, weights typically sum to 1.

name: Weighted Average Contribution Margin Ratio
definitions: The weighted average contribution margin ratio is a composite ratio calculated by weighting the contribution margin ratios of individual products by their respective sales proportions in a multi-product enterprise. It reflects the contribution level of the product mix to overall profitability and is commonly used in cost-volume-profit analysis and break-even point calculations.

name: Weighted Average Correlation
definitions: Weighted average correlation is the portfolio-level correlation measure computed as the weighted mean of each asset's average correlation with the rest of the portfolio, using the assets' portfolio weights as weights. It is used to assess diversification and overall co-movement risk.

name: Weighted Average Cost
definitions: Weighted average cost refers to the average cost calculated based on the weight of each cost item in the total cost.

name: Weighted Average Cost of Capital
definitions: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is the weighted average cost of all capital sources (including equity and debt) of a company, reflecting the overall cost paid by the company for raising and using capital. It is commonly used as the discount rate in investment decisions and corporate valuation.

Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is the average rate of return a company is expected to pay to its security holders to finance its assets, calculated as the weighted average of the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt based on their respective proportions in the capital structure.

Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is the average rate of return a company is expected to pay to all its security holders to finance its assets, weighted by the proportion of each capital component in the firm's capital structure.

Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is the average rate of return a company must pay to its capital providers (debt and equity), weighted by their respective market values. It incorporates the tax shield effect on debt and is used to assess investment decisions, valuation, and capital structure efficiency.

Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is the blended required rate of return a company must earn on its invested capital, weighted by the proportion of debt and equity in its capital structure. It reflects the after-tax cost of debt and the cost of equity, and is widely used for valuation, capital budgeting, and assessing optimal capital structure.

name: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)
definitions: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) refers to the composite cost of capital calculated by weighting the cost of each capital source (such as common stock, preferred stock, bonds, and long-term debt) by its proportion in the total capital structure. It serves as a crucial discount rate for evaluating investment projects and calculating Economic Value Added (EVA).

Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) is the firm's average after-tax required return on invested capital, computed as the market-value-weighted cost of equity and cost of debt. It is commonly used as a discount rate for valuation and capital budgeting decisions.

name: Weighted Average Cost of Equity
definitions: Weighted Average Cost of Equity represents the overall required rate of return on a company's equity, calculated as the sum of each equity component's cost multiplied by its proportion of total equity. It consolidates the costs of different equity sources (e.g., common equity, preferred equity, retained earnings) according to their weights in the equity structure and is expressed as a decimal rate.

name: Weighted Average Cost per Share
definitions: Weighted average cost per share represents the average purchase cost allocated to each share when multiple acquisitions occur at different prices. It is calculated by dividing the total cost of all purchase batches by the total number of shares acquired, and is commonly used to determine the cost basis for capital gains taxation and to assess investment performance.

name: Weighted Average Coupon
definitions: Weighted average coupon (WAC) is the principal-weighted average of the coupon rates in a mortgage pool or fixed-income portfolio. It is calculated by weighting each loan's coupon rate by its outstanding principal balance, indicating the pool's average nominal interest rate.

name: Weighted Average Credit Rating
definitions: Weighted Average Credit Rating (WACR) measures a portfolio’s average credit quality by assigning numeric values to credit ratings and computing the weighted average using each holding’s portfolio weight. It facilitates comparison of overall credit risk across bond funds and fixed-income portfolios.

name: Weighted Average Diluted Common Shares Outstanding
definitions: Weighted Average Diluted Common Shares Outstanding is a composite metric used in calculating diluted earnings per share. It is derived by adding the weighted average number of common shares outstanding used in calculating basic earnings per share to the weighted average number of additional common shares that would be issued assuming the conversion of all dilutive potential common shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, stock options, etc.). This metric reflects the comprehensive impact of potentially dilutive securities on the number of common shares.

name: Weighted Average Life
definitions: Weighted Average Life (WAL) measures the average time to receive principal repayments on an amortizing security, weighting each period by the proportion of principal returned. It reflects principal timing and is commonly used for bonds, loans, and mortgage-backed securities.

name: Weighted Average Loan Age
definitions: Weighted Average Loan Age (WALA) measures the average age of loans in a mortgage-backed securities pool, weighted by each loan’s initial nominal principal, typically expressed in months since origination. It indicates the pool’s seasoning and is used in prepayment and cash flow analysis.

name: Weighted Average Market Capitalization
definitions: Weighted Average Market Capitalization describes the market-cap-weighted structure of an index, where each constituent's weight is proportional to its market capitalization relative to the index's total market capitalization. The constituent weights, often expressed as percentages, indicate each security's contribution to the index based on size.

name: Weighted Average Maturity
definitions: Weighted Average Maturity (WAM) refers to the weighted average of the time to maturity for each security in a mortgage-backed security (MBS) portfolio, with the weight being the outstanding principal balance of each security. It is used to estimate the average remaining term of the underlying mortgages.

Weighted Average Maturity (WAM) measures the average time to maturity of a portfolio's holdings, weighted by each holding's proportion of the portfolio value. It indicates the portfolio's maturity profile and exposure to interest rate risk across fixed-income securities.

name: Weighted Average Number of Additional Ordinary Shares from Assumed Conversion
definitions: This concept is an intermediate adjustment item in calculating diluted earnings per share. It refers to the weighted average number of additional ordinary shares that would be outstanding if all dilutive potential ordinary shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, share options, etc.) were converted into ordinary shares at the beginning of the period or the date of issuance, weighted for the period they were outstanding during the reporting period. Its value is derived through assumption and weighted calculation, rather than being raw data directly obtained from accounting records.

name: Weighted Average Number of Additional Ordinary Shares from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Ordinary Shares
definitions: The weighted average number of additional ordinary shares from conversion of dilutive potential ordinary shares is a composite metric used in calculating diluted earnings per share. It represents the weighted average (by time) of the increased number of shares assuming all dilutive potential ordinary shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, stock options, etc.) are converted into ordinary shares. This metric is derived based on the quantity of potential ordinary shares, conversion ratios, issuance dates, etc., following accounting standards (e.g., assuming conversion at the beginning of the period for those issued in prior periods, and at the issuance date for those issued during the current period). It is used to adjust the denominator of basic earnings per share to reflect the potential dilution effect.

name: Weighted Average Number of Additional Ordinary Shares from Dilutive Potential Ordinary Shares Conversion
definitions: The weighted average number of additional ordinary shares from dilutive potential ordinary shares conversion refers to the weighted average, calculated for the purpose of determining diluted earnings per share, of the increased number of shares assuming the conversion of dilutive potential ordinary shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, and share options) into ordinary shares. This average is computed by applying time-weighting factors from the assumed conversion date to the end of the reporting period for each dilutive instrument. This metric is a composite adjustment to the denominator of diluted earnings per share and is not directly derived from raw financial statement data.

name: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding
definitions: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding is a composite metric calculated using the weighted average method to determine the average number of common shares during the reporting period. It incorporates the time-weighting of factors such as share issuance and repurchase, serving as the key denominator for calculating basic earnings per share.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the average number of common shares calculated with time weighting during the reporting period, used for financial metrics such as earnings per share. It is derived by time-weighting the beginning shares, newly issued shares, and repurchased shares, and is a non-leaf node concept.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the number of shares calculated by weighting the common shares outstanding during the reporting period according to the proportion of time they were outstanding relative to the reporting period. This calculation is used in metrics such as earnings per share to reflect the continuous impact on shareholders' equity due to changes in the number of common shares from events like issuances and repurchases during the reporting period.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the average number of shares calculated by adjusting the beginning number of shares with time weights for issuance or repurchase of common shares during the reporting period, in order to reflect the impact of changes in the number of common shares on the capital base when calculating metrics such as earnings per share.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the average number of common shares outstanding during an accounting period, adjusted for the time-weighting of share issuances or repurchases, and serves as the basis for calculating key financial metrics such as earnings per share.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the average number of common shares calculated on a time-weighted basis during the reporting period, taking into account the timing of share issuances or repurchases. This metric serves as the foundation for calculating key financial ratios such as earnings per share and book value per share, and is not a point-in-time figure directly obtained from the balance sheet.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to an average number of shares calculated using time-weighting over a specific reporting period (such as a quarter or a year), taking into account potential changes in the number of common shares due to factors like new share issuances or share repurchases. It serves as a crucial denominator in calculating key per-share metrics such as earnings per share and sales per share.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the average number of common shares outstanding during a specific reporting period (such as a quarter or a year), calculated by considering the time-weighting factors of share issuances or repurchases within the period. It is used to more accurately reflect the capital base available for sharing the company's profits throughout the entire reporting period.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the number of shares calculated by weighting the common shares outstanding at different points in time during the reporting period according to the proportion of time they were outstanding relative to the total reporting period. This is done to reflect potential changes in the number of common shares due to issuances, repurchases, or other reasons when calculating metrics such as earnings per share.

The weighted average number of common shares outstanding refers to the number of shares calculated by weighting the shares outstanding at different points in time according to their proportion of the total reporting period, in order to more accurately reflect the actual number of common shares available during the entire period when calculating financial metrics such as earnings per share, considering that the number of common shares may change during the reporting period due to reasons such as new share issuances or share repurchases.

name: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding Expected at Period End
definitions: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding expected at period end refers to the average number of common shares calculated on a time-weighted basis, after considering potential changes in the number of common shares during the reporting period (such as new issuances, repurchases, etc.), used to forecast metrics like earnings per share for future periods (e.g., the next reporting period). It is a forward-looking composite indicator.

name: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Period End
definitions: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding at period end refers to the number of shares calculated by weighting the shares issued at different points in time according to their proportion of the reporting period in circulation. This calculation is performed to more accurately reflect the actual number of common shares available throughout the period when computing metrics such as earnings per share for a financial reporting period (e.g., quarter or year), considering that the number of common shares may change due to new share issuances or share repurchases during the period.

name: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for the Next Period
definitions: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding for the next period refers to an average share count calculated based on the time-weighting of common share issuances and repurchases during the next period (typically the next financial reporting period), used for metrics such as earnings per share for the next period. It reflects the average level of common equity actually available to shareholders throughout the entire upcoming reporting period.

name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding Before Changes
definitions: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding before changes refers to the number of ordinary shares issued at the beginning of the period, weighted by the time they were outstanding during the reporting period, calculated before considering changes such as new issuances or repurchases of ordinary shares during the current period. This figure is used to reflect the time-weighting effect of the number of ordinary shares when calculating earnings per share. It serves as one of the base data points for determining the number of ordinary shares corresponding to the net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders when calculating both basic and diluted earnings per share.

name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding During the Period
definitions: Refers to the average number of shares outstanding during the reporting period, weighted by the time they were outstanding. It is the key denominator for calculating basic earnings per share. The calculation is based on the number of shares at the beginning of the period, with subsequent issuances or repurchases of ordinary shares weighted by the portion of the reporting period they were outstanding.

The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the period is a key metric used in calculating financial indicators such as basic earnings per share. It is computed by weighting the number of shares at the beginning of the period, newly issued shares, and repurchased shares by the fraction of the reporting period they were outstanding, reflecting the average scale of ordinary shares in circulation during the reporting period.

name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding Expected
definitions: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding expected refers to the average number of shares calculated by weighting the ordinary shares outstanding during the reporting period based on the time they were outstanding. It serves as the basis for calculating key per-share metrics such as expected earnings per share and expected other comprehensive income per share.

name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding for Basic Earnings Per Share Calculation
definitions: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding for basic earnings per share calculation is a key metric used to compute basic earnings per share. It reflects the impact of changes in the number of ordinary shares during the reporting period on earnings per share using the weighted average method, considering the number of shares at the beginning of the period, newly issued shares, repurchased shares, and their respective time-weighting, typically calculated based on the number of days.

name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in Basic EPS Calculation
definitions: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding is the denominator used in calculating basic earnings per share. It is weighted based on the period the ordinary shares are outstanding during the reporting period, reflecting the impact of changes in the capital structure on earnings per share during the period.

name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in Diluted EPS Calculation
definitions: According to the Application Guidance of Accounting Standards for Business Enterprises No. 34 - Earnings Per Share, the 'Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding' is a fundamental metric for calculating both basic and diluted earnings per share. It reflects the average number of ordinary shares calculated during the reporting period, taking into account changes in the number of ordinary shares due to events such as new share issuances, share repurchases, stock dividends, stock splits, or reverse stock splits, and their respective time weights. This metric is a composite indicator calculated using the weighted average method, rather than raw data directly obtained from accounting records.

name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in the Prior Period
definitions: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding in the prior period is a key concept used to calculate financial metrics such as earnings per share for the previous reporting period. It is calculated based on the time-weighted number of shares at the beginning of the period, newly issued shares, and repurchased shares, reflecting the average number of shares after considering the timing of share changes.
